options.rationale: Antenatal oral antibiotics do not durably eradicate GBS colonisation and are not part of the Australian prophylaxis pathway. Intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis is what reduces vertical transmission and early-onset disease. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for women with a documented immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin AND either clindamycin resistance on GBS isolate or clindamycin susceptibility unknown. Severity of prior disease does not change the first-line agent. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.rationale: A prior baby with GBS sepsis is not itself an indication for caesarean. Elective caesarean on intact membranes before labour eliminates the immediate intrapartum transmission risk but does not obviate GBS prophylaxis in women with strong risk factors, and adds surgical morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined by RANZCOG as three or more consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. The evidence-based workup targets treatable or prognostically important conditions: antiphospholipid syndrome (repeat testing 12 weeks apart to satisfy classification criteria), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced chromosomal translocations, and uterine cavity anomalies (septum, submucosal fibroid, adhesions). Approximately half of couples end investigation with no identified cause; supportive care with early-pregnancy ultrasound in the next conception is offered and cumulative live-birth rates remain reasonable. Empirical progesterone (400 mg vaginally twice daily) started with a positive test may be offered per the RANZCOG algorithm to women with a history of recurrent miscarriage and early pregnancy bleeding.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage per RANZCOG: three or more consecutive first-trimester losses.
First-line workup: APLS (twice, 12 weeks apart), TFTs, parental karyotype, uterine cavity imaging.
Routine inherited thrombophilia and MTHFR screening are NOT recommended.
Empirical vaginal progesterone can be offered when bleeding occurs in the next pregnancy.
About 50% remain unexplained; supportive care and early scan the primary intervention.
explanation.pearls: Do NOT order MTHFR or routine thrombophilia in recurrent miscarriage - the evidence supports lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus anti-beta-2 glycoprotein-I repeated at 12 weeks, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and uterine cavity imaging.

options.rationale: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not routinely recommended in recurrent pregnancy loss workup and has an uncertain evidence base for changing management. Maternal-side treatable causes take priority. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is NOT recommended in recurrent miscarriage: results do not alter management, MTHFR is now specifically discouraged, and false positives lead to unnecessary anticoagulation exposure. Reserve for a personal or family VTE history. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

TORCH infections are not causes of recurrent first-trimester miscarriage. Screening produces prevalence findings without therapeutic implications and delays workup of the causes that do matter. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

The evidence for chronic endometritis as a cause of recurrent pregnancy loss and for empirical doxycycline is limited and this is not a RANZCOG first-line investigation. Consider only in the context of investigation-negative recurrent loss with tertiary specialist input. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

RANZCOG and ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines identify treatable causes: antiphospholipid syndrome (needs two positive tests 12 weeks apart), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced translocations and uterine cavity anomalies. This is the evidence-based first-line panel that changes management. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os, either from a velamentous cord insertion (type I) or between placental lobes in a bilobed or succenturiate placenta (type II). Antenatal diagnosis by second-trimester ultrasound with follow-up transvaginal colour Doppler transforms outcomes: undiagnosed vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50%, diagnosed cases with planned caesarean carry a survival rate approaching 100%. RANZCOG advises inpatient admission from 30-32 weeks (individualised for distance from hospital and clinical stability), a completed corticosteroid course, and planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks. Emergency caesarean with massive transfusion capability follows any antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes or spontaneous labour.
key_points: Vasa praevia carries perinatal mortality above 50% when undiagnosed; near 100% survival with planned birth.
Type I: velamentous cord insertion. Type II: vessels between lobes.
Admit from 30-32 weeks; complete antenatal corticosteroids by 34 weeks.
Planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks (SMFM 34-37, RANZCOG typically 34-36).
Emergency caesarean for any bleeding, rupture of membranes, or labour.
explanation.pearls: In a confirmed vasa praevia, plan the caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after an antenatal corticosteroid course and admit the mother from around 32 weeks - waiting until 39 weeks converts a survivable situation into a fetal exsanguination emergency.

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends inpatient admission for confirmed vasa praevia from around 30-32 weeks with a completed corticosteroid course, given the risk of catastrophic fetal haemorrhage at rupture of membranes. Planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks balances perinatal exsanguination risk against prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Vaginal birth in vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50% because rupture of the fetal vessel at membrane rupture leads to rapid fetal exsanguination. Planned caesarean before labour is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Cerclage does not treat vasa praevia and is not indicated. The condition is a fetal vessel problem, not a cervical competency problem. Vaginal birth remains contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Attempted vaginal birth places the fetus at unacceptable risk of exsanguination at any spontaneous or artificial membrane rupture. Induction of labour does not mitigate this risk and is contrary to RANZCOG guidance. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Delaying planned caesarean to 39 weeks in vasa praevia substantially increases the probability of spontaneous labour or rupture of membranes with catastrophic fetal haemorrhage. RANZCOG recommends birth by 35+6 weeks. Two courses of corticosteroids beyond 34 weeks are not routine. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy and the puerperium raise VTE risk fourfold antenatally and up to twentyfold postnatally, with the peak in the first six weeks post-delivery. RANZCOG stratifies risk by antenatal and postnatal factors: BMI at booking above 30, emergency caesarean, prolonged labour, immobility, peripartum haemorrhage requiring transfusion, pre-eclampsia, prior VTE and known thrombophilia. Women with multiple moderate risk factors after caesarean receive weight-adjusted enoxaparin for six weeks postpartum; LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin except in renal failure. Neuraxial block timing rules apply: first prophylactic LMWH dose is given at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and prophylactic dosing precedes any subsequent catheter removal by at least 12 hours.
key_points: Multiple moderate risk factors (emergency CS + BMI > 40 + weight > 90 kg) meet RANZCOG threshold for 6 week postpartum LMWH.
Weight-adjusted enoxaparin approximates 0.6 mg/kg daily; 91-130 kg dose is around 80 mg daily.
Aspirin is NOT an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent.
DOACs are not recommended while breastfeeding; LMWH and warfarin are compatible.
Timing after neuraxial block: at least 4 hours after catheter removal for LMWH.
explanation.pearls: For postpartum VTE prophylaxis at booking BMI over 40, use enoxaparin 0.6 mg/kg daily (about 80 mg for 118 kg) for six weeks - the risk peak is in the first six weeks post-delivery, and shorter courses miss the majority of pulmonary emboli.

options.rationale: Aspirin is not an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent under RANZCOG or RCOG guidance. Low molecular weight heparin at a weight-adjusted dose is standard for postpartum women meeting risk thresholds, once haemostasis is secured. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

Direct oral anticoagulants including rivaroxaban are not recommended in breastfeeding women because transfer into breast milk is either significant or inadequately characterised. LMWH is breastfeeding-compatible. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

The RANZCOG weight-adjustment schedule delivers approximately 0.6 mg/kg for extended prophylaxis; 40 mg is under-dosing for 118 kg. Ten days does not meet the guideline recommendation of six weeks postpartum LMWH for women with multiple moderate risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

Therapeutic dose LMWH is reserved for confirmed or high-clinical-suspicion VTE, mechanical valve prophylaxis, or specific antiphospholipid syndrome scenarios. It carries substantial bleeding risk and is not indicated for postpartum prophylaxis in the absence of documented VTE. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

Emergency in-labour caesarean plus BMI over 40 plus current weight over 90 kg constitutes multiple moderate-risk factors, meeting the RANZCOG threshold for six weeks postpartum LMWH. Weight-based dosing per RANZCOG is 0.6 mg/kg once daily rounded to available vial size for weights 91-130 kg, approximating enoxaparin 80 mg. Timing after neuraxial anaesthesia respects catheter removal rules. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is defined by abnormal placental adherence (accreta), invasion into myometrium (increta) or through it (percreta). Prior caesarean plus a current anterior placenta praevia is the leading risk profile; two prior caesareans raises accreta risk to around 40%. Antenatal ultrasound features include placental lacunae (Finberg grade), loss of the retroplacental clear space, myometrial thinning, bladder wall interruption and bridging vessels. MRI is not diagnostic in isolation but adds surgical planning value. Standard care is planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with obstetrics, gynaecological oncology or urology, anaesthesia, interventional radiology, blood bank and neonatal intensive care coordinated. Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ is the usual surgical strategy; conservative management with the placenta left in situ and expectant care is offered in select cases.
key_points: Two prior caesareans plus anterior praevia carries around 40% accreta risk.
Key ultrasound features: lacunae (grade 3), loss of clear space, myometrial thinning, bridging vessels.
MRI supports surgical planning, not diagnosis in isolation.
Planned caesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in an accreta centre.
Standard strategy is caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with two prior caesareans and an anterior placenta praevia showing lacunae, loss of the clear space, and bridging vessels at 28 weeks, the correct sequence is MRI plus corticosteroids plus transfer to a placenta accreta centre for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0-35+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.rationale: Delaying elective caesarean to 39 weeks in suspected placenta accreta spectrum substantially increases the probability of an emergency haemorrhage. RANZCOG and international guidance both recommend planned birth between 34 and 36 weeks after a completed corticosteroid course. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.rationale: Placenta praevia with two prior caesareans plus lacunae, loss of clear space, bridging vessels and myometrial thinning meets the ultrasound criteria for likely placenta accreta spectrum. MRI adds surgical planning information. Planned birth at 34+0-35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with multidisciplinary team, blood bank preparation and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia. Prophylactic pre-birth embolisation is not standard practice for antenatally suspected accreta spectrum in Australia; balloon catheters may have a role intraoperatively at select centres, not as an outpatient antenatal intervention. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia and additionally with suspected accreta. Cervical length screening does not alter management here and daily CTG antenatally in an otherwise stable pregnancy adds no value. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.rationale: Emergency delivery at 28 weeks in a stable woman inflicts substantial prematurity morbidity unnecessarily. Planned delivery at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in a suitably resourced centre is the standard, with emergency intervention reserved for antepartum haemorrhage or labour. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined by RANZCOG as failure of placental delivery beyond 30 minutes of active third-stage management. In an actively bleeding woman it converts a common third-stage problem into an obstetric emergency, because the partially-separated placenta prevents effective uterine contraction and creates open sinuses at the placental bed. Definitive treatment is manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia. The standard concurrent package is massive transfusion protocol activation for major PPH, tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial shows a mortality benefit), and single-dose prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole). Ongoing atony after removal escalates through uterotonic ladder, uterine balloon tamponade, uterine compression sutures, uterine artery embolisation, and finally hysterectomy.
key_points: Retained placenta: no delivery of placenta within 30 minutes of active third-stage management.
In a bleeding woman, retained placenta prevents uterine contraction; manual removal is the definitive treatment.
Give IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of birth for any PPH (WOMAN trial mortality benefit).
Uterine balloon tamponade requires an empty uterus, not one containing a retained placenta.
Post-removal atony ladder: oxytocin infusion -> ergometrine -> carboprost -> tamponade -> compression sutures -> embolisation -> hysterectomy.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth reduces death from bleeding by around a third in the WOMAN trial; the retained placenta must be removed in theatre first, because uterine balloon tamponade cannot form around a placenta.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.rationale: A Bakri balloon has no role while the placenta remains in the uterus; the tamponade cannot form around a foreign body of that size. Continued pharmacological uterotonics without addressing the retained placenta will not stop the bleeding and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.rationale: The woman is haemodynamically unstable with a retained placenta and atonic haemorrhage. Manual removal under anaesthesia is the definitive treatment; delay adds ongoing exsanguination. Simultaneous massive transfusion activation, IV tranexamic acid within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial) and prophylactic antibiotics (single-dose cefazolin plus metronidazole) form the standard package. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.rationale: Umbilical vein oxytocin has weak evidence of benefit for retained placenta and no role in an unstable haemorrhaging woman. The definitive treatment remains theatre transfer for manual removal. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.rationale: Bedside manual removal without adequate anaesthesia is painful, unsafe, and produces incomplete removal; it also delays the surgical response if bleeding does not settle. RANZCOG mandates regional or general anaesthesia in an appropriately equipped theatre. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.rationale: Interventional radiology is not the first-line response to retained placenta with ongoing haemorrhage. The retained placenta must be removed; embolisation is considered after removal if atony or focal bleeding persists. Vasopressor use without volume resuscitation and definitive haemostasis worsens end-organ perfusion. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

explanation.summary: Primary PPH management follows the four Ts (tone, trauma, tissue, thrombin) and a stepwise uterotonic ladder: oxytocin (intravenous bolus plus infusion) as first-line, ergometrine second-line if there is no hypertension or cardiac disease, and carboprost third-line.
key_points: Tone first (uterine atony is the commonest cause) - massage plus escalating uterotonics.
Oxytocin first-line, ergometrine second unless hypertension/cardiac disease, carboprost third.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of PPH onset (WOMAN trial).
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly is second-line PPH pharmacology only if the mother is normotensive and has no cardiac disease.

options.rationale: Escalation to a second-line uterotonic acting on a different receptor is more effective than repeating oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)
Carboprost is third-line in Australian sequencing (after oxytocin and ergometrine) and can cause significant bronchospasm. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Misoprostol has a role when parenteral uterotonics are unavailable or ergot is contraindicated; it acts slowly, so it is not the immediate next step when intravenous oxytocin and ergometrine can be given. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Australian PPH sequencing: intravenous oxytocin bolus plus infusion escalates the initial uterotonic, and ergometrine is added as the second-line agent because she is normotensive with no cardiac disease. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; AMH: Uterotonics)
Uterotonic escalation is done in parallel with examination under anaesthesia; deferring pharmacology until theatre wastes time while the atonic uterus keeps bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk.
key_points: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception.
LNG-IUD is first-line for heavy menstrual bleeding in Australia.
Copper IUD increases menstrual blood loss and worsens iron deficiency.
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg LNG-IUD reduces menstrual blood loss by about 90% at 12 months and rescues ferritin, all while providing the most effective reversible contraception.

options.rationale: The traditional low-dose progestogen-only pill requires a three-hour dosing window and is user-dependent; it does not reliably reduce menstrual loss on its own. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)
Combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) in migraine with aura at any age because of increased ischaemic stroke risk. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; UKMEC)
The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but typically INCREASES menstrual blood loss and pain, and would worsen her iron deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG contraception)
Depot progestin is safe in migraine with aura and reduces bleeding, but bone mineral density falls with prolonged use. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; AMH)

Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD is the most effective non-permanent contraception (failure under 0.2%) and is first-line hormonal treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding; as a progestogen-only method it can be used in migraine with aura. (Source: RANZCOG contraception; Family Planning Alliance Australia)

explanation.summary: Intrapartum fetal surveillance is chosen on the balance of risk factors, and colonisation with group B streptococcus, treated with the recommended intravenous antibiotic and with no fever or other complication, does not by itself move a woman from intermittent auscultation to continuous cardiotocography. What does move her is an intrapartum fever, suspected intrauterine infection, significant meconium, oxytocin augmentation, bleeding, or an abnormality heard on auscultation. Applying continuous monitoring to every colonised woman increases immobility, intervention and operative birth without a demonstrated benefit, and conflicts with the low risk pathway she has been offered. In context, the practical compromise many Australian units use is a cannula with intermittent flushing so the antibiotic can be given four hourly while she remains mobile, upright and able to use the shower or bath between doses.
key_points: Carriage alone does not warrant continuous cardiotocography.
Fever, meconium, bleeding, oxytocin or abnormal auscultation do warrant it.
Unnecessary continuous monitoring increases intervention without benefit.
A flushed cannula lets four hourly dosing coexist with mobility in labour.
explanation.pearls: Intermittent auscultation in established labour is performed for one minute immediately after a contraction, every 15 to 30 minutes in the first stage and every 5 minutes in the second stage.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management
Queensland Clinical Guidelines - Early onset group B streptococcal disease

options.rationale: Carriage on its own is not a risk factor that warrants continuous monitoring, so her low risk pathway stands. (Source: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline
RANZCOG - Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy: screening and management

options.rationale: Continuous monitoring is indicated once fever, meconium, oxytocin or an abnormal auscultation appears. (Source: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Monitoring around a dose would make sense for a drug with direct fetal effects, which this is not. (Source: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: A scalp electrode is used when continuous monitoring is indicated and the external trace cannot be maintained. (Source: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline

options.rationale: Fetal blood sampling is used to clarify an abnormal continuous trace, not as a routine addition. (Source: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal os, either overlying a velamentous cord insertion (Type I) or between lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta.
key_points: Vasa praevia: painless antepartum haemorrhage at rupture PLUS sinusoidal or bradycardic CTG.
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes; delay costs the baby.
Neonate needs immediate resuscitation and blood transfusion for anaemia.
explanation.pearls: A sinusoidal CTG with painless blood-stained liquor after membrane rupture is vasa praevia fetal exsanguination; the baby is born by category 1 caesarean and needs immediate neonatal resuscitation and blood transfusion.

options.rationale: Fetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern indicates fetal hypovolaemia and severe anaemia. Labour will lose the baby. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

Fetal bradycardia with sinusoidal pattern after painless ruptured membranes with blood-stained liquor is vasa praevia with fetal exsanguination, which needs category 1 caesarean with the neonatal team ready to resuscitate and transfuse. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)
Ultrasound wastes the survival window in vasa praevia with active exsanguination. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)
Corticosteroids do not treat fetal exsanguination and 37 weeks is past the routine steroid window. Delivery cannot wait. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)
Membranes are already ruptured and the fetal circulation is compromised. (Source: RANZCOG antepartum haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by any of BP >=160/110, thrombocytopaenia (platelets <100), impaired liver function (transaminases twice upper limit), renal insufficiency, or neurological features such as persistent headache or hyperreflexia with clonus.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria include BP >=160/110 OR end-organ features (platelets <100, ALT >2x normal, headache, hyperreflexia with clonus).
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g/h reduces eclamptic seizures (MAGPIE).
Continue magnesium 24 hours after delivery or last seizure.
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour is the Australian first-line for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia; continue for 24 hours after delivery or the last seizure.

options.rationale: Antihypertensive control is essential but does not prevent eclamptic seizures; magnesium is a separate pharmacological intervention. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)
Benzodiazepines are not first-line seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is superior for preventing eclamptic seizures. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

Pre-eclampsia with severe features (BP >=160/110, headache, epigastric pain, platelets <100, ALT >2x normal, hyperreflexia with clonus) warrants magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, which reduces eclamptic seizures (MAGPIE). (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

Betamethasone is indicated for fetal lung maturity at this gestation, but administering steroids without magnesium sulfate leaves her unprotected against eclamptic seizures. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)
Low-dose aspirin is preventive (started before 16 weeks in women at high risk); it has no acute role once pre-eclampsia has developed. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome ranges from mild (self-limiting) to critical (respiratory failure, thrombosis, acute renal failure).
key_points: OHSS is a hypercoagulable, haemoconcentrated, third-space-loss state.
Admission for moderate to severe disease; VTE prophylaxis with LMWH.
Crystalloid volume replacement guided by haematocrit and urine output.
explanation.pearls: In moderate OHSS with haematocrit above 45%, isotonic crystalloid resuscitation plus VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin is the Australian standard; diuretics are avoided while she is intravascularly depleted.

options.rationale: Rising haematocrit (46%), hyponatraemia (130), oliguria on history, pleural effusion, weight gain >3 kg, dyspnoea and tachycardia mark moderate to severe OHSS, which needs admission rather than outpatient care. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)
Surgery is reserved for ovarian torsion, cyst rupture with haemodynamic instability, or ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)
Diuresis in OHSS is contraindicated while patients are intravascularly deplete (rising haematocrit, third-space losses). (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

Moderate to severe OHSS is a high-VTE-risk state (haemoconcentration, oestradiol effect, immobility) and requires admission for isotonic crystalloid, enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis and daily haematocrit, with paracentesis if breathing deteriorates. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement; RCOG green-top guideline)
Corticosteroids have not shown clinically important benefit in OHSS and are not standard therapy. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS statement)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare obstetric emergency that presents during labour or shortly after birth with sudden breathlessness or agitation, then hypoxia, cardiovascular collapse and a consumptive coagulopathy. There is no specific treatment, so management is high-quality ALS with simultaneous haemostatic resuscitation. RANZCOG lists amniotic fluid embolism among the causes of PPH from abnormal coagulation and recommends a massive transfusion protocol, tranexamic acid and early fibrinogen replacement. Before birth, a woman in arrest from 20 weeks also needs left uterine displacement and a resuscitative caesarean; after birth those steps no longer apply, and the uterus is managed as atonic PPH once there is a circulation.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism: sudden peripartum collapse with coagulopathy and bleeding from puncture sites.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given as soon as possible after PPH begins and repeated at 30 minutes if bleeding continues.
RANZCOG replaces fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate when it is below 1.5 to 2 g/L.
Resuscitative caesarean applies only while the fetus is undelivered.
explanation.pearls: RANZCOG's PPH statement lists ergometrine 0.25 mg IM or slow IV, repeated 5-minutely to a maximum of 1 mg, as a second-line uterotonic when there is no contraindication.

sources.label: ANZCOR Guideline 11.2: Protocols for adult advanced life support
RCOG Green-top Guideline 56: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Fibrinolysis during CPR is reserved for arrest from a suspected massive pulmonary embolism in a patient who is not bleeding. ESC 2019 lists active bleeding and bleeding diathesis as absolute contraindications, and she has torrential haemorrhage with a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L. (Source: ESC 2019 Acute Pulmonary Embolism Guidelines)

Ergometrine 0.25 mg is a second-line uterotonic for atonic PPH once the woman has a circulation, but crystalloid alone and a 20-minute wait for blood leave a consumptive coagulopathy untreated. RANZCOG calls early replacement of clotting factors and platelets essential in severe PPH. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43))

Haemostatic brace sutures such as the B-Lynch are a theatre option for atony that persists once she is resuscitated. Moving a woman in cardiac arrest interrupts effective compressions, and a suture does nothing for the arrest or the coagulopathy. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43); ANZCOR Guideline 11.2: Protocols for adult advanced life support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11.2: Protocols for adult advanced life support

options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not a first-line haemostatic agent in obstetric haemorrhage, and withholding red cells during an arrest from bleeding is unsafe. RANZCOG pairs a massive transfusion protocol with fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate) when fibrinogen is below 1.5 to 2 g/L. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43))

Sudden breathlessness, agitation and cardiac arrest minutes after birth, with bleeding from cannula sites and a fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L, is amniotic fluid embolism with consumptive coagulopathy. She needs ALS and simultaneous replacement of blood and clotting factors: RANZCOG supports a massive transfusion protocol, tranexamic acid 1 g IV as soon as possible, and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43); ANZCOR Guideline 11.2: Protocols for adult advanced life support)
source_refs: ANZCOR Guideline 11.2: Protocols for adult advanced life support

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean carries a small risk of uterine rupture, which is why labour is monitored with continuous CTG and oxytocin is used cautiously. Rupture presents non-specifically, and QCG lists abnormal CTG, scar pain, abdominal pain persisting between contractions, loss of station, easily felt fetal parts, vaginal bleeding and maternal instability. Suspected rupture is a category 1 caesarean with expeditious laparotomy and neonatal resuscitation, while the mother is resuscitated for haemorrhage. Delay costs the fetus quickly, and QCG reports hysterectomy in 14 to 33% and perinatal death in up to 13% of ruptures.
key_points: Fetal bradycardia is the most common sign of uterine rupture.
Suspected uterine rupture is a category 1 caesarean.
Suspected uterine rupture and suspected placental abruption are contraindications to acute tocolysis.
Intrauterine resuscitation and CTG reassessment are for reversible causes, not rupture.
explanation.pearls: QCG notes that the classic triad of pain, vaginal bleeding and fetal heart rate abnormality is present in fewer than 10% of complete uterine ruptures.

options.rationale: RANZCOG lists suspected uterine rupture among the contraindications to acute tocolysis, and her contractions have already stopped, so terbutaline adds only maternal tachycardia and hypotension while she bleeds. Terbutaline 250 micrograms suits tachysystole with an abnormal CTG, or buys time for the fetus when theatre is not immediately available. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance (C-Obs 1))

Ergometrine 0.25 mg IM or slow IV is a uterotonic for PPH after the birth. Given with the fetus still in utero and the scar open, it delays birth and does nothing for the cause of the bradycardia. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of postpartum haemorrhage (C-Obs 43))

Contractions that stop, a new constant pain, loss of station, easily felt fetal parts and a prolonged bradycardia in labour after caesarean point to uterine rupture. QCG recommends a category 1 caesarean because there is an urgent threat to the woman and her baby, and she needs large-bore access and blood ready for the haemorrhage that follows. (Source: QCG: Vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC))

Intrauterine resuscitation suits a reversible CTG abnormality such as tachysystole or cord compression. RANZCOG notes that after uterine rupture, fetal hypoxia develops within about 10 minutes, so birth is expedited rather than the CTG reassessed. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance (C-Obs 1))

A category 2 caesarean allows time that this fetus does not have. QCG specifies a category 1 caesarean for suspected uterine rupture, with expeditious laparotomy to reduce morbidity and mortality. (Source: QCG: Vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC))

explanation.summary: Uterine atony causes the majority of primary PPH. RANZCOG stepwise pharmacological escalation is fundal massage, oxytocin (given), ergometrine (contraindicated by chronic hypertension), carboprost, then misoprostol. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours of birth as an adjunct. Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used if medical measures fail. Do not give ergometrine in hypertensive, pre-eclamptic or cardiac disease.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease
Carboprost is contraindicated in asthma
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of birth for any PPH over 500 mL
Bimanual compression and balloon tamponade are used with, not instead of, pharmacology
explanation.pearls: The AMH warns that ergometrine and combination Syntometrine can precipitate hypertensive crisis in eclamptic women - remember to check the antenatal blood pressure before reaching for the ampoule.

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension, pre-eclampsia or cardiac disease because of the risk of hypertensive crisis, stroke and myocardial ischaemia; this woman has documented chronic hypertension. (Source: AMH: Ergometrine)

RANZCOG stepwise PPH management gives ergometrine as second line, then carboprost when ergometrine fails or is contraindicated by hypertension; a history of chronic hypertension makes ergometrine contraindicated so carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic here. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement; eTG: Postpartum haemorrhage)

Bimanual compression is a temporising manoeuvre used alongside pharmacological escalation for ongoing PPH; using it in place of additional uterotonic wastes time and does not address the uterine atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Tranexamic acid should be given for any PPH over 500 mL within three hours as an adjunct, not instead of a second line uterotonic; the atony must be treated pharmacologically at the same time. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

Intrauterine balloon tamponade is second line after failure of medical management and preparation for theatre; pharmacological escalation to a second uterotonic is appropriate before mechanical intervention in a stable woman with atony. (Source: RANZCOG PPH statement)

explanation.summary: This woman has severe pre-eclampsia at 34+2 weeks with cerebral symptoms (headache, blurred vision), HELLP features (platelets 92, ALT 152, LDH raised) and blood pressure well over the severe threshold of 160/110. Management is simultaneous control of blood pressure with IV labetalol or hydralazine, seizure prophylaxis with magnesium sulfate per the Magpie protocol, and antenatal corticosteroids as delivery is planned within 24-48 hours after stabilisation. Delivery mode is determined by cervix and fetal status; caesarean is not automatic.
key_points: Severe pre-eclampsia criteria: BP 160/110, HELLP, neurological symptoms, or end-organ dysfunction
Magnesium sulfate load 4 g IV over 20 min, then 1 g/hour infusion (Magpie protocol)
Monitor magnesium clinically: reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output
Betamethasone if delivery may be delayed 24-48 hours between 24 and 34+6 weeks
explanation.pearls: The AU spelling is magnesium sulfate (INN in AMH), not sulfate - and magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically, not by routine serum levels.

options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms and HELLP features (platelets under 100, ALT over 70) requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis (Magpie trial protocol) alongside blood pressure control and betamethasone before delivery planning. AMH uses the AU spelling magnesium sulfate. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023; RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy statement)

Magnesium sulfate is the evidence-based seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia (Magpie trial) with clear superiority over phenytoin; phenytoin is not first line and gives worse outcomes. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

This woman meets criteria for severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP features and neurological symptoms and requires magnesium sulfate; a blood pressure agent alone leaves her unprotected against eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

Delivery is planned but stabilisation with magnesium sulfate and antihypertensives comes first, and at 34+2 weeks betamethasone should be given if delivery can be safely delayed for 24 hours; skipping stabilisation increases maternal and neonatal risk. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

Benzodiazepines are used to abort an active eclamptic seizure only if magnesium fails; they cause maternal sedation and respiratory depression and have no role in prevention. (Source: SOMANZ hypertension in pregnancy guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: ADIPS diagnostic criteria for GDM on a 75 g OGTT are fasting 5.1, one hour 10.0, two hour 8.5 mmol/L (any one). First line management is medical nutrition therapy from a dietitian, structured physical activity and home glucose self monitoring four times daily targeting fasting under 5.0 and one hour post prandial under 7.4 (or two hour under 6.7). Pharmacotherapy (metformin or insulin) is added if targets are not met within 1-2 weeks, or immediately for severe hyperglycaemia or fetal macrosomia. Insulin remains first line pharmacotherapy in AU, with metformin used in specific settings after counselling on placental transfer.
key_points: ADIPS OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1h 10.0, 2h 8.5 mmol/L
Glucose targets on treatment: fasting under 5.0, 1h post prandial under 7.4, 2h under 6.7
MNT first, pharmacotherapy if targets missed at 1-2 weeks
Insulin first line pharmacotherapy in AU, metformin alternative
explanation.pearls: Metformin crosses the placenta but the MiG trial and long term follow up show broadly reassuring neonatal outcomes; AU practice still starts with insulin more often than metformin, unlike some UK pathways.

options.rationale: A single positive OGTT meeting ADIPS criteria makes the diagnosis and delaying management for a repeat test exposes mother and fetus to four weeks of untreated hyperglycaemia; there is no diagnostic need for confirmation. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

Pharmacotherapy is not first line at diagnosis in the absence of severe hyperglycaemia; ADIPS calls for a trial of medical nutrition therapy with self monitoring first, with metformin or insulin added if glucose targets are not met. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

Insulin is first line pharmacotherapy when nutrition therapy fails or when there is severe hyperglycaemia at diagnosis; the OGTT here is mildly elevated and a trial of medical nutrition therapy is indicated first. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020)

ADIPS first line management of newly diagnosed GDM is medical nutrition therapy, physical activity and home glucose self monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if targets (fasting under 5.0 and two hour post prandial under 6.7 mmol/L) are not met within one to two weeks. (Source: ADIPS consensus 2020; RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

Delivery timing decisions in GDM depend on glycaemic control, fetal growth and complications during ongoing pregnancy, not on the diagnosis alone; this bypasses the need for glucose management and monitoring in the interim. (Source: RANZCOG diabetes in pregnancy statement)

explanation.summary: MEC AU categorises contraception in breastfeeding women. Progestogen only methods (pill, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUS) are all category 1 or 2 from any time postpartum and do not impair lactation. Combined hormonal methods are category 3 in the first six weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (VTE and lactation concerns) and category 2 from 6 weeks onwards. If she declines devices, the progestogen only pill is a category 1 first choice that can start today. Contraception should be discussed by six weeks postpartum because ovulation can return before menses.
key_points: MEC AU 1: progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum
MEC AU 3: combined pill in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding
Ovulation may return before menses so contraception before day 21 if not breastfeeding
LAM is 98% effective only if exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months
explanation.pearls: The progestogen only pill window in AU is often quoted as 3 hours for older levonorgestrel pills and 12 hours for desogestrel and drospirenone - check the product prescribed.

options.rationale: The implant is safe and effective but requires a subdermal insertion which she declined for the same reason as the IUD; the pill matches her stated preference and MEC category 1 status. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

MEC AU category 3 (risks outweigh benefits) for combined pill in the first six weeks postpartum in a breastfeeding woman due to venous thromboembolism and lactation concerns; category 2 after 6 weeks but not first choice while breastfeeding. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

DMPA is safe in breastfeeding but requires an injection which she declined for other reasons and has a slower return to fertility and bone mineral density concerns with long use; the pill better matches her preference. (Source: MEC AU 2021)

LAM requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea and infant under 6 months, and even then has a failure rate of about 2% in typical use; she needs a defined method as she does not want to rely on breastfeeding pattern alone. (Source: FSRH postnatal contraception guideline)

MEC AU category 1 for progestogen only pill in breastfeeding from any time postpartum; it does not affect lactation and can be started immediately with no additional precautions if within 21 days postpartum or amenorrhoeic. It is also compatible with smoking under 15/day if under 35. (Source: MEC AU 2021; FSRH progestogen only pill guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive first trimester losses or two or more with any second trimester loss) warrants structured workup: pelvic imaging for uterine anomaly, parental karyotype, antiphospholipid antibody screen and thyroid and prolactin. In this case the cavity is normal, karyotypes are normal and endocrine screen is normal, so the outstanding test is APL antibodies. APS diagnosis needs a positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti beta 2 glycoprotein 1 antibody confirmed at 12 weeks. Treatment with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH from a positive pregnancy test improves live birth rate in obstetric APS.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage: 3 or more first trimester OR 2 or more with any second trimester loss
Workup: pelvic imaging, parental karyotype, APL antibodies, thyroid, prolactin
APS diagnosis: positive APL confirmed at 12 weeks
Empirical LMWH in unexplained recurrent miscarriage is not evidence based
explanation.pearls: The ISTH APS classification criteria 2023 use domain scoring so a single positive result is not enough - two positive results 12 weeks apart, at least one at moderate to high titre, is needed to confirm.

options.rationale: Empirical LMWH in the absence of documented antiphospholipid syndrome or heritable thrombophilia has not been shown to reduce miscarriage in trials (SPIN, ALIFE); prescribing it exposes her to needle burden and bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ALIFE trial NEJM 2010)

A three dimensional pelvic ultrasound has already shown a normal cavity with no septum and no further imaging is needed unless the ultrasound was unclear; empirical resection has no evidence of benefit without a documented lesion. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage workup includes antiphospholipid antibody screening after 3 or more first trimester losses; diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome requires a positive test confirmed on repeat 12 weeks later, and treatment (aspirin plus low molecular weight heparin) reduces subsequent loss. Her provoked DVT is not itself diagnostic without APL. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement; ISTH APS classification criteria 2023)

Parental karyotypes have already returned normal and repeat testing is not indicated; array comparative genomic hybridisation is a cytogenetic tool for products of conception rather than parental blood in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

PGT-A has not been shown to improve live birth rate in couples with unexplained recurrent miscarriage and normal parental karyotypes; empirical use adds cost, cycle burden and does not address a potentially treatable cause like APS. (Source: RANZCOG recurrent miscarriage statement)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is stratified by peak bile acid: mild (under 40), moderate (40-99) and severe (100 or more micromol/L). Stillbirth risk rises sharply above 100 micromol/L from about 37 weeks. Contemporary guidance recommends delivery at 36 weeks for severe ICP, 38-39 weeks for moderate and 39-40 weeks for mild disease. UDCA improves maternal pruritus and biochemistry but the PITCHES trial did not show reduction in composite fetal outcomes; it is not a substitute for delivery timing. Continuous intrapartum CTG is recommended given the small but definable stillbirth risk.
key_points: Severe ICP: bile acids 100 or more, deliver at 36 weeks
Moderate ICP: 40-99, deliver 38-39 weeks
Mild ICP: under 40, deliver 39-40 weeks
UDCA improves itch but does not remove need for timed delivery
explanation.pearls: Peak bile acids drive the plan - so ongoing measurement matters even after treatment starts, because tier can escalate.

sources.label: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.rationale: Bile acids over 100 micromol/L carry an absolute stillbirth risk that rises from 37 weeks onwards; expectant management until spontaneous labour or 40 weeks is inconsistent with contemporary AU and UK practice for severe ICP. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

RCOG and RANZCOG endorsed bile acid stratification identifies severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 micromol/L as carrying a stillbirth risk that is materially higher than background from 36 weeks; delivery at 36 weeks is recommended with continuous intrapartum CTG. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.rationale: There is no acute fetal compromise on CTG, Doppler or growth to warrant category 1 delivery tonight; the timing decision here is elective planning at 36 weeks, not emergency birth. (Source: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement)
source_refs: RANZCOG intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy statement

options.rationale: Delivery at 39 weeks is appropriate for mild ICP with bile acids under 40 micromol/L; severe ICP with peak bile acids over 100 requires earlier delivery to reduce stillbirth risk. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022)

PITCHES showed UDCA does not reduce fetal composite outcomes but many centres continue it for maternal itch; stopping it does not change delivery timing which is driven by the peak bile acid tier. (Source: RCOG Green Top 43 ICP 2022; PITCHES Lancet 2019)

explanation.summary: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria for tubal ectopic pregnancy are: hCG under 5000 IU/L, no fetal cardiac activity, adnexal mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemodynamic instability, reliable follow up, no contraindications (liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression) and normal baseline blood tests. Single dose regimen is methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with beta hCG on day 4 and day 7; success is a fall of at least 15% between days 4 and 7. Failure or rise triggers a second dose or surgery. Anti-D immunoglobulin should be considered if Rh negative.
key_points: hCG threshold for methotrexate: under 5000 IU/L
Mass size threshold: under 3.5 cm
Requires no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow up
Contraindications: liver, renal, haematologic disease, breastfeeding, immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L (or the presence of cardiac activity, or mass at or above 3.5 cm, or instability, or contraindications to methotrexate) - not the older 3000 IU/L figure.

options.rationale: The pregnancy is not intrauterine on ultrasound so curettage of an empty uterus is not indicated and can delay treatment of the extrauterine pregnancy; location has already been established sonographically. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

Surgical management is preferred for haemodynamic instability, severe pain, contraindications to methotrexate or when medical management fails; in a stable woman meeting all methotrexate criteria, medical management avoids surgical morbidity and preserves the contralateral tube. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

Salpingostomy carries a persistent trophoblast rate around 4-15% and adds no live birth benefit over salpingectomy when the contralateral tube is healthy; it is not preferred over methotrexate in a stable woman meeting medical criteria. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

Expectant management is reserved for women with declining beta hCG under 1000, an asymptomatic clinical picture and clear evidence of resolution; a rising or stable hCG at 1820 with a visible adnexal mass has too high a rupture risk to observe without treatment. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS)

This tubal ectopic meets RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, no cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm, no significant pain, no haemorrhage, reliable follow up, no contraindications and normal bloods. Single dose methotrexate has resolution rates around 85-90% in appropriately selected cases. (Source: RANZCOG ectopic pregnancy GPS; eTG: Ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates 10-15% of monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies and is staged by the Quintero classification: stage I (oligo-poly), II (donor bladder not visible), III (abnormal Doppler in either twin), IV (hydrops), V (demise). Stage II or higher between 16 and 26 weeks is treated by fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the intertwin anastomoses which has been shown superior to serial amnioreduction (Eurofetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is right at the upper margin of the classic laser window; urgent transfer to a fetal therapy centre is time critical.
key_points: MCDA chorionicity mandates fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks
Quintero staging: I oligo-poly, II bladder gone, III abnormal Doppler, IV hydrops, V demise
Stage II+ at 16-26 weeks: fetoscopic laser preferred over amnioreduction
Delivery is a fallback when laser is not feasible or when demise is imminent
explanation.pearls: The absence of the lambda sign at 11-13 weeks confirms monochorionicity - a determination that cannot be reliably made retrospectively later in pregnancy, which is why every twin pregnancy must have chorionicity documented at the nuchal scan.

options.rationale: Selective reduction is reserved for cases with severe growth restriction and imminent demise of the donor threatening the recipient by exsanguination through anastomoses, or major structural anomaly; laser is offered before reduction as it preserves both twins where possible. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

Amnioreduction is inferior to laser for TTTS at 16-26 weeks (Eurofetus trial: survival of at least one twin 76% laser vs 51% amnioreduction) and delays definitive therapy; if a fetal therapy centre is inaccessible amnioreduction is a temporising measure at best. (Source: Eurofetus trial NEJM 2004)

At 26+3 weeks with reassuring CTGs and normal ductus venosus flow, immediate delivery carries very high extreme prematurity morbidity that is worse than the risk of transferring for laser therapy; delivery is reserved for irretrievable Doppler deterioration or fetal distress. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement)

TTTS stage III (Quintero: oligohydramnios pocket under 2 in donor, polyhydramnios pocket over 8 in recipient, empty donor bladder plus abnormal Doppler with absent end diastolic flow) at 16-26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of intertwin anastomoses; laser improves at least one twin survival compared with amnioreduction (Eurofetus trial). At 26+3 weeks she is at the outer margin and referral is time critical. (Source: RANZCOG multiple pregnancy statement; ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

TTTS with abnormal Doppler is a treat now diagnosis, not a watch and wait; without laser the composite mortality of untreated stage III TTTS at this gestation approaches 80-90%. (Source: ISUOG monochorionic twin surveillance guideline)

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean requires a low transverse uterine scar, a resolved or non recurring indication, appropriate inter delivery interval, continuous cardiotocograph monitoring and immediate access to obstetric, anaesthetic and theatre teams to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of the decision. Facility rather than obstetric factors are the reason planned vaginal birth after caesarean is declined here. Anterior placenta not overlying the scar is safe; anterior placenta overlying the previous caesarean scar prompts placenta accreta workup. Inter delivery interval and previous indication are not disqualifying in this scenario.
key_points: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of decision is a RANZCOG facility requirement for vaginal birth after caesarean.
Low transverse scar with resolved indication is a favourable feature.
Anterior placenta over the scar (not off the scar) prompts placenta accreta workup.
explanation.pearls: A 30 minute theatre recall for elective work is not the immediate response needed for uterine rupture; refer to a facility with in house theatre for planned vaginal birth after caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean
NSW Health Maternity - vaginal birth after caesarean

options.rationale: The indication for the previous caesarean does not itself preclude a planned vaginal birth after caesarean; a low transverse scar with a resolved non recurring indication is a good candidate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.rationale: An inter delivery interval of 18 to 24 months and above is considered acceptable; 3 years does not preclude a planned vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.rationale: 36 weeks is not a preclusive gestation; term vaginal birth after caesarean is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.rationale: RANZCOG requires the ability to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of a decision, meaning immediate access to anaesthetics and theatre for uterine rupture. A 30 minute recall for elective theatre with 15 minute anaesthetic on call overnight does not meet that immediate response requirement and makes planned vaginal birth after caesarean inappropriate at this facility. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.rationale: An anterior placenta not overlying the scar and normally sited does not preclude planned vaginal birth after caesarean; placenta accreta risk with anterior placenta over the scar would. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

explanation.summary: The Australasian intrapartum prophylaxis pathway for group B streptococcus uses benzylpenicillin as first line; a woman with immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin has cephalosporins relatively contraindicated. Clindamycin may be used only when the isolate is sensitive and no inducible resistance is detected on D test; where either is unavailable or resistance is present, vancomycin is the recommended alternative. Erythromycin is no longer routinely recommended. Vancomycin is dosed at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes to reduce infusion related hypersensitivity. Adequate prophylaxis is at least one dose 4 hours before birth.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line; anaphylaxis is a hard contraindication.
Clindamycin requires proven susceptibility and no inducible resistance on D test.
Vancomycin is the fallback where clindamycin cannot be used, 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over 60 minutes.
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance, intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis is vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is contraindicated because of her documented immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Cephalosporins share a small cross reactivity with penicillins and are relatively contraindicated when the reaction was immediate anaphylaxis; select an alternative not sharing the beta lactam core. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: The isolate is resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance; clindamycin cannot be relied on for group B streptococcus prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Erythromycin has variable resistance in group B streptococcus and poor placental transfer; it is not recommended as intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: With immediate penicillin anaphylaxis and clindamycin resistance on D test, vancomycin is the recommended prophylaxis at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes until delivery. Sensitivity to vancomycin does not need to be reported for empiric intrapartum use. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is graded by symptoms, haemoconcentration, ascites, renal function and thromboembolic markers. Moderate cases with haematocrit under 0.45 L/L, weight gain under 5 kg, adequate urine output, ability to tolerate oral fluids and stable social supports can be managed as outpatients with a daily weight and urine diary, thromboprophylaxis in high risk cases and a same next day review. Admission is reserved for severe features (haematocrit >=0.45 L/L, oliguria, pleural effusion, hyponatraemia, coagulopathy). Paracentesis, albumin infusion and prophylactic surgery are all reserved for specific severe scenarios.
key_points: Moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (haematocrit <0.45, urine output preserved) can be managed as outpatient with structured monitoring.
Severe features prompt admission: haematocrit >=0.45, oliguria, pleural effusion, coagulopathy, tense ascites.
Prophylactic laparoscopy of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable.
explanation.pearls: A moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with haematocrit 0.44 L/L, tolerating oral fluid and preserved urine output goes home with a monitoring diary and next day review.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.rationale: This is moderate ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with weight gain <5 kg, haematocrit <0.45 L/L, normal renal function, adequate oral intake, no pleural effusion or thromboembolism and a stable social situation; outpatient management with structured monitoring is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.rationale: Paracentesis is reserved for severe or critical ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with respiratory compromise, tense ascites, or oliguria refractory to conservative therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.rationale: Neither high dose albumin nor dopamine renal dose are supported for prevention of renal injury in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and both add risk. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.rationale: Ovarian abscess is not a routine consideration in this scenario; markers are not consistent with sepsis and empirical antibiotics are not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a specific surgical emergency with characteristic pain, and prophylactic surgery of hyperstimulated ovaries is contraindicated because they are friable. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 1 Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome

explanation.summary: Atonic postpartum haemorrhage after adequate oxytocin needs a different uterotonic mechanism. Ergometrine causes ergot mediated vasoconstriction and precipitates hypertensive crisis in women with pre eclampsia or hypertension. Carboprost (15 methyl prostaglandin F2 alpha) is the preferred second line agent when ergometrine is contraindicated; the main contraindication for carboprost itself is asthma. Misoprostol 800 microg rectally is an option in low resource settings or where parenteral prostaglandin is unavailable. Concurrent tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
key_points: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia.
Carboprost 250 microg intramuscularly, repeat every 15 minutes to 2 mg total, asthma is the main contraindication.
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous is a standard adjunct in postpartum haemorrhage.
explanation.pearls: A woman with gestational hypertension and ongoing atonic postpartum haemorrhage gets carboprost as the second line uterotonic, not ergometrine.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre eclampsia because of ergot mediated vasoconstriction and severe hypertensive crisis risk; her blood pressure and gestational hypertension exclude this. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Carboprost is the appropriate second line uterotonic when ergometrine is contraindicated by hypertension; it can be repeated every 15 minutes up to a total of 2 mg with asthma being the main contraindication to consider. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Misoprostol may be used but has slow onset and is less effective as monotherapy in ongoing bleeding; parenteral carboprost is preferred when available in ongoing haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Repeating oxytocin in a woman already on an oxytocin infusion at 250 mL/hour with ongoing haemorrhage is not the next step; escalate to a different uterotonic mechanism. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

options.rationale: Glyceryl trinitrate is a uterine relaxant used for a trapped placenta or uterine inversion, not for atonic bleeding after a complete placenta. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is characterised by unprotected fetal vessels traversing or lying close to the internal cervical os. Membrane rupture with these vessels present precipitates fetal exsanguination within minutes. Australian guidance recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient admission where the woman lives at a distance from a maternity unit, and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity risk against catastrophic haemorrhage risk. Vaginal birth is contraindicated. Suspicion is triggered on morphology scan features such as bilobed placenta, low lying placenta or velamentous cord insertion, then confirmed on transvaginal colour Doppler.
key_points: Vasa praevia risk factors: bilobed placenta, low lying placenta, velamentous cord insertion.
Vaginal birth contraindicated; deliver by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids.
Consider inpatient admission from 32 weeks if geography or bleeding raises risk.
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is delivered by planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, not at term.

sources.label: SMFM Consult Series 37: Diagnosis and management of vasa previa

options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated in vasa praevia because rupture of membranes can precipitate fetal exsanguination; delivery must be by planned caesarean before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

32 weeks is too early to deliver an asymptomatic woman with vasa praevia and no evidence of bleeding or labour; corticosteroids given intrapartum are too late for maximal benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

RANZCOG recommends antenatal corticosteroids at 32 to 34 weeks, inpatient monitoring (particularly for women living far from a maternity unit) and planned caesarean at 34 to 36 weeks to balance prematurity against catastrophic haemorrhage from ruptured fetal vessels at membrane rupture. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Planned caesarean at 39 weeks carries an unacceptable risk of spontaneous rupture of membranes and fetal exsanguination in the interval; delivery must be planned before labour. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

Fetal vessels overlying the internal os do not resolve reliably and expectant management delays needed delivery; planned early caesarean is the intervention. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Magnesium toxicity in a pre eclamptic woman on magnesium sulfate is a clinical diagnosis: loss of patellar reflexes, reduced respiratory rate, drowsiness and oliguria all indicate rising levels. Because renal clearance dominates elimination, oliguria drives accumulation. The clinical assessment does not wait for the level; the infusion is stopped and intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes antagonises the neuromuscular effect. Ventilatory support is added if respiration is compromised. Once stable the infusion may be recommenced at a lower rate with closer monitoring and dose adjustment for renal function.
key_points: Magnesium toxicity is clinical: absent reflexes, respiratory depression, oliguria.
Antidote is calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes; stop the infusion first.
Oliguria drives accumulation; adjust the rate for reduced renal clearance.
explanation.pearls: Absent patellar reflexes and respiratory rate 10 /min on magnesium sulfate is toxicity: stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenous over 10 minutes.

sources.label: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Magnesium sulfate in pre eclampsia

options.rationale: The clinical picture is magnesium toxicity, not seizure recurrence; increasing the infusion worsens toxicity, and aggressive blood pressure reduction below 140/90 risks fetal compromise. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Waiting for a level in the face of areflexia, respiratory depression and oliguria risks respiratory arrest; clinical toxicity mandates action before the level returns. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Loop diuresis carries risk of hypotension and does not immediately antagonise the neuromuscular effect; calcium gluconate is the antagonist to give during clinical toxicity. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and reduced urine output are clinical signs of magnesium toxicity; the appropriate step is to stop the infusion, give calcium gluconate 1 g over 10 minutes as an antagonist, and support respiration and monitor closely without waiting for the level. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are second line for magnesium refractory seizures; here the clinical problem is magnesium toxicity not seizure and diazepam risks compound respiratory depression. (Source: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy)
source_refs: SOMANZ guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism has three overlapping phases: sudden cardiopulmonary collapse from pulmonary vasoconstriction and right ventricular failure, hypoxia and neurological dysfunction, and consumptive coagulopathy with a marked and early drop in fibrinogen. Management is supportive: airway and ventilation, haemodynamic support with noradrenaline and consideration of pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and aggressive correction of coagulopathy targeting fibrinogen above 2 g/L with cryoprecipitate and platelets above 50 x10^9/L. Ergometrine, heparin and recombinant activated factor VII are variously contraindicated or unproven; the primary haemostatic priority is fibrinogen replacement.
key_points: Amniotic fluid embolism coagulopathy is fibrinogen consumption first; cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen above 2 g/L.
Ergometrine is contraindicated because of pulmonary vasoconstriction risk.
Anticoagulation is not indicated during active haemorrhage from amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation.
explanation.pearls: In amniotic fluid embolism with fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, cryoprecipitate targeted to above 2 g/L is the survival step; do not give ergometrine, heparin or recombinant activated factor VII.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism
National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guideline Module 5 Obstetrics

options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII is not first line in amniotic fluid embolism and has an increased thrombotic and pulmonary vascular complication risk in this setting; correction of fibrinogen and platelets and empirical haemostatic products come first. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.rationale: Cell salvage is a useful adjunct in obstetric haemorrhage but does not correct the coagulopathy and does not treat the pulmonary vasoconstrictive component of amniotic fluid embolism; it is not the priority. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.rationale: Ergometrine is contraindicated in this haemodynamic and pulmonary state; the pulmonary vasoconstriction would worsen right ventricular failure. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.rationale: Anticoagulation would worsen active haemorrhage and is not indicated in amniotic fluid embolism related disseminated intravascular coagulation which is predominantly consumptive and fibrinolytic. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

options.rationale: Fibrinogen falls first and fastest in amniotic fluid embolism related consumptive coagulopathy; targeted cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen above 2 g/L reduces mortality more than fresh frozen plasma alone at low fibrinogen. Concurrent platelets are kept above 50 x10^9/L in the actively bleeding patient. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 60 Amniotic fluid embolism

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic placenta praevia at term is delivered by elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in AU per RANZCOG, balancing the maternal risk of antepartum haemorrhage against neonatal prematurity morbidity. Symptomatic praevia (bleeding) or high risk features (previous bleed, low anterior placenta with previous caesarean) may prompt delivery from 34 to 36+6 weeks, in which case antenatal betamethasone is given. Cell salvage, cross matched blood, senior obstetric and anaesthetic involvement and a written surgical plan are standard for high risk cases. Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete praevia regardless of parity. Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess for accreta if the placenta is anterior and overlies a previous scar.
key_points: Elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks in asymptomatic praevia.
Antenatal betamethasone if delivery is expected before 34+6 weeks.
Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in complete placenta praevia regardless of parity.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic complete placenta praevia at term: elective caesarean at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks; antenatal betamethasone reserved for expected delivery before 34+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Guideline
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists Optimal Timing of Elective Birth statement

options.rationale: 36+0 is earlier than the RANZCOG recommended timing for asymptomatic placenta praevia and requires antenatal steroids because of prematurity risk; timing without prior bleeding is 36+0 to 37+6 in some guidance but Australian practice defaults to 37+0 to 37+6 for asymptomatic praevia.
