options.rationale: The 250 international unit dose covers sensitising events before 12 completed weeks, such as miscarriage, termination or ectopic pregnancy managed in the first trimester. At 13 weeks that dose may be insufficient for the fetomaternal bleed possible at this placental mass. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Waiting to detect anti-D antibodies means waiting for the sensitisation that prophylaxis exists to prevent, and once alloimmunisation occurs it cannot be reversed for this or any future pregnancy. Antibody screening is surveillance, not prophylaxis. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)

Vaginal bleeding after 12 weeks is a sensitising event, and the Australian dose changes at that gestation because the volume of fetal red cells in the circulation rises with placental mass. From 12 weeks onward the dose is 625 international units, given as soon as possible and within seventy two hours. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh D immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Quantification of fetomaternal haemorrhage is used from 20 weeks to decide whether additional doses beyond the standard one are needed, not to decide whether to treat at all. Delaying the dose while awaiting the result risks breaching the seventy two hour window. (Source: National Blood Authority: Anti-D guidelines)

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes identifies a woman whose pancreatic reserve was unable to meet the insulin resistance of late pregnancy, and roughly half go on to develop type 2 diabetes within a decade. Insulin is stopped at delivery because that resistance disappears with the placenta, but the underlying tendency does not. The Australian pathway is a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum, which is early enough that women are still engaged with maternity services and late enough that the physiology has settled. Women who test normal then need repeat screening every one to three years, and sooner if they are planning another pregnancy. Needing insulin antenatally, as here, marks a higher risk group in whom the follow up test is most often abnormal.
key_points: Stop insulin at delivery; the insulin resistance of pregnancy resolves with the placenta
Reclassify with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks postpartum
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin are less sensitive in this window
Repeat screening every one to three years lifelong after a normal result
Test before any subsequent pregnancy, not just at the next booking visit
explanation.pearls: Write the six to twelve week oral glucose tolerance test request before she leaves the ward and copy it to her general practitioner, because completion rates in Australia sit near half and the commonest reason given is that nobody handed over the test; a woman who needed insulin antenatally has roughly a one in five chance of an abnormal result at that first visit.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.rationale: Testing in the first days after birth measures a rapidly changing physiological state as placental hormones fall, so results neither confirm nor exclude persisting diabetes. The reclassification window deliberately waits for that transition to finish. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.rationale: A fasting sample alone is the least sensitive option after gestational diabetes, because post load hyperglycaemia commonly persists while fasting values normalise. Using it as the reclassification test underdiagnoses impaired glucose tolerance. (Source: RACGP: Management of type 2 diabetes)

Self monitoring after birth is not a diagnostic pathway and produces scattered postprandial values that cannot be mapped onto diagnostic thresholds. Women whose home readings look acceptable still turn out to have impaired glucose tolerance on formal testing. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin reflects the preceding two to three months, which in this window still includes the pregnancy itself and is further distorted by delivery related blood loss and red cell turnover. It is a reasonable interval test later, not the reclassification test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

options.rationale: Postnatal reclassification uses a full oral glucose tolerance test at six to twelve weeks, once the insulin resistance of pregnancy has resolved, because a proportion of women have persistent diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance that fasting testing alone misses. Lifelong periodic screening follows because the risk of type 2 diabetes remains elevated. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of gestational diabetes

explanation.summary: The renewed Australian program screens primarily for oncogenic human papillomavirus, with management determined by genotype and, where available, reflex cytology. Types 16 and 18 account for most cervical cancer and carry a substantially higher immediate risk of high grade disease than the other oncogenic types, so their detection means direct colposcopy referral whatever the cytology shows. Self collection was extended to all screening participants to reach under screened and never screened women, who make up the majority of cervical cancer cases in Australia. A self collected vaginal sample is valid for the human papillomavirus test but cannot yield useful cytology, which is why type 16 or 18 on such a sample goes straight to colposcopy while other oncogenic types require a clinician collected sample for triage.
key_points: Types 16 and 18 trigger direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types on a self collected sample need clinician collected cytology to triage
Self collection is not valid for cytology because it misses the transformation zone
Never screened and under screened women account for most cervical cancers in Australia
Vaccination does not alter management of an existing positive result
explanation.pearls: When a never screened woman accepts self collection, book the colposcopy or the follow up sample during the same consultation rather than waiting for the result to arrive, because the group most likely to accept self collection is also the group most likely to be lost between a positive result and the referral that follows it.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to intermediate risk results, meaning oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 with negative or low grade cytology. Applying it to type 16 leaves prevalent high grade disease untreated for a year. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.rationale: Detection of type 16 or 18 carries a high enough risk of high grade disease that referral is immediate regardless of cytology, and a self collected sample cannot be used for cytology because it does not sample the transformation zone. Adding a clinician collected test first only delays the colposcopy that is already indicated. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.rationale: Self collected polymerase chain reaction testing performs equivalently to clinician collection for detecting oncogenic human papillomavirus, so a confirmatory repeat adds no information. Treating the first positive as provisional is a common reason these women are lost to follow up. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.rationale: This is the pathway for oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 found on a self collected sample, where cytology triages who needs colposcopy. With type 16 the referral threshold is already met and cytology cannot lower it. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Guidelines

options.rationale: Vaccination does not clear an established infection or treat existing disease, and returning her to the routine interval ignores a result that already meets the referral threshold. Vaccination is a separate conversation after the colposcopy pathway is under way. (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook: Human papillomavirus)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes precedes about a third of preterm births and exposes the fetus to ascending infection from the moment the barrier is lost. Antibiotics given for latency prolong the interval to delivery, reduce chorioamnionitis and reduce neonatal infection and surfactant requirement. Erythromycin is the agent of choice because the large randomised comparison found amoxicillin with clavulanic acid raised necrotising enterocolitis rates despite similar latency benefit. The course runs ten days or until labour establishes. Corticosteroids are given for lung maturity, magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection if birth before 30 weeks is imminent, and surveillance for chorioamnionitis by maternal observations, fetal heart rate and inflammatory markers continues throughout.
key_points: Erythromycin for ten days or until labour is the latency antibiotic of choice
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided because of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
Intrapartum group B streptococcal prophylaxis is additional, not a substitute
Corticosteroids for lung maturity and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before 30 weeks
Monitor for chorioamnionitis with observations, cardiotocography and inflammatory markers
explanation.pearls: A rising baseline fetal heart rate is often the earliest sign of chorioamnionitis and precedes maternal fever, so a baseline that has climbed from 145 to above 160 beats per minute between daily traces should prompt review for delivery even when the temperature and C reactive protein are still normal.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Erythromycin prolongs the interval to delivery, reduces neonatal infection and reduces the need for surfactant without the bowel injury seen with clavulanate containing regimens. Ten days, or until labour begins if sooner, is the standard course. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Intrapartum penicillin addresses group B streptococcal transmission at birth but does nothing for the ascending infection that shortens latency after membranes rupture. It is given in addition to the latency course when labour starts, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Withholding antibiotics forfeits a proven reduction in neonatal morbidity, and surveillance cultures identify colonisation rather than the subclinical chorioamnionitis that drives preterm labour here. The benefit of the latency course does not depend on a positive culture. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and bacterial vaginosis organisms but has not been shown to prolong latency or improve neonatal outcomes in this setting. It is not part of the standard regimen when membranes rupture preterm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This combination prolonged latency but was associated with a significantly higher rate of necrotising enterocolitis in the neonates, which is why it is specifically avoided in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. The harm outweighed the latency benefit. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Emergency contraception choice turns on three variables: time since intercourse, where the woman is in her cycle, and her body weight. The copper intrauterine device is the most effective option by a wide margin, with a failure rate below one in a thousand, and it works up to five days after intercourse or up to five days after the earliest estimated ovulation. Oral methods act by delaying ovulation, so they fail if the luteinising hormone surge has already begun, and both levonorgestrel and ulipristal lose efficacy as body weight rises. Ulipristal is licensed to five days and levonorgestrel to three. A woman who accepts a device gains both the emergency effect and long-acting contraception in a single visit, which is why it is offered first rather than mentioned as an alternative.
key_points: Copper device is effective to five days and is unaffected by body weight
Levonorgestrel is licensed to seventy two hours and weakens above about 70 kg
Ulipristal is licensed to five days but efficacy also falls with rising weight
Oral methods work by delaying ovulation and fail once the surge has started
The hormonal intrauterine device is not an emergency method
explanation.pearls: Ulipristal blocks progesterone receptors, so starting a progestogen contraceptive within five days of taking it reduces its effect and can also reduce the contraceptive cover of the pill being started; if a woman takes ulipristal and wants to begin an oral contraceptive, wait five days and use condoms in between.

sources.label: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.rationale: The hormonal device does not reliably prevent implantation after intercourse has already occurred, so it is not an emergency method despite being excellent ongoing contraception. It can be placed once this cycle is shown not to be a pregnancy. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.rationale: The copper device remains effective up to five days after intercourse, is far more effective than any oral option, and its performance is unaffected by body weight. It also provides the ongoing contraception she is asking for, and swabs are taken at insertion rather than waiting for results. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.rationale: Levonorgestrel is licensed only to seventy two hours and its efficacy declines above about 70 kg, so at five days and at this weight it offers little protection. Doubling the dose is sometimes used but the evidence for that practice is weak. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Day five is within the window for the copper device, and intercourse on cycle day 11 sits squarely in the fertile period so the risk is real. Declining to act converts a preventable exposure into a wait and see. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

options.rationale: Ulipristal is licensed to five days and outperforms levonorgestrel, but its efficacy falls with increasing body weight and it is substantially less effective than a copper device at this point in the cycle. It also delays rather than provides ongoing contraception. (Source: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines)
source_refs: Family Planning Australia: Contraception clinical guidelines

explanation.summary: Urinary incontinence in women is separated first into stress, urgency and mixed patterns, because the treatments diverge completely: stress incontinence responds to pelvic floor training and, if that fails, to a continence procedure, while urgency incontinence responds to bladder retraining and then to drug treatment. The initial assessment needs only a history, a bladder diary, an examination for prolapse and pelvic floor function, a urine dipstick to exclude infection, haematuria and glycosuria, and a post-void residual. Behavioural treatment achieves substantial improvement in around half of women with an overactive bladder and carries no adverse effects, so it precedes any prescription. When drug treatment is needed, antimuscarinics and beta 3 agonists are roughly equivalent in efficacy, and the choice turns on adverse effects, with anticholinergic load a genuine concern in older women. Vaginal oestrogen is a useful adjunct where there is urogenital atrophy, and refractory cases proceed to specialist options including intravesical botulinum toxin and sacral neuromodulation.
key_points: Separate stress from urgency first because the treatments diverge completely
Dipstick, bladder diary, prolapse assessment and post-void residual are the initial workup
Behavioural treatment helps around half of women and precedes any drug
Oxybutynin carries the highest anticholinergic burden and is a poor choice in older women
Urodynamics is for treatment failure, unclear patterns or before continence surgery
explanation.pearls: Topical vaginal oestrogen is worth adding here alongside the bladder training: atrophic changes of the urethra and trigone contribute to urgency and frequency after menopause, and low dose vaginal preparations produce negligible systemic absorption, so they are usable even in women for whom systemic hormone therapy is not appropriate.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Urodynamic testing is reserved for symptoms that fail conservative treatment, for mixed or unclear patterns, and before surgery for stress incontinence, because in a clear storage pattern with a negative dipstick and a normal residual it does not change the first line plan. It also carries cost, discomfort and a risk of infection. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Antimuscarinic treatment is second line after behavioural measures, and oxybutynin in particular is the agent most associated with dry mouth, constipation and cognitive impairment in older women, with accumulating evidence linking long term anticholinergic load to dementia. If a drug is needed later, a more selective agent or a beta 3 agonist is preferred. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A sling treats leakage on effort by supporting the urethra, and she has none: no leak on coughing, sneezing or lifting, and none demonstrable on examination. Operating on the wrong mechanism can worsen urgency and cause voiding difficulty. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A beta 3 agonist avoids the anticholinergic burden and is a good second line choice in this age group, but drug treatment still follows a proper trial of behavioural measures because roughly half of women improve substantially without any medication. Blood pressure also needs monitoring on this agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Urology)

Urgency with urge leakage and nocturia, with no stress component, no prolapse, a negative dipstick and a normal residual, is an overactive bladder, and first line treatment is behavioural: a bladder diary, timed voiding with progressively lengthened intervals, reduction of caffeine and of evening fluids, weight loss, and supervised pelvic floor muscle training which suppresses detrusor contractions as well as supporting the urethra. Eight cups of caffeinated drinks a day is a directly modifiable contributor. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Hirsutism means coarse terminal hair in an androgen dependent distribution and is quantified with the modified Ferriman Gallwey score, with a threshold around four to six in most populations. The critical triage is between the common causes, overwhelmingly polycystic ovary syndrome and idiopathic hirsutism, and the rare serious ones: an androgen secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour, non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome. Red flags for a tumour are rapid progression over months rather than years, frank virilisation with clitoromegaly, deepening of the voice or temporal balding, onset well after adolescence, and a total testosterone above roughly 5 nmol/L or twice the upper limit of normal. Non-classical adrenal hyperplasia is screened for with an early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone in the follicular phase. Treatment of the hair itself is combined hormonal contraception first, with an antiandrogen added after six months if the response is insufficient, alongside mechanical or laser hair removal, and any assessment of response requires at least six months because of the length of the hair growth cycle.
key_points: Rapid onset, virilisation or testosterone above about 5 nmol/L suggests a tumour
Early morning 17 hydroxyprogesterone screens for non-classical adrenal hyperplasia
Combined hormonal contraception is first line for hirsutism in polycystic ovary syndrome
Antiandrogens are added after six months and require reliable contraception
Assess response no earlier than six months because of the hair growth cycle
explanation.pearls: Warn her that the contraceptive will stop new terminal hairs developing but will not remove the ones already there, since existing terminal hair does not revert to fine vellus hair, which is why laser or electrolysis is offered alongside rather than after the hormonal treatment and why unrealistic expectations are the usual reason women abandon it at three months.

sources.label: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.rationale: Metformin improves insulin resistance, menstrual regularity and ovulation in this condition and has a place, but its effect on hair growth is minimal and it is not recommended as treatment for hirsutism. It would be the right choice if the target were cycle regulation or metabolic risk. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.rationale: Androgen receptor blockade is effective and is added after six months if the first line treatment has not achieved enough, but used alone in a woman of reproductive age it requires reliable contraception because of the risk of undervirilisation of a male fetus. The sequence, not the drug, is what is wrong here. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.rationale: Imaging for an androgen secreting tumour is warranted with rapid onset over months, virilisation such as clitoromegaly, deepening voice or temporal balding, or a testosterone above about 5 nmol/L, and none of those apply to a gradual two year history with a modest elevation. Her pelvic ultrasound has already been done and shows no mass. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Gradual hirsutism with oligomenorrhoea since adolescence, a modestly raised testosterone, normal adrenal androgens and normal 17 hydroxyprogesterone is polycystic ovary syndrome, and combined hormonal contraception is first line for the hair because it suppresses ovarian androgen production and raises sex hormone binding globulin. Six months is the minimum interval for assessing response because the hair growth cycle takes that long to turn over. (Source: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome)
source_refs: International evidence-based guideline for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome

options.rationale: Five alpha reductase inhibitors have some efficacy for hirsutism but are not approved for this use in women, carry the same teratogenic risk to a male fetus as other antiandrogens, and are not recommended ahead of the established options. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Chlamydia is the most frequently notified sexually transmitted infection in Australia, with the highest rates in people aged fifteen to twenty nine, and it is asymptomatic in about three quarters of infected women, which is why antenatal screening and annual screening of sexually active people under thirty are both recommended. Treatment differs by setting: outside pregnancy the preferred regimen is doxycycline for seven days, reflecting evidence of superior cure rates particularly at rectal sites, while in pregnancy a single dose of azithromycin is used because tetracyclines are contraindicated. A test of cure is not routine for uncomplicated genital infection but is recommended in pregnancy, after rectal infection, where adherence is uncertain and where an alternative regimen was used, and it is performed at four weeks because nucleic acid tests detect residual non-viable organism before then. Partner notification covering sexual contacts from the preceding six months is an integral part of management, and retesting for reinfection at three months is advised because reinfection from an untreated partner is common. Untreated maternal infection risks preterm birth and neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.
key_points: Around three quarters of infections in women are asymptomatic, hence routine screening
Doxycycline for seven days outside pregnancy; single dose azithromycin in pregnancy
Test of cure at four weeks is recommended in pregnancy, not routinely otherwise
Partner notification covers contacts from the preceding six months
Retest for reinfection at three months regardless of the initial cure
explanation.pearls: Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis presents between five and fourteen days after birth, later than the gonococcal form which appears in the first two to five days, and it is treated with oral rather than topical erythromycin because the organism also colonises the nasopharynx and can cause an afebrile pneumonia at four to twelve weeks of age.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A seven day tetracycline course is the preferred regimen outside pregnancy because it has higher cure rates, particularly for rectal infection, but tetracyclines are avoided in pregnancy because of deposition in developing teeth and bone. The duration is not the issue; the class is. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: A single dose macrolide is the recommended treatment for genital chlamydia in pregnancy, being effective and safe in all trimesters, and a test of cure is performed at four weeks specifically because pregnancy is one of the situations where confirming eradication matters, given the risks of preterm birth and of neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia. Her partner is treated at the same time to prevent reinfection. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: Amoxicillin is a recognised alternative in pregnancy when a macrolide cannot be used, but it has lower microbiological cure rates and there is concern about driving latent infection, so it is second line rather than the default. Omitting the test of cure compounds the problem. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: Untreated infection in pregnancy is associated with preterm birth, premature rupture of membranes and low birth weight, and with neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia acquired during vaginal birth, so deferral exposes both mother and baby to preventable harm. Asymptomatic infection is treated exactly as symptomatic infection is. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: A cephalosporin injection is the treatment for gonorrhoea, which her swab specifically excluded, and it has no useful activity against this intracellular organism. The pairing of the two infections in practice makes this an easy substitution to make by reflex. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: Medical abortion with sequential mifepristone and misoprostol is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and can be provided in general practice by a prescriber who has completed the required training, including by telehealth with local pathology and ultrasound. The woman needs to know that bleeding is typically heavier than a period with clots and cramping over several hours, that it usually settles over one to two weeks, and that she should present for bleeding soaking two pads an hour for two hours, fever, or severe pain not relieved by simple analgesia. Confirmation of success matters because around two to five per cent of treatments fail or leave retained tissue, and the ongoing pregnancy rate is under one per cent; the standard confirmation is a low sensitivity urine pregnancy test at two weeks or a fall in serum hormone of more than eighty per cent at one week from a pre-treatment baseline. Routine ultrasound is avoided because it detects clinically irrelevant intrauterine echoes and drives unnecessary surgery. Contraception is discussed at the same visit and can be started immediately, including insertion of an intrauterine device once the abortion is confirmed complete.
key_points: The combination regimen is approved in Australia to sixty three days of gestation
Confirm success with a low sensitivity urine test at two weeks or an eighty per cent hormone fall at one week
Routine post-treatment ultrasound drives unnecessary surgical intervention
Anti-D immunoglobulin is not required before ten weeks gestation
Contraception can be started immediately, with device insertion once completion is confirmed
explanation.pearls: A standard high sensitivity urine pregnancy test detects down to about 25 IU/L and can stay positive for four weeks or more after a completely successful medical abortion, which is why the low sensitivity test with a threshold near 1000 IU/L is used instead and why a positive standard test at two weeks causes avoidable alarm.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: This was long standing practice, but current Australian guidance no longer recommends anti-D immunoglobulin for spontaneous or induced abortion before ten weeks gestation, because the volume of fetal red cells at that gestation is below the threshold needed to cause sensitisation. Giving it exposes her to a blood product she does not need. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: The combination regimen is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and she is within that window, and confirmation of success uses a low sensitivity urine test that turns negative once the hormone falls below about 1000 IU/L, at two weeks. This avoids the false positives of a standard high sensitivity test, which remains positive for weeks after a completely successful treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Prostaglandin alone has a complete abortion rate around eighty per cent compared with more than ninety five per cent for the sequential combination, so it is reserved for settings where the antiprogestogen is unavailable. A single hormone measurement without a baseline for comparison is also uninterpretable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Being rhesus negative is not a contraindication to medical treatment, and surgical aspiration is an equally valid option chosen for patient preference, gestation beyond the approved window, or contraindications such as suspected ectopic pregnancy, an intrauterine device in place, chronic adrenal failure or long term corticosteroid use. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Routine scanning after medical abortion is specifically discouraged because retained blood and debris in the cavity look abnormal on ultrasound in many women who are entirely well, and acting on that appearance leads to unnecessary surgical intervention. Scanning is reserved for continuing symptoms, heavy bleeding, or a persistently positive test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it typically presents in women in their late thirties and forties with progressively heavier and more painful periods, often with deep dyspareunia and a chronically enlarged tender uterus. Its distinguishing examination finding is a uniformly enlarged globular uterus that is tender, as opposed to the irregular firm contour of fibroids or the fixed retroverted nodular uterus of deep endometriosis. Transvaginal ultrasound has largely replaced the old idea that it can only be diagnosed after hysterectomy, and the features to look for are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, a globular shape, subendometrial echogenic lines and an interrupted or indistinct junctional zone. Iron deficiency is very common and needs treating in its own right alongside the bleeding. Treatment is stepwise: the intrauterine progestogen first, then combined hormonal or oral progestogen options, with antifibrinolytics and anti-inflammatories as adjuncts, then embolisation or ablation, and hysterectomy as the definitive cure for women who have completed their family.
key_points: A uniformly enlarged, globular, tender uterus distinguishes it from fibroids on examination
Ultrasound features include myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone
The intrauterine progestogen is first line and treats both bleeding and pain
Antifibrinolytics reduce bleeding by about a third but do not help the pain
Iron deficiency accompanies it commonly and is treated in parallel
explanation.pearls: Treat the iron deficiency as a separate problem rather than assuming it will correct once the bleeding is controlled: a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L means stores are exhausted, oral iron on alternate days is better absorbed than daily dosing because of the hepcidin response, and symptoms of fatigue often improve before the haemoglobin does.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: Embolisation has reasonable results in this condition and is a genuine option, but it is a radiological intervention with a significant post-procedural pain syndrome and is reserved for women who have failed medical management. It is more established for discrete fibroids, which her scan specifically excludes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the only definitive cure and is entirely appropriate for a woman who has completed her family and failed medical treatment, but she has had no medical treatment at all and has asked to avoid an operation. Offering surgery first inverts the usual ladder. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Ovarian suppression shrinks the uterus and stops the bleeding effectively but causes vasomotor symptoms and bone loss, so it is limited to six months without add back therapy and is generally used to prepare for surgery rather than as ongoing treatment. It is a bridging agent, not a first line one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: A globular tender uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and loss of the junctional zone on ultrasound is adenomyosis, and the intrauterine progestogen is first line because it treats both the heavy bleeding and the pain by producing endometrial and adenomyotic decidualisation and atrophy, with typical reductions in blood loss above eighty per cent. It also provides contraception and preserves the uterus, which is what she has asked for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: An antifibrinolytic reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a useful non-hormonal option for a woman who wants to conceive or declines hormones, but it does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia that are half her problem here. The difference from the correct answer is that one treats both symptoms and one treats a single symptom partially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Menopause before the age of forty is premature ovarian insufficiency and between forty and forty five is early menopause, and both are managed differently from menopause at the usual age. The central principle is that these women are deficient in a hormone their peers still produce, so treatment is framed as replacement until at least the average age of natural menopause, around fifty one, rather than as a short course weighed against the risks described in trials of older women. Untreated, they face accelerated bone loss with a high lifetime fracture risk, increased cardiovascular disease, and probably increased cognitive decline, which is why hormone therapy is first line for their bone protection ahead of bisphosphonates. Either standard menopausal hormone therapy or a combined oral contraceptive can be used, with the contraceptive preferred where pregnancy is still possible, which it occasionally is. Investigation at diagnosis includes karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and adrenal and thyroid autoantibodies, and bone density is measured at diagnosis and repeated every few years. Calcium intake of around 1300 mg a day and vitamin D sufficiency support whichever agent is chosen.
key_points: Menopause before forty five is replacement, not optional symptom relief
Hormone therapy is continued until at least the average age of menopause
It is first line for bone protection in this group, ahead of bisphosphonates
Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures
Karyotype, fragile X premutation and autoantibody testing belong in the initial workup
explanation.pearls: Her vitamin D of 48 nmol/L sits just below the target of at least 50 nmol/L year round, and correcting it matters before starting any antiresorptive agent, because giving a potent bisphosphonate or denosumab to a vitamin D deficient patient can precipitate symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are first line for postmenopausal osteoporosis at the usual age, but in women with early menopause they are second line because they do not replace the oestrogen deficiency that is causing the loss, and long term use in a woman who may need treatment for four decades raises concerns about atypical femoral fracture. They become appropriate if oestrogen is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

Denosumab is effective but commits the patient to indefinite six monthly injections, because stopping it causes a rebound loss of bone density with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures unless another agent is substituted immediately. That is a poor commitment to make at forty seven when a physiological alternative exists. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

Menopause before forty five is treated as replacement of a hormone she should still be producing rather than as optional symptom relief, and hormone therapy is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause around fifty one, for bone density, cardiovascular and cognitive protection. The usual risk calculus from trials in women over sixty does not apply, and she has no contraindication. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

A selective oestrogen receptor modulator increases spinal density and reduces vertebral fracture but not hip fracture, raises the risk of venous thrombosis, and causes or worsens hot flushes, which is a particular problem in a woman who is already oestrogen deficient. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

Exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D repletion are necessary for everyone and will be part of her plan, but as the entire treatment for established osteoporosis in a woman with five years of untreated oestrogen deficiency ahead of her, they allow avoidable further loss. Lifestyle alone is the answer for osteopenia without other risk factors. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are classified as third degree when the anal sphincter complex is involved, subdivided into less than half of the external sphincter torn, more than half torn, and involvement of the internal sphincter, and fourth degree when the anal epithelium is breached. Risk factors are a first vaginal birth, forceps delivery, a birth weight above 4 kg, a prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia and occipitoposterior position. Repair is performed in theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia and good lighting, by an appropriately trained clinician, using either overlap or end to end technique for the external sphincter, with the internal sphincter repaired separately end to end when torn. Aftercare is a course of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives rather than constipating agents, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with specialist review at around three months. The risk of recurrence at a subsequent vaginal birth is around five to seven per cent, and elective caesarean is offered to women who have persisting symptoms or abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, while asymptomatic women with normal studies may plan a vaginal birth.
key_points: Third degree tears are subdivided by how much of the external sphincter is torn
Antibiotics and laxatives, not constipating agents, protect the repair
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and specialist review at around three months are standard
Recurrence risk at a subsequent vaginal birth is roughly five to seven per cent
Elective caesarean is offered for persisting symptoms or abnormal investigations
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about incontinence of flatus and about faecal urgency at every review rather than about faecal incontinence alone, because loss of control of wind and an inability to defer a motion for more than a few minutes are the earliest and commonest symptoms of a sphincter defect, and women very rarely volunteer them.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care

options.rationale: Repair of an anal sphincter injury is followed by a course of broad spectrum antibiotics to reduce wound infection and breakdown, a stool softening laxative so that the first motions do not strain the repair, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with review in a dedicated clinic at around three months where continence is assessed and endoanal ultrasound and manometry are considered. That review, rather than a decision made now, determines the advice about the next birth. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: The immediate measures are right but waiting for symptoms misses the women who will benefit most, since occult sphincter defects and reduced squeeze pressures are common while continence is preserved in the early months and deteriorates years later. Structured follow up is what allows the next birth to be planned properly. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Committing her to abdominal birth on the day after the injury pre-empts the assessment that should decide it: a woman who is fully continent with normal investigations at review can be supported to birth vaginally, and elective caesarean is reserved for those who are symptomatic or have abnormal studies. Omitting antibiotics also increases wound breakdown. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: This gets the bowel management exactly backwards. Constipating the patient produces a hard bolus that has to be passed eventually and is far more likely to disrupt the repair than soft regular motions, which is why a stool softener and not a constipating agent is prescribed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Imaging and pressure studies belong at the specialist review months later, when oedema has resolved and the findings reflect the healed anatomy rather than acute swelling, and doing them now would be uninterpretable. Physiotherapy alone also omits the antibiotics and laxatives that protect the repair. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Vasomotor symptoms are the commonest reason women stop adjuvant endocrine therapy early, and non-adherence to tamoxifen translates directly into higher recurrence and mortality, so treating the flushes is oncological treatment rather than a comfort measure. Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen, its potent active metabolite, so strong inhibitors of that enzyme are avoided: paroxetine and fluoxetine are the ones to know, along with bupropion and quinidine, while venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram and citalopram are weak inhibitors and are considered safe. Effective non-hormonal options in order of evidence are the serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin at night where sleep disturbance dominates, clonidine, and cognitive behavioural therapy or hypnosis, which have good trial evidence and no interactions at all. Vaginal oestrogen is a separate question for genitourinary symptoms and is used cautiously and usually with oncologist involvement, particularly for women on aromatase inhibitors.
key_points: Untreated flushes drive early discontinuation of endocrine therapy and worsen outcomes
Systemic hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer
Tamoxifen requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to form its active metabolite
Avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion; venlafaxine and escitalopram are acceptable
Gabapentin at night and cognitive behavioural therapy are effective alternatives
explanation.pearls: If flushes at night are the dominant problem, gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime is worth knowing as an alternative to the antidepressants because it reduces night time flushes by a similar margin, has no interaction with tamoxifen at all, and its sedation is useful rather than a drawback when the symptom is waking her four times a night.

options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and is contraindicated after a receptor positive breast cancer, where trial evidence showed an increase in new breast cancer events. The transdermal route changes the thrombotic risk profile but not the hormonal one. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

This class does reduce flushes, but paroxetine and fluoxetine are potent inhibitors of the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, and using them together lowers that metabolite substantially with observational evidence of increased breast cancer mortality. The drug class is right and this particular member is the one to avoid. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

Aromatase inhibitors do not work in a woman who is still menstruating unless ovarian function is suppressed, and adding ovarian suppression would deepen the oestrogen deficiency and make the flushes considerably worse. It also changes her cancer treatment without her oncologist, when the request was to manage the symptoms. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

Low dose vaginal oestrogen is used cautiously for genitourinary symptoms in selected women after breast cancer, but systemic absorption is minimal by design, so it has no effect on hot flushes. It answers a different symptom from the one she has presented with. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the best studied non-hormonal option for vasomotor symptoms and typically reduces flush frequency by about sixty per cent, and venlafaxine is specifically preferred in women on tamoxifen because it is a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that generates the active metabolite. Treating the symptom effectively is also what protects five years of adjuvant endocrine therapy she is otherwise about to abandon. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate given to the mother shortly before very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, with a number needed to treat of roughly 60 at gestations below 30 weeks. The Australian and New Zealand guideline sets the threshold at anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks, and treatment is given as a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion, ideally with at least four hours before birth although benefit is not abandoned if less time is available. Monitoring is clinical: respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output, with the infusion stopped if toxicity appears. Normal renal function matters because magnesium is renally cleared. Steroids and neuroprotection serve different endpoints and both are given when time permits.
key_points: Neuroprotective magnesium applies to anticipated birth before 30 completed weeks
Loading dose then infusion, ideally at least four hours before birth
Monitor respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output for toxicity
Renal impairment demands dose reduction because magnesium is renally cleared
Steroids reduce respiratory morbidity and do not replace neuroprotection
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the earliest reliable sign of magnesium toxicity and appears well before respiratory depression, so check reflexes hourly and treat their disappearance as a reason to stop the infusion and recheck the level rather than waiting for the respiratory rate to fall below 12 breaths per minute.

sources.label: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines
RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: A repeat course is considered when the first was given more than seven days earlier and birth is again threatened, but it cannot be completed in a woman delivering within hours and would delay the intervention that can be. Magnesium takes precedence when time is short. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

Antenatal magnesium given to women expected to give birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors, and this birth is imminent at 29 weeks and 4 days. The loading dose and infusion are started as soon as birth is anticipated rather than held back. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulfate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: The Australian threshold is birth before 30 completed weeks, and 29 weeks and 4 days sits inside it. Reading the threshold as 29 weeks or as 28 weeks is the commonest reason eligible women miss the treatment. (Source: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulfate clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: ANZ Antenatal magnesium sulphate clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Nifedipine is an oral agent and tocolysis at 6 cm with regular contractions is very unlikely to stop labour. Its purpose is to buy time for steroids or transfer, both of which are already complete here. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

Group B streptococcal prophylaxis is reasonable in preterm labour of unknown carriage status and would usually be given, but it addresses neonatal sepsis rather than the neurological outcome that defines the window closing here. It is an addition, not the answer to what matters most now. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Venous thromboembolism remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in Australia, and the daily risk peaks in the first postnatal weeks rather than during pregnancy. Risk is scored from a combination of previous events, thrombophilia, mode of birth, body mass index, age, parity and immobility. A previous unprovoked thrombosis is a high risk marker in its own right and mandates prophylaxis antenatally and for six weeks postnatally, while intermediate risk combinations attract ten days. Prophylaxis is with low molecular weight heparin, which does not cross into breast milk in clinically relevant amounts. Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in breastfeeding women. The practical failure mode is not choosing the wrong drug but stopping it at discharge.
key_points: Previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism means six weeks of postnatal prophylaxis
Intermediate risk combinations attract ten days rather than six weeks
Most postnatal events occur after discharge, so the script must leave with her
Enoxaparin and warfarin are compatible with breastfeeding, direct oral agents are not
Prophylactic dosing is used even when the previous event was unprovoked
explanation.pearls: Restart low molecular weight heparin at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and do not remove the catheter within twelve hours of a prophylactic dose, because spinal haematoma is the complication that turns a correct prophylaxis decision into a permanent injury.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Stopping at discharge leaves the highest risk weeks uncovered, since most postnatal events occur after the woman goes home. Stockings are an adjunct and do not substitute for pharmacological prophylaxis in a high risk woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: A previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism places her in the high risk group, for whom prophylaxis continues six weeks postnatally rather than stopping at discharge. The postnatal period carries the highest daily thrombotic risk of the whole pregnancy, and the caesarean and body mass index add to it. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended while breastfeeding because they are excreted in breast milk and infant safety data are lacking. Enoxaparin and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Therapeutic dosing is for treating an acute event or for women on long term anticoagulation, not for prophylaxis after a remote treated thrombosis. It raises the risk of wound haematoma and secondary postpartum haemorrhage without added benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Ten days covers intermediate risk, such as an emergency caesarean with one or two minor risk factors and no thrombotic history. A previous unprovoked event moves her above that band. (Source: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum follows implantation over a uterine scar where decidua is deficient, so villi anchor into or through myometrium. Incidence has risen in step with the caesarean rate, and the combination of placenta praevia with previous caesareans is the classic antenatal warning. Sonographic features are lacunae, loss of the hypoechoic clear zone, myometrial thinning, and bridging vessels extending towards the bladder. Outcomes are determined almost entirely by whether the diagnosis is made antenatally and the delivery planned: a scheduled operation at 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with blood bank support, experienced surgeons and critical care halves maternal morbidity compared with emergency delivery. The operative principle is to deliver the baby through an incision away from the placenta and not to attempt separation.
key_points: Praevia plus previous caesarean is the combination that should prompt the diagnosis
Plan birth at 34 to 36 weeks before labour or a large bleed forces the issue
Deliver through an incision away from the placenta and do not attempt separation
Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta in situ is the standard operation
Antenatal diagnosis and a planned team are the strongest predictors of outcome
explanation.pearls: Ask every woman with an anterior low placenta how many caesareans she has had, because the risk of accreta spectrum in the presence of praevia climbs from roughly 3 percent with one previous caesarean to more than 40 percent with three or more, and that single history question changes the ultrasound from routine to targeted.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Expectant management leaving the placenta in situ is reserved for women who strongly desire uterine preservation and accept a high rate of delayed haemorrhage, sepsis and eventual hysterectomy. Methotrexate does not hasten placental involution and is not recommended as part of that strategy. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Manual removal is the specific manoeuvre that converts a controlled operation into torrential haemorrhage when the villi are invading myometrium, and embolisation cannot keep pace with that rate of loss. Interventional radiology has a role in planned balloon occlusion, not as a rescue after avoidable bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

The imaging describes placenta accreta spectrum, where attempting to remove the placenta provokes catastrophic haemorrhage from vessels that cannot retract. Planned delivery before labour at a centre with the right team, with the placenta left in place and hysterectomy performed, gives the lowest maternal blood loss and morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Magnetic resonance imaging helps define posterior placentation or the extent of parametrial spread, but it does not outperform good ultrasound for the diagnosis itself and adds nothing when the sonographic signs are this clear. Deferring the plan wastes the planning time that determines the outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

Waiting to term in a woman who has already bled twice courts an emergency delivery out of hours without the assembled team, which is the setting in which most maternal deaths from this condition occur. The gestation is deliberately traded against that risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus without a primary rash, classically on the palms and soles and worse at night, and is confirmed by raised serum bile acids once other liver disease is excluded. The important shift in the last decade came from pooled individual patient data showing that stillbirth risk is not uniform across the condition: it is essentially background when bile acids are below 40 micromol/L, slightly elevated between 40 and 99, and rises sharply above 100 micromol/L, particularly after 35 weeks. Management therefore stratifies by concentration, with birth at 35 to 36 weeks for severe disease and closer to term for milder disease. Ursodeoxycholic acid remains reasonable for symptom relief but the randomised evidence shows it does not prevent perinatal death, so it must not be used as a reason to delay delivery.
key_points: Bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more define the high stillbirth risk group
Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks for that group, later for milder disease
Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itch but does not reduce perinatal death
Cardiotocography does not predict the sudden fetal death seen in this condition
Diagnosis requires exclusion of viral, autoimmune and structural liver disease
explanation.pearls: Take the bile acid sample non fasting, because postprandial values run higher and the risk thresholds published from the pooled data were derived largely from non fasting samples; a fasting level reported as 85 micromol/L may sit above 100 micromol/L after a meal and place the woman in a different management band.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Obstetric cholestasis

options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid improves pruritus and lowers biochemistry modestly but the large randomised trial found no reduction in perinatal death, preterm birth or neonatal unit admission. Treating the number rather than the risk delays the intervention that does change outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Stillbirth risk in this condition is concentrated in women whose bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more, in whom the risk rises steeply from the mid thirties of gestation, so birth is brought forward to 35 to 36 weeks. Below that concentration the risk approximates background and delivery can wait until closer to term. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Transaminase level correlates poorly with perinatal risk in this condition, whereas the bile acid concentration is the variable that tracks stillbirth. Using the wrong marker as the trigger leaves an already high risk pregnancy undelivered. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

There is no evidence that abdominal birth improves outcome in this condition, and immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes prematurity without a corresponding gain over waiting the short interval to 35 to 36 weeks. Induction is the usual route once the decision to deliver is made. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

Term delivery is appropriate for mild disease but not once bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L. Surveillance is the deeper problem here: stillbirth in this condition is a sudden arrhythmic event and a normal trace does not predict the next few days. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first five months after birth in a woman with no previously known cardiac disease. Multiple pregnancy, older maternal age, hypertensive disease and multiparity all increase risk. The presentation overlaps almost completely with normal late pregnancy and early postnatal symptoms, which is why the median time to diagnosis is measured in weeks, and the discriminating features are orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, a raised jugular venous pressure and hypoxaemia. Echocardiography confirms a reduced ejection fraction and excludes valvular and pericardial causes. Treatment follows standard heart failure principles adapted for breastfeeding, using furosemide, beta blockade and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor postnatally, with anticoagulation considered when the ejection fraction is severely reduced.
key_points: Presents from the last month of pregnancy to five months after birth
Orthopnoea and a raised jugular venous pressure separate it from deconditioning
Twins, older maternal age and hypertensive disease raise the risk
Echocardiography is the diagnostic test and should not wait for outpatient booking
Postnatal treatment uses agents compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Captopril, enalapril and quinapril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best breastfeeding safety data and should be chosen over perindopril or ramipril in a woman who wants to keep feeding, because being told to wean is a common reason women stop taking the drug that most improves their ejection fraction.

sources.label: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: Her haemoglobin has risen from 104 to 118 g/L, so anaemia is resolving while her symptoms are worsening, and anaemia does not raise the jugular venous pressure or produce upper lobe venous diversion. Attributing postnatal breathlessness to blood loss is the commonest reason this diagnosis is delayed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: She is afebrile with symmetrical basal crackles, oedema and a raised venous pressure, none of which fit infection, and the radiograph shows congestion rather than consolidation. Treating this as pneumonia sends home a woman in decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pulmonary embolism deserves consideration in any breathless postnatal woman, but orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, bilateral crackles and cardiomegaly with venous diversion point to a congested circulation rather than an obstructed one. Echocardiography will answer both questions faster. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Deconditioning does not cause orthopnoea, a raised venous pressure, hypoxaemia or an abnormal chest radiograph. Normalising these findings in a postnatal woman is precisely the pattern that turns a treatable cardiomyopathy into a late presentation. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: The clinical picture is pulmonary congestion with a raised venous pressure and radiographic changes, which requires imaging of ventricular function now and treatment of the congestion while that is arranged. Peripartum cardiomyopathy characteristically declares itself in the first month after birth and carries significant mortality if missed. (Source: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Heart Foundation of Australia: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined as four or more episodes in twelve months and affects around five to eight per cent of women of reproductive age. Confirming the diagnosis by culture rather than treating on symptoms alone is essential at this point, because the differential includes bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus and vulvodynia, and because species identification matters: Candida glabrata and Candida krusei are intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole and require boric acid pessaries or nystatin instead. Predisposing factors worth excluding are diabetes, immunosuppression, pregnancy, recent antibiotics and corticosteroid use, but most women with recurrent disease have none of them and it is better understood as an abnormal inflammatory response to normal vaginal colonisation. Treatment is an induction phase followed by six months of weekly suppression, which controls symptoms in around nine out of ten women during treatment, though roughly half relapse in the year after it stops and may need a further course. Partner treatment, bowel decolonisation and dietary sugar restriction have all been tested and do not work.
key_points: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease
Culture identifies non-albicans species that are intrinsically fluconazole resistant
Induction followed by six months of weekly suppression is the effective regimen
Around half relapse after treatment stops and may need a further course
Partner treatment and bowel decolonisation do not reduce recurrence
explanation.pearls: If the culture grows Candida glabrata rather than albicans, fluconazole will fail regardless of the regimen, and the usual next step is intravaginal boric acid 600 mg nightly for fourteen days, which is compounded rather than commercially available and is toxic if swallowed, so it must be labelled clearly and kept away from children.

sources.label: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Treating each episode as it arises is exactly what has been happening and has produced four episodes in a year, because a single dose clears the symptomatic infection without altering the propensity to recur. Episodic treatment is the correct approach for isolated infections, not for a recurrent pattern. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: This is not a sexually transmitted infection and randomised trials of treating the male partner show no reduction in recurrence for the woman, so partner treatment is reserved for a man with symptomatic balanitis. It also misses the need for a maintenance regimen. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles against this organism and as required use leaves the same episodic pattern in place. Topical azoles are a reasonable alternative to oral treatment where tablets cannot be used, but the regimen rather than the route is the problem here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

The idea that recurrence comes from a gastrointestinal reservoir was tested and abandoned, since oral nystatin does not reduce vaginal recurrence. The organism persists in the vagina at low density between episodes rather than being reintroduced from the bowel. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: Four or more culture confirmed episodes in twelve months defines recurrent disease, and the treatment that changes the pattern is an induction phase of three doses forty eight to seventy two hours apart followed by six months of weekly suppression, which keeps around ninety per cent of women free of symptoms while it is running. The culture confirming a fluconazole sensitive albicans species is what makes this regimen appropriate rather than a topical alternative. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

explanation.summary: A hydrosalpinx is a distally obstructed, dilated, fluid filled fallopian tube, most often the late consequence of pelvic inflammatory disease, and in Australia chlamydia is the usual antecedent, frequently asymptomatic at the time. It matters out of proportion to its size because the accumulated fluid intermittently refluxes into the uterine cavity, where it impairs implantation both mechanically and through its inflammatory and embryotoxic content, roughly halving live birth rates in assisted reproduction and approximately doubling miscarriage. Randomised evidence supports removing the affected tube, or occluding it proximally when dense adhesions make excision hazardous, before embryo transfer, and this restores success rates to those of comparable women without the condition. Surgical technique matters because dissection close to the tube preserves the mesosalpingeal blood supply to the ovary and avoids compromising ovarian reserve, which is a genuine concern when the woman will undergo ovarian stimulation afterwards. A hydrosalpinx large enough to be visible on ultrasound, rather than only on contrast imaging, appears to have the greatest adverse effect, and is the group in which the case for surgery is strongest.
key_points: A hydrosalpinx roughly halves live birth rates and doubles miscarriage in assisted reproduction
Fluid refluxing into the cavity is mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo
Salpingectomy, or proximal occlusion where adhesions prevent it, precedes embryo transfer
Aspiration gives only transient benefit because the fluid reaccumulates
Careful dissection close to the tube preserves the ovarian blood supply
explanation.pearls: The tube found to be diseased at surgery also carries a risk that outlasts the fertility question: women with tubal damage have a markedly increased chance that any future pregnancy is ectopic, so an early ultrasound at around six weeks is arranged for every subsequent pregnancy, including one conceived through assisted reproduction.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care
Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.rationale: A fluid filled obstructed tube roughly halves implantation and live birth rates in assisted reproduction and about doubles the miscarriage rate, because the fluid refluxes into the cavity and is both mechanically and biochemically hostile to the embryo. Removing the tube, or occluding it proximally where adhesions make removal unsafe, restores pregnancy rates to those of women without the condition, and it is done before transfer rather than after a failed cycle. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Proceeding without treating the tube spends a funded cycle at roughly half the expected success rate and exposes her to a higher miscarriage risk, when the intervention that corrects it is a single day procedure. Waiting for failure means the cycle is lost before the problem is addressed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Needle aspiration at the time of collection is easy and appealing but the fluid reaccumulates within days to weeks in most cases, so the benefit does not last through the implantation window, and it carries a risk of introducing infection into the pelvis. It is a fallback where surgery is refused or unsafe. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: The tubal damage here is the healed structural consequence of an infection cleared eleven years ago, and her current test is negative, so antibiotics cannot reopen a scarred and dilated tube. Antibiotic cover is used around instrumentation of the tract rather than as treatment for the damage itself. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care)
source_refs: Australian STI Management Guidelines for use in primary care

options.rationale: Opening the distal tube gives poor live birth rates when the tube is dilated and its lining destroyed, and it leaves a functionally useless conduit with a high risk of ectopic implantation and of the fluid simply reaccumulating. Reconstruction is considered only for mild disease in a woman declining assisted reproduction. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory vulval condition, commonest after menopause, that produces itch, pallor, fissuring and progressive architectural loss with resorption of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. First line treatment is an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, applied daily for an induction period and then titrated to the lowest frequency that maintains control, with long term maintenance reducing both symptoms and, on cohort evidence, the risk of malignant progression. The lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma in women with this condition is around two to five per cent, and it arises through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, which is human papillomavirus independent, occurs in older women and is much more aggressive than the usual human papillomavirus related type seen in younger women.
