The practical rule is that any focal area which is fixed, thickened, ulcerated, eroded, bleeding or simply not responding to adequate treatment is biopsied rather than re-treated. Lifelong review is recommended, and patients are taught to self examine and to present with any new lump, ulcer or bleeding rather than waiting for a scheduled appointment.
key_points: Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line, with long term maintenance
Lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma is around two to five per cent
Differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia is human papillomavirus independent and aggressive
Biopsy any area that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or unresponsive to adequate treatment
Adequate steroid use is confirmed by quantity used, not by the prescription alone
explanation.pearls: A useful adherence check in this condition is the quantity of ointment consumed: a 30 g tube should last roughly twelve weeks on maintenance and about four weeks during induction, so a patient whose disease is uncontrolled while a single tube has lasted a year is under-treated, whereas one who has used the expected amount and still has a focal lesion needs a biopsy.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Escalating the frequency is reasonable when the whole vulva is under-treated, but she has used adequate quantities and every other area has responded, so a single focal region that has not is behaving differently from the surrounding disease. A further eight weeks of topical treatment delays a diagnosis that is time critical. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Superimposed candidiasis is a genuine cause of persistent symptoms in women on long term ultrapotent steroid to the vulva, and it presents with itch, erythema and satellite lesions rather than a firm hyperkeratotic plaque, and her swab grew no Candida. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

A calcineurin inhibitor is a recognised second line agent for lichen sclerosus that fails corticosteroid, but it is relatively contraindicated in this setting because of theoretical concern about local immunosuppression in skin already at risk of squamous malignancy, and using it would suppress the signal being investigated. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Any area of lichen sclerosus that fails to respond to three months of adequately applied ultrapotent corticosteroid, or that is fixed, thickened, ulcerated or eroded, must be biopsied, because differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma arise on this background and can look like resistant disease. A punch biopsy taken from the thickest part of the abnormal area is the appropriate technique. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Ablative treatment destroys the tissue without providing histology, so an early invasive cancer would be both inadequately treated and rendered unstageable. Laser has no established role in lichen sclerosus and this option repeats the error of treating before diagnosing. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

explanation.summary: The assessment of an adnexal mass in a postmenopausal woman rests on combining ultrasound morphology, the CA125 concentration and menopausal status, conventionally through the risk of malignancy index, which multiplies an ultrasound feature score by a menopausal score by the marker value. Ultrasound features that raise concern are multilocularity, solid areas, papillary projections, bilateral lesions, ascites and intra-abdominal metastases, and a cyst with none of these scores zero. Simple unilocular anechoic cysts are common after menopause, are found in roughly one in five women on transvaginal scanning, and carry a risk of malignancy well below one per cent, so they are managed conservatively with a repeat scan rather than operated on. CA125 is unreliable in isolation because it is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and raised by endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, heart failure, liver disease and any peritoneal irritation, which is why it is never used as a screening test in the general population. Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre is indicated for a high index, because operating within such a centre improves staging quality and survival.
key_points: The risk index combines ultrasound score, menopausal status and the marker value
Simple unilocular anechoic cysts carry a malignancy risk well under one per cent
CA125 is normal in about half of stage 1 disease and is never used alone
Conservative surveillance with a repeat scan at four to six months is standard
A high index warrants referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgery
explanation.pearls: Tell her what to come back for rather than only when: persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal or pelvic pain and urinary urgency occurring on most days for more than a few weeks are the symptom cluster associated with ovarian cancer, and new symptoms of that kind matter more than the next scheduled scan.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: Referral to a specialist centre is reserved for a high risk of malignancy index or for ultrasound features suggesting malignancy, and her index is at the bottom of the scale with a completely simple cyst and a normal marker. Staging surgery for a benign simple cyst carries all the morbidity and none of the benefit. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Surgery is offered for symptomatic cysts, for cysts above about 5 cm that are enlarging or complex, or where the woman prefers it after discussion, and none of those apply to an asymptomatic simple cyst found incidentally. Oophorectomy also carries operative risk and is not required to make the diagnosis. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Simple unilocular anechoic cysts under about 5 to 10 cm in postmenopausal women carry a risk of malignancy well under one per cent, and with a normal marker the calculated risk index here is at the lowest level, so conservative surveillance is appropriate. Repeat imaging at four to six months confirms stability or resolution, and most such cysts resolve or remain unchanged. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for characterising a lesion that is indeterminate on ultrasound, particularly for distinguishing endometriomas, dermoids and fibroids, and this cyst is not indeterminate: it has every feature of a simple benign cyst. Additional imaging adds cost and anxiety without changing the plan. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: The marker is normal in around half of early stage ovarian cancers and is raised in many benign conditions, so it is never used alone to exclude malignancy and is interpreted only alongside the ultrasound morphology and menopausal status. One period of surveillance to confirm stability is what makes conservative management safe. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)

explanation.summary: A request for permanent contraception from a young woman without children tests the difference between counselling and gatekeeping. A competent adult can consent to sterilisation at any age in Australia, and refusing on the basis of age or parity is not clinically defensible, yet the doctor still owes her an accurate comparison of the options before referral. The comparison genuinely favours long-acting reversible methods on the numbers: the etonogestrel implant fails in roughly 0.05 per cent of users a year and intrauterine devices in about 0.1 to 0.8 per cent, against a cumulative ten year failure rate of around 1.9 per cent for tubal occlusion with the added risk that a pregnancy after the procedure is more likely to be ectopic. Regret after sterilisation is reported by around one in five women sterilised before the age of thirty compared with under one in twenty afterwards, and it is higher again after nulliparity and after a decision made around the time of a birth or a relationship change. Counselling covers permanence, the failure rate, the ectopic risk, the surgical risks and the alternatives including vasectomy, and if she still chooses the procedure after that, the referral is made without further obstruction.
key_points: A competent adult may consent to permanent contraception at any age in Australia
Implants and intrauterine devices match or beat tubal occlusion for effectiveness
Pregnancy occurring after tubal occlusion is more likely to be ectopic
Regret is higher when sterilisation occurs before thirty and after nulliparity
Counsel fully, then refer if she still chooses the procedure
explanation.pearls: If she proceeds to a tubal procedure, current Australian practice is complete removal of both tubes rather than clipping or ligation, because the distal tube is now understood to be the origin of most high grade serous ovarian cancers and salpingectomy at the time of another operation is the one accessible risk reducing step available to the general population.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.rationale: Referral without a comparison of the options is not respect for autonomy but an incomplete consent process, since a decision can only be informed if she knows that reversible methods match or beat the procedure for effectiveness. Referral remains entirely appropriate once that conversation has happened and she still wants it. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Long-acting reversible methods have failure rates of around 0.05 to 0.2 per cent a year, which equals or betters tubal occlusion, while avoiding a general anaesthetic and remaining reversible, and they solve the specific problem that is failing her now, which is a method requiring daily action. Recommending it is a clinical recommendation rather than a refusal: if she considers it and still wants a permanent procedure, she is referred. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

There is no age threshold for permanent contraception in Australia and a competent adult may consent to it, so refusing on age alone is paternalistic and has already driven her from two practices. Younger age and nulliparity are associated with higher rates of later regret, which is a reason to counsel carefully rather than to refuse. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper than tubal occlusion and deserves discussion, but it is his decision to make in his own consultation, and a method that depends on the relationship continuing does not protect her if it ends. It cannot be recommended as her contraceptive plan. (Source: Family Planning Australia)

Switching to another daily tablet ignores the reason her current method is failing, which is that she cannot reliably take a pill every day, and the progestogen only pill is less forgiving of late doses than the combined pill. It also causes irregular bleeding in a substantial proportion of users. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia describes fetal vessels running unsupported through the membranes over the internal os, typically arising from a velamentous cord insertion or connecting the lobes of a bilobed or succenturiate placenta. In vitro fertilisation, a low lying placenta in the second trimester and multiple pregnancy all raise the risk, which is why targeted transvaginal colour Doppler is performed when those features appear. When the diagnosis is missed, membrane rupture tears the vessels and the fetus exsanguinates into the vagina, with perinatal mortality historically above half. When it is made antenatally and birth is planned by caesarean before labour, survival exceeds 95 percent. Australian practice is corticosteroids and inpatient admission from around 32 weeks with delivery at 34 to 36 weeks, balancing prematurity against the unpredictable timing of membrane rupture.
key_points: Velamentous cord insertion and bilobed or succenturiate placentas are the substrates
Diagnosis is by transvaginal colour and pulsed wave Doppler confirming fetal vessels
Planned caesarean before labour at 34 to 36 weeks is the management
These vessels do not migrate away from the os as gestation advances
Antenatal diagnosis is the single variable that determines survival
explanation.pearls: Painless vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture with an immediate fetal bradycardia or a sinusoidal trace is fetal blood until proven otherwise and calls for immediate delivery, not for maternal resuscitation, because the mother is haemodynamically well while the baby is the one bleeding.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Vasa praevia

options.rationale: Waiting for bleeding means waiting for fetal haemorrhage, and even an immediate response in a fully staffed unit rarely reaches the baby in time because the total fetal blood volume at this gestation is only around 250 mL. Admission is to shorten the response time for the unexpected, not to be the plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Around a third of women labour or rupture membranes before 37 weeks, and this condition gives no warning and no time to intervene once that happens. Waiting to 39 weeks trades a modest gain in maturity for the specific catastrophe the diagnosis predicts. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Any plan involving labour exposes the vessels to spontaneous or artificial rupture, and controlled amniotomy does not protect vessels that tear with uterine activity or with the presenting part descending. Vaginal birth is not an option once these vessels are confirmed. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Unprotected fetal vessels overlying the os rupture when the membranes do, and the fetal blood volume is so small that exsanguination occurs within minutes. Planned abdominal birth before labour, with steroids and inpatient proximity to theatre, converts a condition with very high perinatal mortality into one with survival above 95 percent. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

options.rationale: Unlike a low lying placenta, which migrates as the lower segment forms, vessels running within the membranes do not move away from the os. Building a plan around resolution that does not occur risks the woman labouring while the decision is still open. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and vasa praevia

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates roughly one in 200 trials of labour after caesarean, and abnormal fetal heart rate patterns, usually a prolonged deceleration or bradycardia, are the presenting feature in the great majority. Classical teaching emphasises scar pain, but working epidurals mask it, so the reliable signs are fetal, haemodynamic and mechanical: sudden bradycardia, maternal tachycardia and hypotension out of proportion to visible loss, fresh vaginal bleeding, loss of the previously recorded station, and cessation of effective contractions. Recognition is the whole task, because the treatment is immediate laparotomy with delivery and repair or, occasionally, hysterectomy. Neonatal outcome deteriorates rapidly beyond about ten to twenty minutes from the onset of the bradycardia, so investigations that add minutes are themselves harmful.
key_points: Abnormal fetal heart rate is the commonest presenting sign of scar rupture
An epidural masks scar pain, so absence of pain is not reassuring
Loss of station and fresh bleeding with maternal tachycardia complete the picture
Immediate laparotomy is the treatment, not further fetal assessment
Contractions often become infrequent and the uterus feels soft after rupture
explanation.pearls: Recheck the station yourself rather than accepting the last documented value, because a presenting part that has risen between two examinations is close to specific for rupture and is the single finding most often missing from the notes of cases reviewed after a poor outcome.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is appropriate for a bradycardia caused by uterine hyperstimulation, but the tocograph shows infrequent contractions and a soft uterus, which is the opposite pattern. Spending ten minutes reassessing here uses up the interval in which the baby and the mother are salvageable. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Scalp sampling is invalid during a prolonged deceleration and requires several minutes that this situation does not have. It also answers the wrong question, since the maternal signs already indicate a surgical emergency independent of the fetal blood gas. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

She is not fully dilated and the presenting part has risen, so the prerequisites for instrumental birth are absent, and traction on a head that is being displaced by a ruptured uterus worsens the tear. The recent station is misleading because it describes where the head was before the event. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

A prolonged bradycardia with loss of station, fresh bleeding, maternal tachycardia and hypotension during a trial of labour is uterine rupture until proven otherwise, and the only treatment is immediate surgical delivery and repair. Maternal and fetal survival both fall sharply with every ten minutes of delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation is correct for a bradycardia caused by aortocaval compression or hypotension after an epidural top up, neither of which explains fresh bleeding and a presenting part that has risen. These measures delay the laparotomy that is the actual treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

explanation.summary: Twin to twin transfusion syndrome complicates about one in ten monochorionic pregnancies and arises from unbalanced arteriovenous anastomoses within the shared placenta. Diagnosis rests on the liquor discrepancy alone, defined in Australia as a deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other, and staging then follows the Quintero system: stage one is the liquor discrepancy, stage two adds a non visible donor bladder, stage three adds critically abnormal Dopplers, stage four hydrops and stage five death of either twin. Fetoscopic laser ablation divides the offending anastomoses and is the treatment of choice from about 16 to 26 weeks, with survival of at least one twin above 80 percent. Untreated advanced disease carries mortality above 90 percent, so recognition and immediate referral matter more than any bedside intervention.
key_points: Deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm in one sac and above 8 cm in the other defines the condition
A non visible donor bladder and abnormal Dopplers mark advancing Quintero stages
Fetoscopic laser ablation is first line between about 16 and 26 weeks
Amnioreduction gives worse survival and more neurological injury than laser
Selective growth restriction differs because liquor volumes remain normal
explanation.pearls: Establish chorionicity at the first trimester scan and record it in the handheld notes, because a lambda sign at 11 weeks excludes this condition entirely while a T sign commits the woman to fortnightly scanning from 16 weeks, and chorionicity cannot be reliably determined once the second trimester is well advanced.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Growth discordance surveillance is the pathway for selective fetal growth restriction, a different complication of a shared placenta in which liquor volumes stay normal. Here the liquor discrepancy with an absent and a distended bladder defines a condition that progresses over days. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Amnioreduction relieves the pressure and prolongs the pregnancy but leaves the anastomoses intact, so the randomised comparison showed worse survival and more neurological injury than laser. It is reserved for gestations beyond the laser window or where laser is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Delivery at 20 weeks is below the threshold of viability and guarantees the loss of both twins, so it cannot be the response to a treatable condition. Steroids have no role at this gestation. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Selective reduction is considered when one twin is already severely compromised or has a lethal anomaly and the other is at risk, not as first line when both twins are alive with a treatable vascular imbalance. It forfeits one healthy twin unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

options.rationale: Laser ablation treats the cause by dividing the vascular connections that drive the transfusion, and it gives higher survival and markedly lower neurological morbidity than drainage for disease at this stage and gestation. Australian practice is urgent referral to one of the small number of centres offering the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic twin pregnancy

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome follows gonadotrophin stimulation and is mediated by vascular endothelial growth factor released from luteinised granulosa cells, producing capillary leak with ascites, pleural effusions and intravascular depletion. Late onset disease appearing more than a week after retrieval is driven by endogenous human chorionic gonadotrophin from an implanting pregnancy and tends to be more severe and more prolonged than the early form. Severity is graded on symptoms, haematocrit, white cell count, renal function and the presence of tense ascites or hydrothorax. Management is supportive and rests on three pillars: intravascular volume replacement, thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin, and drainage of tense ascites, which relieves dyspnoea and often restores urine output by lowering intra abdominal pressure. Diuretics and surgery both make things worse in the absence of specific indications.
key_points: Capillary leak means intravascular depletion despite visible fluid overload
Late onset disease implies an implanting pregnancy and runs a longer course
Replace volume, anticoagulate, and drain tense ascites
Diuretics worsen haemoconcentration and renal impairment
Leucocytosis is part of the syndrome and does not indicate infection
explanation.pearls: Thrombosis in this syndrome occurs characteristically in the internal jugular and subclavian veins rather than the legs, and can appear weeks after the ascites has resolved, so neck or arm swelling in a woman who had a stimulated cycle in the past two months warrants imaging even if she now feels well.

options.rationale: The hyponatraemia here is dilutional and resolves with correction of the underlying leak, so hypertonic saline treats a number rather than the patient and risks overcorrection. Fluid restriction is directly contrary to the need to refill the intravascular space. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

Surgery on friable enlarged ovaries risks haemorrhage and rupture and does nothing for the ascites that is driving her symptoms. Operative intervention is reserved for torsion, rupture with bleeding, or an unrelated surgical diagnosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

Leucocytosis above 15 x10^9/L is characteristic of this syndrome itself and does not indicate infection in an afebrile woman with a clear ultrasound diagnosis. Antibiotics and further imaging delay the drainage and anticoagulation that change the course. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

Diuresis in a woman who is intravascularly depleted worsens the haemoconcentration and the acute kidney injury, even though she looks overloaded. Furosemide is considered only after the intravascular compartment has been restored and oliguria persists. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

The pathology is capillary leak with intravascular depletion despite total body fluid overload, so the circulation is refilled while the third space is drained to relieve pressure on the diaphragm and renal veins. Thromboprophylaxis is mandatory because haemoconcentration and high oestradiol make this one of the strongest acquired thrombotic states in gynaecology. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy alters the handling of most antiseizure medicines through increased volume of distribution, increased renal clearance, reduced protein binding and, for lamotrigine specifically, strong induction of uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase by rising oestrogen. Lamotrigine clearance can more than double by the third trimester, and the resulting fall in concentration is the commonest reason for seizure deterioration in an adherent woman. Australian practice is to establish a preconception target concentration in a woman who is seizure free, measure at least each trimester, and increase the dose to maintain that individual target rather than to a population range. Seizure control matters because convulsions carry risks of trauma, abruption, fetal hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and driving restrictions apply as they would outside pregnancy. Because clearance falls rapidly after birth, the dose must be brought back down over the first one to two weeks postpartum to avoid toxicity.
key_points: Oestrogen induced glucuronidation markedly increases lamotrigine clearance
Falling concentration is the usual cause of breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman
Set an individual preconception target and measure at least each trimester
Seizure risks to mother and fetus outweigh the risk of this drug
Reduce the dose over one to two weeks after birth as clearance falls
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum taper on the discharge plan at the time you increase the dose antenatally, because clearance returns towards baseline within days of delivery and a woman left on her third trimester dose typically presents at two weeks with ataxia, diplopia and vomiting from toxicity.

options.rationale: Oestrogen driven induction of glucuronidation increases lamotrigine clearance markedly from the first trimester, so the same dose produces falling concentrations and breakthrough seizures in an adherent woman. Dosing is adjusted upward against serial levels with a planned reduction in the days after birth as clearance returns to baseline. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Eclampsia requires hypertension or proteinuria or other features of the disease, and her blood pressure, urinalysis and reflexes are all normal with a known seizure disorder to explain the events. Magnesium is not a treatment for epilepsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Changing agent mid pregnancy exposes the fetus to two drugs during the transition and risks further seizures while neither is at an effective level. Levetiracetam is a reasonable preconception choice but is not the response to a predictable fall in concentration. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Adding a second agent increases fetal exposure and side effects without correcting the pharmacokinetic change that caused the breakthrough. The simpler and safer step is to restore the concentration that previously controlled her seizures. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Generalised convulsions carry maternal and fetal risks including trauma, hypoxia, placental abruption and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, all of which outweigh the risk of this drug, which has one of the lowest malformation rates in the class. Reducing the dose inverts the risk balance. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury complicates about 3 percent of vaginal births and up to 6 percent of first vaginal births, with forceps delivery the strongest modifiable risk factor. Counselling about a subsequent birth depends on two things: whether she has symptoms, and what the sphincter looks like and does on testing. A woman who is asymptomatic with a normal endoanal ultrasound and normal manometry can be supported to have a vaginal birth with a small risk of recurrence. A woman who is symptomatic, or who has a significant structural defect with abnormal pressures, should be advised that a further vaginal birth carries a substantial risk of worsening incontinence, and elective caesarean is recommended. All women with a previous severe tear should be assessed in a dedicated perineal clinic before the next birth rather than at the time of labour.
key_points: Forceps delivery is the strongest modifiable risk factor for sphincter injury
Symptoms plus an ultrasound defect and abnormal manometry favour abdominal birth
Asymptomatic women with normal tests may be supported for vaginal birth
Routine episiotomy does not protect a previously injured sphincter
Secondary repair is for completed families, not to enable a vaginal birth
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about loss of control of wind and about bowel urgency rather than about incontinence of stool, because women consistently under report this and the question phrased as faecal incontinence is answered no by the majority who in fact have symptoms that would change the birth plan.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Perineal care

options.rationale: A woman who remains symptomatic after a previous severe tear and who has both a structural defect and abnormal manometry faces a high risk of irreversible deterioration in continence with another vaginal birth. In that specific combination abdominal birth is the recommended option rather than one of several equivalents. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not protect a sphincter that is already deficient and adds its own morbidity, and the evidence for prophylactic episiotomy in this group is not supportive. It offers false reassurance in the highest risk situation. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Avoiding forceps lowers but does not remove the risk, and a further tear or simple stretching of a compromised sphincter can convert manageable urgency into daily faecal incontinence. This is reasonable counselling for a woman who is asymptomatic with normal tests, which she is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Sphincter repair is not performed in pregnancy, and its results deteriorate over time so it is reserved for women with disabling incontinence who have completed their families. It cannot be used to make a vaginal birth safe. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Six months of physiotherapy has already failed and nine further weeks will not repair a structural defect, while deferring the decision leaves her at risk of presenting in labour without a plan. Physiotherapy continues alongside the decision rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects roughly one in seven Australian women and the average delay from first symptom to diagnosis has historically been six to eight years, much of it spent being told that severe period pain is normal. The current Australian guideline explicitly abandons laparoscopy as the requirement for diagnosis: a clinical diagnosis can be made from the symptom pattern, and empirical treatment started, because a normal ultrasound excludes endometrioma and deep disease but says nothing about superficial peritoneal implants. First line treatment is a regular non-steroidal anti inflammatory taken from before the pain begins, combined with continuous hormonal suppression using a combined pill, a progestogen or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. Symptoms that persist after three to six months of adequate treatment prompt gynaecology referral, at which point laparoscopy becomes both diagnostic and therapeutic.
key_points: A normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal endometriosis
Clinical diagnosis and empirical treatment come before any surgery
Continuous rather than cyclical hormonal dosing suppresses symptom cycles
Non-steroidal anti inflammatory taken before the pain starts works better than after
Refer when three to six months of adequate medical treatment fails
explanation.pearls: Pain on opening the bowels or on passing urine that occurs only during menstruation is far more specific for endometriosis than the severity of the cramping itself, and asking that single cyclical question separates the teenagers who need treatment now from the much larger group with primary dysmenorrhoea.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Empirical medical treatment is first line in adolescents with symptoms suggesting endometriosis, because a normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal disease and a good response avoids surgery altogether. Continuous rather than cyclical dosing suppresses the menstruation that drives the pain. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is useful for mapping deep infiltrating disease before complex surgery, not for diagnosis in an adolescent who has not yet had medical treatment. A normal scan would not change the plan and an incidental finding could lead to unnecessary surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is no longer required to make the diagnosis, and operating on a teenager before medical treatment has been tried exposes her to surgical risk and to a negative result that does not exclude the condition. Surgery follows failed medical management, not precedes it. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: These agents are reserved for disease that has failed first line hormonal treatment, and in an adolescent they raise particular concern about bone mineral density during the years of peak accrual. Starting there skips several safer and effective steps. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.rationale: Pain causing regular school absence and pain on defaecation during menstruation are the features that separate this from ordinary period pain, and normalising them is why Australian women wait years for a diagnosis. Reassurance without treatment leaves a modifiable problem untreated. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

explanation.summary: Bleeding after the menopause carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma and always requires assessment. In women not on tamoxifen, transvaginal ultrasound is a valid first test and an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has a high negative predictive value, allowing some women to avoid instrumentation. Tamoxifen changes that calculus completely: it acts as a partial oestrogen agonist on the endometrium, producing polyps, hyperplasia, subendothelial cystic change and stromal oedema that thicken the measurement without indicating malignancy, while also roughly doubling to trebling the risk of carcinoma. There is no reliable sonographic cut off in these women, and the pathology is typically focal, so hysteroscopy with directed biopsy rather than blind sampling is the appropriate investigation. Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound for the same reason.
key_points: Postmenopausal bleeding carries about a one in ten risk of endometrial cancer
The 4 mm sonographic threshold does not apply to women taking tamoxifen
Tamoxifen related pathology is focal, so blind sampling can miss it
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the investigation of choice
Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened by ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Keep the tamoxifen going while the endometrium is investigated, and involve the treating oncologist before any decision to switch to an aromatase inhibitor, because in a postmenopausal woman that switch removes the endometrial risk but brings bone loss and arthralgia that need their own management plan.

options.rationale: A blind sample misses focal lesions, and tamoxifen associated pathology is characteristically focal within polyps, so a benign result cannot be accepted as excluding carcinoma. Hysteroscopy allows the lesion to be seen and sampled directly. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

The 4 mm threshold applies to women not taking this drug, and in any case exceeding it is an indication for biopsy rather than for repeat imaging. Rescanning a woman who is bleeding delays diagnosis by a further three months. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

Stopping adjuvant endocrine therapy for a hormone sensitive breast cancer has real oncological consequences and must not be done on the basis of bleeding that has not been investigated. The drug is usually continued while the endometrium is assessed. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

Tamoxifen produces subendometrial cystic change and stromal oedema that inflate the measured thickness and make sonographic thresholds unreliable, so imaging cannot be used to triage. Direct visualisation with targeted biopsy is required because this drug raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma and of polyps. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

No validated thickness threshold exists for women on this drug, and reporting a measurement as reassuring is the specific error the sonographic appearance invites. Bleeding after the menopause requires tissue whatever the number. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial cancer)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma and is the symptom that makes this the most curable of the gynaecological cancers, because it declares itself while disease is still confined to the uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is used as a triage tool rather than a diagnostic one: a thin regular endometrium at or below 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and permits observation, while anything above that threshold requires tissue. Obesity drives risk through peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrone in adipose tissue, producing unopposed oestrogen exposure, and diabetes and nulliparity compound it. Recurrent bleeding despite a reassuring initial assessment always warrants repeat investigation, because the negative predictive value applies to a single episode rather than to a pattern.
key_points: Endometrial thickness above 4 mm with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue sampling
A thickness at or below 4 mm with a single episode of bleeding permits observation
Obesity, diabetes, nulliparity and late menopause all raise endometrial cancer risk
Hysteroscopy adds direct visualisation and detects focal lesions that blind sampling misses
Recurrent bleeding after a reassuring scan mandates repeat assessment regardless
explanation.pearls: Around 90% of women with endometrial carcinoma present with abnormal bleeding, which is why any postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation within weeks, and why the 4 mm cut-off applies only to women not taking menopausal hormone therapy.

options.rationale: A thickness of 9 mm is already well above the threshold at which sampling is indicated, so repeating the same measurement cannot reclassify her. Interval imaging in this setting delays a diagnosis in which stage at presentation drives survival. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Progestogen therapy is a treatment for confirmed hyperplasia without atypia and may mask bleeding from an undiagnosed carcinoma. Treating the symptom before establishing the histology removes the only warning sign the patient has. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Cervical screening looks for a different disease at a different site and a negative human papillomavirus result does not address the endometrium at all. Her cervix is visibly healthy, so the bleeding source needs to be sought above the internal os. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

An endometrial thickness above 4 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue diagnosis, and at 9 mm with obesity and diabetes her risk of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma is substantial. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation as well as sampling, which matters because focal lesions can be missed by blind biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

CA125 is used in the assessment of an adnexal mass rather than of endometrial bleeding, and it is neither sensitive nor specific for early endometrial carcinoma. Using a normal result as a gate to referral would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cysts are found incidentally on a large proportion of pelvic scans in women of reproductive age, and most represent the normal physiology of follicular development or corpus luteum formation rather than disease. Sonographic characterisation does most of the diagnostic work: a unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation and no internal vascularity is described as simple and is effectively never malignant. Size then sets the follow-up, with the commonly used premenopausal thresholds being no follow-up below 50 mm, annual imaging between 50 and 70 mm, and further assessment with magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral above 70 mm where ultrasound cannot see the whole cyst. The important harm to avoid is overtreatment, since surgery on a young woman's ovary costs follicles permanently.
key_points: Simple premenopausal cysts under 50 mm need no follow-up imaging
Simple cysts of 50 to 70 mm are followed with yearly ultrasound
Cysts above 70 mm warrant magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral
The risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and misleads before menopause
Any solid component, thick septation or internal vascularity moves the cyst out of the simple category
explanation.pearls: A haemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst shows a characteristic lacy reticular internal pattern with no Doppler flow within the clot, and repeating the scan in the early follicular phase of the next cycle, around day 5 to 10, shows resolution and avoids an unnecessary referral.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Ovarian Cysts in Premenopausal Women

options.rationale: Surgery on a physiological cyst removes normal ovarian cortex and reduces ovarian reserve for no benefit, and carries operative and adhesion risk. Cystectomy is reserved for persistent symptomatic cysts, suspicious features or acute complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

Combined hormonal contraception reduces the incidence of new functional cysts over time but does not hasten resolution of one already present. Prescribing it as treatment for this finding implies the cyst needs treating, which it does not. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

Repeat imaging is reserved for simple cysts between 50 and 70 mm, which are followed yearly, and for any cyst with complex features. Scanning a 42 mm simple cyst generates incidental findings and anxiety without changing management. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

The risk of malignancy index is validated in postmenopausal women and performs poorly before menopause, where CA125 rises with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and pelvic inflammation. Applying it to a simple cyst in a young woman generates false positives and unnecessary surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

A simple unilocular cyst under 50 mm in a premenopausal woman is a physiological finding that resolves spontaneously in the great majority of cases and carries no malignant potential. Australian and international guidance is explicit that cysts of this size and appearance need no follow-up imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy to supply expanded maternal red cell mass, the fetus and the placenta, and a short interpregnancy interval means stores have had little chance to recover. Ferritin is the best single measure of iron stores but is an acute phase reactant, so a normal or raised value alongside a normal C-reactive protein is interpretable while a raised value with inflammation is not. Treatment matters beyond maternal symptoms, because antenatal iron deficiency is associated with low birth weight, preterm birth and reduced neonatal iron endowment that affects infant development. The hepcidin response to an oral dose suppresses absorption for around 24 hours, which is the physiological basis for alternate-day rather than divided daily dosing.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms/L indicates deficiency even when haemoglobin is only mildly reduced
Oral iron on alternate days is absorbed more efficiently than the same total dose split daily
Take iron away from food, tea, coffee and calcium, with vitamin C to aid absorption
Intravenous iron is for oral failure, intolerance, malabsorption or late gestation
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so interpret it alongside C-reactive protein
explanation.pearls: Expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L within 2 to 4 weeks of starting adequate oral iron, and treat failure to achieve that as a trigger to check adherence and reconsider the diagnosis rather than simply escalating the dose.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when absorption is impaired, or when the gestation is too advanced for an oral response. At 20 weeks with no oral trial yet, it commits her to an infusion and its risks unnecessarily. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Diet cannot replete established deficiency within the timeframe of a pregnancy, and non-haem iron from a vegetarian diet is absorbed less efficiently than haem iron. Dietary advice belongs alongside supplementation rather than instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

A ferritin below 30 micrograms/L confirms depleted stores and oral iron is first line in the second trimester when there is time to respond before delivery. Alternate-day dosing produces greater fractional absorption than daily dosing because it avoids the hepcidin rise that a dose triggers for the following 24 hours. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Divided daily dosing raises hepcidin and reduces the fraction absorbed from each subsequent dose, and taking iron with food further impairs uptake through phytate and calcium binding. The problem is dose frequency and timing rather than the drug itself. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Folate and B12 deficiency cause macrocytosis rather than the microcytosis present here, and B12 is worth checking in a vegetarian but does not explain these indices. Deferring iron for a fortnight while a parallel test returns wastes treatment time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's physical, social and emotional quality of life rather than by a measured volume, so the history of flooding, clots and time off work is the diagnosis. The PALM-COEIN system separates structural causes, which are polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy, from non-structural ones including coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial and iatrogenic causes, and it directs the workup. A normal ultrasound with regular ovulatory cycles points to a primary endometrial disorder of haemostasis, which is the setting in which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system performs best. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of these women and must be treated alongside the bleeding rather than assumed to resolve with it.
key_points: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by quality of life impact, not by measured millilitres
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line when the cavity is structurally normal
Tranexamic acid and non-steroidal agents are non-hormonal options for women avoiding hormones or seeking pregnancy
Short luteal-phase progestogen courses are ineffective for heavy bleeding
Treat coexisting iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Around one in five women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche has an underlying bleeding disorder, most commonly von Willebrand disease, so bleeding that dates from the very first period warrants a coagulation screen and von Willebrand studies rather than empirical treatment alone.

options.rationale: Non-steroidal agents reduce blood loss by around a fifth and help dysmenorrhoea, making them useful adjuncts, but they are the weakest of the medical options for volume. Used alone they are unlikely to correct bleeding severe enough to cause this degree of iron depletion. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Long-course oral progestogen does reduce bleeding but requires daily tablets for three weeks of every cycle, is poorly tolerated and is less effective than an intrauterine device. Short luteal-phase courses are ineffective and should not be used at all. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Ablation is effective but is a surgical procedure that mandates reliable contraception afterwards because pregnancy following ablation carries serious risk. It is considered after medical therapy has failed rather than before it has been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss more than any other medical therapy and is first line for heavy bleeding with a structurally normal cavity. It simultaneously provides the contraception she wants without committing her to a permanent procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a reasonable option for a woman wanting non-hormonal treatment or trying to conceive, but the magnitude of benefit is smaller and it provides no contraception. It is the alternative when an intrauterine device is declined or unsuitable. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary human papillomavirus testing every five years from age 25 to 74, with partial genotyping that separates types 16 and 18 from the other oncogenic types. That split exists because 16 and 18 cause around 70% of cervical cancers and carry a much higher risk of prevalent high grade disease, so they are referred to colposcopy immediately while the other types are triaged on cytology. Self collection is now available to every screening participant as a way of reaching women who have been under-screened, and its performance for high grade disease is equivalent to clinician collection. Reflex cytology cannot be performed on a self collected vaginal sample, so a woman needing cytology triage must return for a clinician collected specimen, but that requirement does not apply when the result is type 16 or 18.
key_points: Human papillomavirus 16 or 18 detected means direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types are triaged with reflex cytology and often repeated at 12 months
Self collection has equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease and is available to all participants
Reflex cytology is not possible on a self collected sample, so cytology triage needs a clinician collected one
Under-screened women carry the highest burden of cervical cancer in Australia
explanation.pearls: Cervical screening starts at 25 years or two years after first sexual activity if later, and in Australia any symptomatic woman with abnormal bleeding or postcoital bleeding needs a co-test with cytology and speculum examination regardless of when she last screened.

options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to women with oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 whose reflex cytology is negative or low grade. Applying it to a type 16 result in a woman screened once in eleven years risks allowing established high grade disease to progress. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Detection of human papillomavirus type 16 or 18 leads straight to colposcopy regardless of cytology, because these two types account for the large majority of cervical cancers and confer the highest immediate risk of high grade disease. The absence of reflex cytology on a self collected sample does not alter that pathway. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Vaccination is prophylactic and does not clear an infection that is already established or treat existing cervical disease. Offering it as an alternative to assessment misapplies a preventive intervention to a diagnostic problem. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Self collected samples tested with a polymerase chain reaction assay have equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease to clinician collected samples, so the result does not need confirmation. Repeating it duplicates a reliable test and postpones definitive assessment. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

Cytology triage determines management for the other oncogenic types, where a negative or low grade result allows a 12-month repeat, but types 16 and 18 bypass that triage entirely. Waiting on cytology here would delay colposcopy without any possibility of changing the destination. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer is the gynaecological malignancy with the poorest survival in Australia, largely because the early symptoms of bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency and abdominal pain are non-specific and commonly attributed to gastrointestinal causes for months. The risk of malignancy index multiplies a menopausal score, an ultrasound morphology score and the CA125 value, and a result above 200 is the accepted trigger for referral to a gynaecological oncology service. The reason the destination matters so much is that survival correlates strongly with the completeness of cytoreduction, which requires a surgeon able to perform bowel resection, splenectomy and diaphragmatic stripping as needed. Where disease is too extensive for primary debulking, neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval surgery is the alternative, and that decision is made by the multidisciplinary team rather than at the point of referral.
key_points: A risk of malignancy index above 200 mandates gynaecological oncology referral
The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology score and CA125
Survival improves when surgery is performed by a subspecialist in a specialist centre
Bloating, early satiety and abdominal pain lasting weeks warrant investigation in women over 50
Completeness of cytoreduction is the strongest surgical determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Any woman diagnosed with high grade serous ovarian cancer in Australia should be offered germline and tumour BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing at diagnosis, because a pathogenic variant both opens access to PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy and triggers cascade testing of her relatives.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when ultrasound findings are indeterminate and the mass could be a fibroid, an endometrioma or a dermoid, which is not the case here. Adding a fourth imaging study to an already convincing picture only delays referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

Ascitic cytology can be useful when neoadjuvant chemotherapy is being considered and a tissue diagnosis is needed without surgery, but that decision belongs to the oncology team. A negative cytology does not exclude malignancy, so a normal result would not change the referral. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Her risk of malignancy index is far above the threshold of 200 that mandates specialist referral, combining a postmenopausal score, a CA125 of 640 kU/L and multiple suspicious ultrasound features. Survival is measurably better when cytoreductive surgery for ovarian cancer is performed by a subspecialist in a centre with the full multidisciplinary team. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

Serial CA125 has a role in monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, not in deciding whether to investigate a suspicious mass. A six week delay in a woman with ascites and omental disease allows measurable progression. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Operating locally on a likely advanced ovarian malignancy risks incomplete staging, tumour rupture with upstaging, and port site seeding, and a general list cannot deliver the debulking these women need. Speed is valuable but does not compensate for the wrong operation in the wrong place. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

explanation.summary: CA125 is a glycoprotein shed by mesothelial and Mullerian epithelium under almost any inflammatory stimulus, so its specificity for ovarian cancer is poor in premenopausal women and good only after menopause, when the benign causes largely disappear. That difference is why the risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and why applying it to a young woman with endometriosis produces a false alarm. The sonographic appearance carries far more weight than the marker: an endometrioma shows homogeneous low level ground glass echoes with no solid component and no internal Doppler flow, and site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility on the probe add to the picture. Managing this woman well means addressing pain and subfertility together, since surgical excision of an endometrioma removes healthy cortex and can lower ovarian reserve, so the decision to operate is weighed against assisted reproduction.
key_points: CA125 rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation and pregnancy
The risk of malignancy index is validated after menopause and misleads before it
Ground glass internal echoes with no solid component or vascularity characterise an endometrioma
Site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility indicate adhesive pelvic disease
Endometrioma excision can reduce ovarian reserve, so weigh surgery against assisted reproduction
explanation.pearls: Ovarian endometriomas larger than 3 cm reduce antral follicle count in the affected ovary even before surgery, so an anti-Mullerian hormone level measured before any planned cystectomy gives the couple a realistic baseline for counselling about fertility outcomes.

options.rationale: Aspiration of an endometrioma yields old altered blood that is unhelpful cytologically, and recurrence after aspiration alone approaches certainty. Puncturing a cyst that has not been excluded as malignant also risks peritoneal spill. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

CA125 is expressed by any inflamed coelomic epithelium, so endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, menstruation and pregnancy all raise it, and the risk of malignancy index is not validated before menopause. The ground glass appearance without vascularity and the fixed tender pelvis describe an endometrioma in a woman whose pressing clinical problem is subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

CA125 fluctuates with the menstrual cycle and with disease activity in endometriosis, so serial values in this setting generate noise rather than information. There is no threshold or trajectory that would reclassify a sonographically benign endometrioma. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

Subspecialist referral is driven by a high risk of malignancy index in a postmenopausal woman or by suspicious morphology such as solid papillary projections, thick septations, vascularity or ascites, none of which is present. Referring on the marker alone would subject a young woman to oncological surgery for benign disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

Medical suppression reduces endometriosis-associated pain but induces a hypo-oestrogenic state that prevents conception, which directly opposes her goal of pregnancy. It also shrinks endometriomas only modestly and they recur on cessation. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome results from a germline pathogenic variant in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2, or in EPCAM, and it substantially raises lifetime risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial and other cancers. Endometrial cancer precedes the colorectal cancer in a large share of affected women, which makes the gynaecologist the person most likely to make the diagnosis for the whole family. Testing follows a sequence: immunohistochemistry or microsatellite instability testing on tumour tissue, then MLH1 promoter methylation analysis when MLH1 and PMS2 are both lost to distinguish sporadic epigenetic silencing from inherited disease, and finally germline testing. Identifying a variant changes management for the patient through colonoscopic surveillance and aspirin chemoprophylaxis, and for relatives through cascade testing and risk-reducing surgery.
key_points: Endometrial cancer is the sentinel cancer in about half of women with Lynch syndrome
Tumour mismatch repair immunohistochemistry is the first triage test and uses existing tissue
Loss of MLH1 and PMS2 needs promoter methylation testing to separate sporadic from inherited causes
Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted through either parent
Confirmation triggers colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin prophylaxis and cascade family testing
explanation.pearls: Regular aspirin reduces colorectal cancer incidence in Lynch syndrome by around half with the benefit emerging after several years of use, which is why it is offered to confirmed carriers alongside one to two yearly colonoscopy starting at 25 years for MLH1 and MSH2 carriers.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted equally through the paternal line, so a father with early bowel cancer is as informative as a mother would be. This is a common misconception about gynaecological cancer risk that leads to missed diagnoses. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

Endometrial cancer is the sentinel malignancy in around half of women with Lynch syndrome, and her age under 50 with a father and aunt affected by Lynch spectrum cancers raises that possibility strongly. Immunohistochemistry for the four mismatch repair proteins on existing tumour tissue is the standard first triage test and requires no new sample. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

Germline testing is the confirmatory step and is appropriate once tumour triage suggests mismatch repair deficiency or when family history alone is compelling enough to bypass triage. Going straight to a blood panel in every case tests many women whose tumours are mismatch repair proficient. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

Grade 1 disease with superficial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion is low risk and does not usually require adjuvant radiotherapy at all. The genetic question is independent of adjuvant treatment and should not be deferred behind it. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Colonoscopic surveillance is exactly what a confirmed diagnosis would trigger, but the interval and starting age depend on which gene is involved, and testing unaffected daughters before the family variant is known is uninformative. The sequence runs from tumour to germline to cascade testing. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

explanation.summary: Antenatal iron deficiency anaemia matters most for what it does to a woman's tolerance of blood loss at delivery, since postpartum haemorrhage is common and a woman entering labour with a haemoglobin of 86 g/L has no reserve. Intravenous iron preparations such as ferric carboxymaltose deliver a large replacement dose in a single short infusion and are established as safe after the first trimester, with the main issues being transient hypophosphataemia, infusion reactions and skin staining from extravasation. The threshold for moving from oral to intravenous therapy is set by intolerance, malabsorption, failure to respond, severity of the anaemia, and how much time remains before delivery. A low lying placenta adds weight to correcting the anaemia early, because it raises the probability of significant peripartum bleeding.
key_points: Intravenous iron is indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption, non-response or late gestation
It is considered safe from the second trimester onwards
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, active bleeding or severe symptomatic anaemia near delivery
Antenatal anaemia reduces tolerance of postpartum haemorrhage and increases transfusion need
Confirm the diagnosis with ferritin plus C-reactive protein before infusing
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes transient hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority of recipients, so a woman needing repeat infusions or reporting persistent bone pain or weakness afterwards should have a serum phosphate checked rather than being given more iron.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Erythropoiesis stimulating agents are used in anaemia of chronic kidney disease rather than in uncomplicated iron deficiency, where the limiting factor is substrate rather than erythropoietin. Giving it alongside oral iron she cannot absorb compounds the error. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Two preparations have already failed for the same reason, and taking iron with food to reduce symptoms substantially reduces the fraction absorbed. Persisting orally spends weeks she does not have before delivery. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia near delivery, active bleeding or haemodynamic compromise, and it carries alloimmunisation risk that matters in a woman who may have further pregnancies. She is stable, so iron replacement is the correct pathway. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.rationale: The diagnosis is already secure with a microcytic anaemia, a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L and a normal C-reactive protein, so repeat testing adds nothing. Four weeks of observation takes her to 34 weeks with untreated severe anaemia and a possible placenta praevia. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

She has documented intolerance of two oral preparations, a haemoglobin of 86 g/L and only ten weeks left, which is too little time for oral therapy to correct stores even if she could take it. Intravenous iron is safe from the second trimester onwards and raises haemoglobin faster and more completely than oral replacement. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Fibroid management is driven by location far more than by size, which is why the submucosal, intramural and subserosal distinction and the degree of intracavitary extension determine the operation. Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity and disrupt the endometrium, producing heavy bleeding and interfering with implantation, and they are the group for which removal has the clearest fertility benefit. Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is needed to grade the intracavitary component because standard ultrasound often cannot tell an intramural fibroid indenting the cavity from a true submucosal one. Where more than half the fibroid lies within the cavity the lesion can usually be resected in a single hysteroscopic procedure, whereas a deeper lesion may need a staged approach to avoid perforation and excessive fluid absorption.
key_points: Location rather than size determines the operative approach to fibroids
Submucosal fibroids cause heavy bleeding and impair implantation
Saline infusion sonohysterography grades the intracavitary component before surgery
Hysteroscopic resection avoids a myometrial incision and preserves the uterus for pregnancy
Embolisation and ablation are both unsuitable when future fertility is desired
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit is monitored continuously during hysteroscopic resection because absorption of hypotonic distension medium causes dilutional hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema, and the procedure is stopped at a deficit of around 1000 mL with hypotonic fluid in a healthy woman.

options.rationale: A submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume in the cavity is accessible transcervically, and hysteroscopic resection removes it without any uterine incision, preserving the myometrium for a future pregnancy. Submucosal fibroids are the subtype with the clearest adverse effect on both bleeding and implantation, so removal addresses her two problems together. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

Agonist therapy shrinks fibroids and corrects anaemia before surgery, which is a legitimate adjunct, but the effect reverses on cessation and the drug prevents conception while it is given. It is preparation for an operation rather than a definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

Abdominal or laparoscopic myomectomy is the approach for intramural and subserosal fibroids that cannot be reached from the cavity, and it creates a myometrial scar that raises the small risk of uterine rupture in labour. Choosing it for a predominantly intracavitary fibroid imposes an unnecessary uterine incision. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

Ablation destroys the endometrium and is absolutely contraindicated in a woman planning pregnancy, since subsequent conception carries high rates of abnormal placentation and loss. It also performs poorly when the cavity is distorted by a submucosal fibroid. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms but is relatively contraindicated when future fertility is desired, because of effects on ovarian reserve and on placentation. A submucosal fibroid can also slough after embolisation and cause prolonged discharge or infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is the gynaecological emergency most often missed, and the single commonest reason is misplaced confidence in Doppler ultrasound. The ovary receives blood from both the ovarian artery and the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, so arterial flow is frequently still detectable in a torted ovary, and because the thin walled veins and lymphatics obstruct before the arteries do, the earliest and most reliable sonographic sign is unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema rather than absent flow. Most torsion occurs around a lead point, typically a benign cyst or dermoid between 5 and 10 cm, since very large masses are less mobile and small ovaries rarely twist. Management has shifted decisively towards conservative detorsion even when the ovary appears necrotic, because gross appearance correlates poorly with recoverable function and the risk of thromboembolism from untwisting has not been borne out.
key_points: Present Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because of the dual arterial supply
Unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema is the more reliable sonographic sign
Waxing and waning severe pain suggests intermittent torsion and should not reassure
A lead point mass of 5 to 10 cm is the usual precipitant
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy even for a dusky ovary
explanation.pearls: Oophoropexy is considered after detorsion when there is no lead point mass, when torsion is recurrent, or when the contralateral ovary has already been lost, since the underlying problem in those cases is an abnormally long utero-ovarian ligament rather than the mass itself.

options.rationale: Waiting for arterial flow to disappear means waiting for the ovary to infarct, since loss of arterial signal is a late finding rather than the diagnostic threshold. The waxing and waning pain characteristic of intermittent torsion is precisely the window in which surgery preserves the ovary. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

Appendicitis is a reasonable differential given the right sided pain and mild inflammatory response, but the ultrasound has already identified an enlarged oedematous ovary containing a known mass, which explains the presentation. Imaging that irradiates a young woman while the ovary twists trades a small diagnostic gain for a large time cost. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

Magnetic resonance imaging can show ovarian oedema and a twisted pedicle, but obtaining it out of hours is slow and it changes nothing about the need for surgery in a patient with this history and these findings. No imaging result would make observation safe. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

Preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because the ovary has a dual blood supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries and venous and lymphatic obstruction precede arterial compromise, producing the oedematous enlargement seen here. Torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis, and untwisting rather than removing the ovary is now standard because the great majority regain function even when the ovary looks dusky. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

Pelvic inflammatory disease typically produces bilateral pain with cervical motion tenderness, discharge and a more indolent onset rather than abrupt pain during exertion with vomiting. The mildly raised white cell count here reflects the stress response and tissue ischaemia rather than infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen acts as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, antagonising the receptor in breast tissue while behaving as a partial agonist in the endometrium, which is why it both reduces breast cancer recurrence and raises endometrial cancer risk several-fold in postmenopausal women. It characteristically produces subendometrial stromal hypertrophy with cystic change, endometrial polyps and adenomyotic change, all of which thicken and distort the sonographic endometrial stripe without any malignancy being present. The practical consequence is that the 4 mm triage threshold, which depends on a thin uniform endometrium having a high negative predictive value, breaks down entirely in these women, and ultrasound cannot be used to decide who needs sampling. Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound for the same reason, since it generates procedures without improving outcomes, but any bleeding is investigated promptly.
key_points: Tamoxifen is an endometrial partial agonist and raises endometrial cancer risk after menopause
It causes subendometrial cystic change that invalidates the usual thickness threshold
