Any bleeding on tamoxifen requires hysteroscopy and directed biopsy, not ultrasound triage
Lesions are often focal polyps, so blind sampling can miss them
Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole do not carry the endometrial risk of tamoxifen because they lower oestrogen synthesis rather than acting at the receptor, which is one reason a postmenopausal woman who develops endometrial pathology on tamoxifen is often switched rather than simply monitored.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Switching to an aromatase inhibitor removes the endometrial stimulus and may well be discussed once the histology is known, but changing adjuvant breast cancer therapy does not investigate the bleeding that has already occurred. The sequence is to obtain tissue first and involve the oncologist afterwards. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial stromal cystic change that inflates the sonographic measurement and blurs the interface, so the thickness threshold used in other postmenopausal women is not valid and cannot be used to triage her. Hysteroscopy allows the cavity to be seen directly and focal lesions to be sampled under vision, which blind sampling would miss. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Magnetic resonance imaging stages a carcinoma that has already been diagnosed histologically and cannot distinguish benign tamoxifen change from malignancy. Using it as a diagnostic filter ahead of tissue reverses the order of assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: The sonographic appearance is indeed a recognised tamoxifen effect, but she has bled, and bleeding is the symptom that demands tissue regardless of how well the imaging is explained. Attributing a symptom to a known drug effect without excluding malignancy is the central error in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

Blind pipelle sampling detects diffuse disease well but samples only a fraction of the cavity, and the lesions tamoxifen causes are characteristically focal polyps rather than a uniform process. A benign pipelle result would therefore not exclude a focal carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia in pregnancy is so commonly due to iron deficiency that the diagnosis is often assumed, but ferritin with a concurrent C-reactive protein separates the two causes reliably, and a normal or high ferritin redirects the workup to haemoglobinopathy. Several features point that way here: the degree of microcytosis is out of proportion to the modest fall in haemoglobin, the red cell count is raised rather than reduced, the Mentzer index falls well below 13, and iron therapy previously failed. Beta thalassaemia trait carries little consequence for the woman herself, but if her partner also carries a beta variant each pregnancy has a one in four chance of transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia major. That is why partner testing is urgent rather than routine, since chorionic villus sampling is available from around 11 weeks and amniocentesis from 15 weeks, and the counselling that precedes either takes time.
key_points: Ferritin with C-reactive protein distinguishes iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait
Disproportionate microcytosis with a raised red cell count suggests a haemoglobinopathy
Previous failure of iron therapy is a strong historical clue
Partner testing is urgent because prenatal diagnostic options are time limited
Alpha thalassaemia may need DNA studies because electrophoresis can be normal in carriers
explanation.pearls: The Mentzer index, the mean cell volume divided by the red cell count, is below 13 in thalassaemia trait and above 13 in iron deficiency, and here it is about 11, which flags the diagnosis from the full blood count alone before any specialised test is ordered.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.rationale: Sequential testing is standard in many settings but costs weeks at exactly the point in pregnancy when chorionic villus sampling remains an option. Timing matters: with ancestry pointing to risk on both sides, parallel testing preserves the full range of reproductive choices. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.rationale: A ferritin of 96 micrograms/L with a normal C-reactive protein excludes iron deficiency as the cause of a mean cell volume of 64 fL, and a raised red cell count with disproportionate microcytosis is the classic thalassaemia trait picture. Because both partners have ancestry from high prevalence regions, partner testing must happen in parallel so that prenatal diagnosis remains available within the first trimester if both carry a variant. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.rationale: A film showing target cells and basophilic stippling would support the suspicion but adds little to indices this characteristic, and reticulocytes do not discriminate. Deferring to 28 weeks removes every prenatal diagnostic option the couple might want. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

Non-invasive prenatal testing screens for common aneuploidies and does not detect haemoglobinopathies in routine Australian practice. Offering it here substitutes an unrelated screening test for carrier testing of the parents. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.rationale: Her stores are replete, so giving iron cannot raise the haemoglobin and repeats the failed teenage trial she has already described. Continued supplementation in a thalassaemia carrier risks iron overload over time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmissible protozoal infection that is far more common in remote and regional Australian communities than in metropolitan populations, and nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced wet mount microscopy because its sensitivity is much higher. In pregnancy it is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, although treatment has not been shown to reverse that risk, so the indication for treating is symptom relief and interruption of transmission. Metronidazole is the drug of choice in every trimester and while breastfeeding. Partner treatment without the need for the partner to be tested is standard, and patients should be advised to avoid sex until 7 days after both have completed therapy. A positive result should prompt a full sexually transmissible infection screen, since coinfection is common.
key_points: Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days is preferred over single-dose therapy because of higher cure rates
Metronidazole is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy and during breastfeeding
Treat partners empirically without waiting for their test results and advise no sex for 7 days after both finish
Tinidazole is a second-line alternative outside pregnancy, not a pregnancy option
A positive result should prompt screening for other sexually transmissible infections
explanation.pearls: Vaginal pH is the fastest bedside discriminator: candidiasis sits below 4.5, while trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis both run above 4.5, so a normal pH essentially excludes trichomoniasis.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Tinidazole is effective against Trichomonas vaginalis but Australian product information advises against its use in pregnancy because human safety data are far thinner than for metronidazole. It is the acceptable alternative outside pregnancy when metronidazole fails. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Clotrimazole treats candidiasis, which presents with a thick white discharge and a vaginal pH below 4.5 rather than the frothy discharge and pH of 5.5 here, and it has poor activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A 7-day oral metronidazole course is the preferred Australian regimen because cure rates exceed those of single-dose therapy, particularly in women with human immunodeficiency virus and in pregnancy, and metronidazole is regarded as safe in all trimesters. Concurrent partner treatment is essential since reinfection is otherwise the rule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Single-dose metronidazole is an accepted option where adherence is a concern, but randomised data show higher rates of treatment failure than the 7-day course, which is why the longer regimen is preferred. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Deferring treatment leaves symptoms untreated and leaves the infection transmissible, and metronidazole has a long record of safe use across pregnancy including the first trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined by four or more episodes in 12 months, and the diagnosis requires culture confirmation because up to half of women who self-treat for thrush have another cause such as dermatitis, lichen sclerosus or bacterial vaginosis. Speciation matters because Candida glabrata and Candida krusei respond poorly to fluconazole. The recognised contributors worth excluding are poorly controlled diabetes, immunosuppression, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and high-dose oestrogen exposure. Management is a fluconazole induction phase followed by 6 months of weekly suppression, with counselling that relapse after cessation is common. Partner treatment is not indicated for candidiasis, which distinguishes it clearly from trichomoniasis.
key_points: Four or more culture-confirmed episodes in 12 months defines the recurrent form
Induction with three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart, then weekly suppression for 6 months
Speciate before treating, since Candida glabrata needs boric acid or nystatin rather than fluconazole
Exclude diabetes, immunosuppression and recent antibiotics as contributors
Partner treatment is not indicated, unlike in trichomoniasis
explanation.pearls: Fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy at any dose above a single 150 mg exposure, so pregnant women with recurrent disease are suppressed with topical clotrimazole instead; check the pregnancy test before writing a 6-month oral script.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.rationale: Four or more culture-proven episodes in a year defines recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, which is managed with an induction phase of three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart followed by weekly suppression for 6 months. Around 90 per cent of women remain free of symptoms while on suppression, although roughly half relapse after it stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.rationale: Single-dose treatment of each episode is appropriate for sporadic candidiasis but does nothing to break the recurrence cycle, which is the actual problem once four or more episodes occur in a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Boric acid is reserved for non-albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, which is intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole; the culture here confirms Candida albicans, for which azoles remain the right class. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles for vulvovaginal candidiasis and, like any single course, treats the current episode without addressing recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Topical suppression timed to the menstrual cycle is a second-line option when oral therapy is contraindicated or refused, but oral fluconazole suppression has better evidence and much better adherence. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts that can obstruct, producing a cyst that may then become infected. Most abscesses are polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora rather than being sexually transmitted, but gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing is still performed because they are recoverable in a minority. Definitive management aims to create a permanent drainage tract rather than simply emptying the cavity, which is why the Word catheter and marsupialisation outperform simple incision. A new Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 raises the possibility of a vulval or Bartholin gland carcinoma and warrants biopsy rather than blind drainage. Antibiotics are an adjunct, indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunosuppression or pregnancy.
key_points: Word catheter insertion after incision creates an epithelialised tract and is first-line for a first abscess
The catheter stays in place for 4 to 6 weeks; simple incision alone recurs frequently
Marsupialisation and gland excision are escalation options, not first-line choices
Antibiotics are adjunctive and indicated for cellulitis, systemic illness, immunosuppression or pregnancy
A new Bartholin mass after age 40 requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: Place the incision inside the hymenal ring on the mucosal surface rather than on the labial skin, since an external incision predisposes to a chronic draining fistula.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.rationale: Antibiotics alone will not resolve a tense fluctuant collection, and the delay prolongs severe pain; antibiotics are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, immunosuppression or systemic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Simple incision relieves pain immediately but the incision seals within days and recurrence rates are in the order of 10 to 15 per cent or higher, which is precisely the problem the Word catheter was designed to solve. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.rationale: Gland excision carries risks of significant bleeding from the underlying venous plexus, dyspareunia and scarring, and is reserved for repeated failure of simpler measures or where malignancy is suspected in a woman over 40. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.rationale: A Word catheter is left in for 4 to 6 weeks so that the tract epithelialises and a permanent drainage channel forms, which reduces recurrence compared with simple incision while remaining a bedside procedure under local anaesthetic. It is the first-line definitive treatment for a first presentation abscess. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.rationale: Marsupialisation is comparably effective at preventing recurrence but requires theatre and general anaesthesia, so it is generally kept for recurrence after a Word catheter rather than used first. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

explanation.summary: Australia has seen a sustained resurgence of infectious syphilis, with congenital cases returning in several jurisdictions, which is why repeat third trimester screening has been reinstated in many antenatal programs alongside booking and delivery testing. Staging determines the regimen: early syphilis, meaning primary, secondary or early latent infection acquired within the past 2 years, is treated with benzathine penicillin, while late latent disease or infection of unknown duration requires three weekly doses. A documented negative test within the previous 2 years is what allows infection to be staged as early. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably crosses the placenta at treponemicidal concentrations, so a woman with genuine penicillin allergy must be desensitised rather than given an alternative. Response is monitored by a fourfold fall in the rapid plasma reagin titre, and the neonate requires assessment and follow-up regardless of maternal response.
key_points: A negative test within the past 2 years stages the infection as early and shortens the regimen
Pregnant women with early syphilis receive a second benzathine penicillin dose one week after the first
Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the fetus; allergic women are desensitised rather than substituted
Three weekly doses are reserved for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration
Monitor treatment response with a fourfold fall in rapid plasma reagin titre and notify the case
explanation.pearls: Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of the first dose: in the third trimester it can provoke uterine contractions and transient fetal heart rate abnormalities, so treat where fetal monitoring is available.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin does not reliably cross the placenta, so it cannot be relied on to treat the fetus. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: A negative result at 10 weeks with a titre of 1:32 now establishes infection acquired within the past 18 weeks, which is early syphilis, and Australian guidance adds a second dose one week after the first when the woman is pregnant to reduce the risk of treatment failure and congenital infection. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the fetus as well as the mother. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.rationale: A single dose is the standard regimen for early syphilis outside pregnancy, but a second dose is added in pregnancy because of the higher stakes of treatment failure for the fetus. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Three weekly doses is the regimen for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration; a documented negative test 18 weeks earlier dates this infection as early and makes the longer course unnecessary. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Doxycycline is the non-pregnant alternative for penicillin-allergic patients; it is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of effects on fetal teeth and bone, and it does not treat the fetus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture, meaning one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, defines osteoporosis clinically in anyone over 50 regardless of what the bone density shows. Secondary causes are screened for before committing to long-term therapy, which is why calcium, vitamin D, thyroid function, renal function and coeliac serology were checked here. Oral bisphosphonates are first-line in Australia, with zoledronic acid or denosumab used where oral therapy is not tolerated or absorption is doubtful. Alendronate requires an upright posture for 30 minutes with plain water on an empty stomach, so reflux, oesophageal stricture and inability to sit up are the practical contraindications. Treatment is generally reviewed after 5 years of oral therapy, when a drug holiday may be considered for lower-risk patients, whereas denosumab must never simply be stopped without transitioning to another antiresorptive.
key_points: A minimal trauma fracture after age 50 defines osteoporosis irrespective of T-score and triggers therapy
Oral bisphosphonates are first-line; denosumab and zoledronic acid follow where oral therapy is unsuitable
Screen for secondary causes with calcium, vitamin D, thyroid, renal function and coeliac serology before starting
Stopping denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive causes rebound vertebral fractures
Anabolic therapy is reserved for severe established disease meeting strict Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria
explanation.pearls: Ask about jaw pain and dental plans before starting any antiresorptive: invasive dental work is best completed beforehand, since osteonecrosis of the jaw risk on osteoporosis doses is low but concentrated around extractions.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention
Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

options.rationale: Anabolic therapy is restricted on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme to severe established osteoporosis with a T-score of -3.0 or below plus two or more fractures, one of which must have occurred on antiresorptive therapy. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Supplements support antiresorptive therapy but do not substitute for it, and her vitamin D is already adequate at 78 nmol/L; leaving a woman with a minimal trauma fracture on supplements alone forgoes proven fracture reduction. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and is a reasonable choice for a woman under 60 who also wants vasomotor symptom relief, but she has no such symptoms and declines it, and it is not the first-line agent for established osteoporosis with a fracture. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

options.rationale: Denosumab is equally effective but is generally reserved for intolerance of or contraindication to oral bisphosphonates, largely because missing a dose produces rapid bone loss and a rebound risk of multiple vertebral fractures, which demands reliable 6-monthly adherence. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: A minimal trauma fracture after the age of 50 establishes osteoporosis irrespective of the T-score and meets Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria for antiresorptive therapy, and an oral bisphosphonate is first-line because it is effective, inexpensive and forgiving of an occasional missed dose. Her normal renal function and absence of reflux make alendronate suitable. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it is being diagnosed far more often now that magnetic resonance imaging and high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound are used to assess heavy menstrual bleeding. The classic combination is heavy bleeding with progressive dysmenorrhoea and a symmetrically bulky, tender uterus, which distinguishes it from the asymmetrical, non-tender enlargement of fibroids. A junctional zone of 12 mm or more is the accepted imaging threshold. Management in a woman who wants to keep her uterus starts with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, with tranexamic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or combined hormonal contraception as adjuncts. Iron deficiency is almost always present by the time a woman presents and should be treated in parallel, since correcting the bleeding alone will not restore her stores quickly.
key_points: A junctional zone of 12 mm or more with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first-line uterus-conserving treatment, helping both bleeding and pain
Endometrial ablation performs poorly in adenomyosis because the disease lies deep in the myometrium
Exclude endometrial pathology with a biopsy in women over 45, or younger with risk factors, before committing to medical therapy
Treat the accompanying iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre confirms iron deficiency regardless of haemoglobin, and oral iron taken on alternate days rather than daily achieves better absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose.

options.rationale: Embolisation has a role in symptomatic adenomyosis, with reported symptom improvement in many women, but it is an invasive second-line option after medical therapy has failed rather than a first recommendation. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual loss by around a third and is a reasonable adjunct, but it does nothing for her worsening dysmenorrhoea and is less effective than the intrauterine system for bleeding of this severity. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

A junctional zone of 12 mm or more on magnetic resonance imaging with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis, for which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective uterus-conserving treatment, reducing both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. It also provides contraception, which suits a woman who has completed her family and declines hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Ablation destroys only the superficial endometrium, so it performs poorly where glandular tissue lies deep within the myometrium, and failure rates in adenomyosis are high with a real chance of later hysterectomy. The distinguishing point against the intrauterine system is depth of disease, not severity of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue effectively but causes hypo-oestrogenic side effects and bone loss, so its role is short-term, usually to bridge to surgery, rather than as ongoing management at 42. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm, and about half of cases are idiopathic. The three causes that must be actively excluded are maternal diabetes, fetal structural anomalies that impair swallowing, and congenital infection or anaemia producing hydrops. Impaired swallowing covers oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, neurological conditions with poor swallowing and any mass effect in the neck or chest. A stomach that cannot be visualised on repeated attempts alongside increased liquor is a specific pairing that should prompt tertiary imaging and planning for delivery where paediatric surgery is available. Polyhydramnios itself increases the risk of preterm labour, malpresentation, cord prolapse at membrane rupture and postpartum haemorrhage from uterine overdistension, so the birth plan is altered even when no cause is found.
key_points: Diagnostic thresholds are a deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more, or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm
Exclude maternal diabetes, fetal structural anomaly and congenital infection before accepting an idiopathic label
Increased liquor with a non-visualised fetal stomach suggests upper gastrointestinal obstruction
Anticipate malpresentation, cord prolapse at rupture of membranes and postpartum haemorrhage
Amnioreduction is symptomatic relief for severe maternal compromise, not a diagnostic step
explanation.pearls: Rupture membranes in a woman with polyhydramnios in a setting equipped for immediate caesarean, since the risk of cord prolapse is highest with a high presenting part and a sudden large fluid loss.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

options.rationale: With diabetes excluded by a normal glucose tolerance test and alloimmunisation excluded by a negative antibody screen, a structural cause of impaired fetal swallowing becomes the leading explanation, and a non-visualised stomach on repeated attempts points directly to an upper gastrointestinal obstruction. Detailed imaging changes the birth plan by identifying a baby who will need a paediatric surgical centre. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: Repeat testing is occasionally done where polyhydramnios or macrosomia appear after a normal early test, but her estimated fetal weight is on the 55th centile and the non-visualised stomach demands a structural explanation first. (Source: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

options.rationale: Congenital infection is a recognised cause of increased liquor, but it characteristically produces hydrops, growth restriction or intracranial calcification, none of which is present, so serology is a reasonable parallel test rather than the priority. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: Amnioreduction is reserved for severe maternal respiratory compromise or intractable discomfort and carries risks of membrane rupture, abruption and infection; it treats a symptom without establishing the cause. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: Serial surveillance is appropriate once a cause has been sought and none found, but adopting it now would leave an unexplained structural finding undiagnosed until birth in a hospital that may lack paediatric surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus

explanation.summary: Oligohydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm and the first task is always to establish whether it is isolated or a marker of another process. Ruptured membranes are excluded by history, speculum examination and a point-of-care test, and placental insufficiency is excluded by normal growth and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Renal tract anomalies and exposure to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or angiotensin blockade are the other causes to consider. Truly isolated oligohydramnios is associated with a modest increase in stillbirth, meconium-stained liquor and cord compression in labour, which is why surveillance is intensified and birth is planned in the 36 to 37 week window rather than at term. When the liquor is low because of growth restriction, the timing decision is driven by the Doppler findings instead, and delivery is often much earlier.
key_points: A single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm defines oligohydramnios
Exclude ruptured membranes and growth restriction before calling it isolated
Isolated oligohydramnios is managed with twice weekly surveillance and planned birth at 36 to 37 weeks
Where growth restriction coexists, Doppler findings rather than liquor volume drive the timing of birth
Ask about non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and renin-angiotensin drug exposure, and check the fetal renal tract
explanation.pearls: The single deepest vertical pocket is preferred over the amniotic fluid index for diagnosing oligohydramnios, because the index diagnoses more cases and leads to more inductions and caesareans without improving perinatal outcome.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes the morbidity of late preterm birth on a fetus with normal growth, normal Dopplers and a reactive cardiotocograph, none of which indicates compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)

Maternal hydration produces a small transient increase in liquor volume but does not alter outcome, and a 4-week interval leaves a pregnancy with a recognised stillbirth risk unmonitored. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: A corticosteroid course is appropriate when preterm birth is genuinely planned or threatened within 7 days, which is not the case here; giving it now and delivering at 34 weeks repeats the error of unnecessary late preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

Isolated oligohydramnios with normal growth and normal Dopplers carries a modestly increased risk of stillbirth and intrapartum compromise without evidence of current placental insufficiency, so the balance is struck by surveillance now and birth in the late preterm to early term window rather than immediate delivery. Ruptured membranes and growth restriction have both been excluded, which is what makes this the isolated form. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.rationale: Expectant management to term ignores the observed rise in stillbirth and intrapartum compromise associated with persistently reduced liquor, and weekly monitoring alone is less than the recommended surveillance intensity. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiepileptic drugs, with major congenital malformation rates around 10 per cent and a dose-dependent risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and it should be avoided in women of childbearing potential wherever an alternative works. The clinical problem in this consultation is different: the exposure has already occurred and the neural tube closed weeks ago, so the decision is about seizure safety from here on. Uncontrolled generalised tonic-clonic seizures in pregnancy carry risks of maternal trauma, fetal hypoxia, status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and epilepsy consistently features among indirect causes of maternal death in Australian and United Kingdom mortality reports. Management therefore centres on urgent specialist review, high-dose folic acid, a detailed anomaly scan, monitoring of drug levels across pregnancy, and planning for the postnatal period including vitamin K and safe infant care advice.
key_points: Neural tube closure completes by about 6 weeks, so stopping valproate at that point does not reverse the risk already incurred
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both recognised causes of maternal death
Start folic acid 5 mg daily and refer urgently to a joint obstetric and neurology clinic
Arrange a detailed anomaly scan and monitor antiepileptic levels, which fall across pregnancy
Any change of agent is made by the specialist team with a supervised cross-taper, not same day in general practice
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine plasma concentrations can fall by more than half by the third trimester because of oestrogen-driven glucuronidation, so levels are checked each trimester and the dose is reduced again within 2 weeks of birth to avoid toxicity.

options.rationale: An abrupt halving of the dose risks breakthrough seizures without meaningfully reducing teratogenic risk at this gestation, since organogenesis of the neural tube is already complete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Neural tube closure is complete by about 6 weeks of gestation, so stopping valproate now cannot undo that risk, while abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both of which are among the leading causes of maternal death in Australian reports. Any change of agent belongs to a specialist review arranged urgently, not to a single consultation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

High-dose folic acid is indeed indicated and will be started, but coupling it with abrupt cessation of an effective anticonvulsant exposes her to seizure recurrence for no fetal benefit at 6 weeks. This is the most tempting option because half of it is correct. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

Levetiracetam is usually the preferred agent in pregnancy, but she has a documented history of severe mood disturbance on it, and any cross-taper in an established patient requires neurology supervision rather than a same-day switch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

This combines abrupt withdrawal with a 6-week gap in supervision, which is the worst combination of seizure risk and lost opportunity to plan monitoring, fetal surveillance and delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum without another identifiable cause, and it is a leading cardiac contributor to maternal mortality in Australia. Orthopnoea and waking gasping distinguish it from the ordinary breathlessness of late pregnancy and the early puerperium, and natriuretic peptide is a useful discriminator because it stays near normal in physiological breathlessness. Treatment after birth follows standard heart failure principles, with drug choice adjusted for lactation rather than abandoned because of it: enalapril, captopril, metoprolol, furosemide and hydralazine with nitrate are all usable. Anticoagulation is considered when the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, because the puerperium is already prothrombotic and mural thrombus is well described. Contraception counselling is essential, since a subsequent pregnancy carries a significant risk of relapse, particularly if ventricular function has not normalised.
key_points: Peripartum cardiomyopathy arises in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum with no other cause
After birth, enalapril and captopril are the preferred angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors during breastfeeding
Beta blockade with metoprolol is added for reverse remodelling; furosemide treats congestion only
Consider anticoagulation where the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, given puerperal thrombotic risk
Counsel about contraception and the risk of relapse in a future pregnancy, especially if function does not normalise
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine added to standard therapy has been studied in peripartum cardiomyopathy on the basis of the prolactin fragment hypothesis, but it requires lactation suppression and anticoagulation cover and is not routine Australian practice.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: Digoxin is compatible with breastfeeding and may help rate control, but it does not modify remodelling, and deferring disease-modifying therapy for 6 weeks wastes the period in which recovery is most achievable. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers lack the breastfeeding safety data that older angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors have, and there is no need to stop breastfeeding when compatible alternatives exist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Sacubitril with valsartan has no safety data in lactation and is not a first-line initiation agent in the puerperium, and routine lactation suppression is not required; cabergoline in peripartum cardiomyopathy remains an investigational adjunct rather than standard care. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Once the baby is born the teratogenic objection to renin-angiotensin blockade no longer applies, and enalapril and captopril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best data in lactation, passing into milk in negligible amounts. Adding a beta blocker completes the two agents that drive reverse remodelling, and recovery of ejection fraction in peripartum cardiomyopathy is best when therapy starts early. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: This reflects the common misconception that lactation blocks all heart failure therapy; diuresis relieves congestion but leaves the ventricle without any remodelling therapy during the window when recovery is most likely. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation for a mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is one of the clearest examples of a decision that trades maternal against fetal risk, and no option is free of harm. Warfarin gives the best protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy, with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, when exposure occurs between 6 and 12 weeks. That risk is strongly dose dependent, which is why the 5 mg daily threshold has become the pivot of the decision: at or below it, continuation is recommended, and above it, a first trimester switch to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin with anti-Xa monitoring is offered. Warfarin is stopped and replaced with heparin from around 36 weeks so that the fetus is not anticoagulated at delivery, since fetal liver immaturity means the fetal international normalised ratio exceeds the maternal one. Care belongs in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic in a centre with cardiac surgical backup.
key_points: The warfarin dose threshold of 5 mg daily decides whether to continue warfarin or switch in the first trimester
Embryopathy risk is concentrated in exposure between 6 and 12 weeks and is dose dependent
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves and in pregnancy
Switch to heparin at around 36 weeks so the fetus is not anticoagulated at birth
Valve thrombosis carries high maternal and fetal mortality, which is why heparin strategies are not automatically safer
explanation.pearls: Monitor therapeutic low molecular weight heparin in mechanical valve pregnancies with peak anti-Xa levels 4 to 6 hours after a dose, targeting about 1.0 to 1.2 IU/mL, since weight-based dosing alone is unreliable as pregnancy alters clearance.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is grossly inadequate for a mechanical mitral prosthesis and would expose her to a high risk of valve thrombosis, which carries substantial maternal and fetal mortality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves in any patient after trials showed excess thromboembolism and bleeding, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and falls to around 3 per cent or less at doses of 5 mg daily or under, so at 3 mg daily continuation offers the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis for a small fetal risk, and this is the recommended strategy for low-dose warfarin. Weekly monitoring accounts for the shifting warfarin requirement across pregnancy, and the switch to heparin is planned near term rather than now. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.rationale: Substituting low molecular weight heparin through the first trimester avoids embryopathy but carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis, and it is the preferred strategy only when the warfarin dose needed exceeds 5 mg daily or the woman declines warfarin after counselling. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.rationale: An intravenous infusion for 6 weeks is impractical and carries risks of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, osteoporosis and line infection, and unfractionated heparin is reserved for the peripartum period when rapid reversibility matters. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary and hypothalamus. The progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium and a patent outflow tract are present, and a negative result is followed by an oestrogen and progestogen challenge to separate an unresponsive endometrium from simple anovulation. Failure of both challenges in a woman with normal gonadotrophins and normal oestradiol points to the endometrium or the outflow tract, and intrauterine adhesions are the dominant cause when there has been recent uterine instrumentation, particularly repeated evacuation of a puerperal uterus or curettage in the presence of infection. Ultrasound may show a thin irregular endometrium with echogenic areas but cannot exclude adhesions, so hysteroscopy remains the definitive test. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, often with measures to prevent re-adhesion, and fertility outcomes depend heavily on the severity of disease at the time of diagnosis.
key_points: Work through secondary amenorrhoea by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary, hypothalamus
A failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge with normal gonadotrophins localises the problem to the endometrium or outflow tract
Repeated evacuation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment; ultrasound cannot exclude adhesions
Normal oestradiol with no vasomotor symptoms argues strongly against premature ovarian insufficiency
explanation.pearls: The risk of adhesions rises sharply when evacuation is performed on a postpartum or post-miscarriage uterus rather than a non-pregnant one, and repeat procedures within a fortnight carry the highest risk of all; this is a specific argument for expectant or medical management of retained products where it is safe.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.rationale: Ovulatory hormone levels with a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge locate the problem in the outflow tract rather than the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, and repeated instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment, since adhesions are divided under direct vision. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.rationale: Ovarian reserve testing investigates premature ovarian insufficiency, which is excluded here by a normal follicle stimulating hormone and a clearly normal oestradiol, alongside the absence of any vasomotor symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

Pituitary imaging is indicated with a raised prolactin, headache, visual field loss or hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, none of which is present; her gonadotrophins and oestradiol confirm an intact axis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

This would provide exogenous hormone to an endometrium that has already failed to respond to a formal oestrogen and progestogen challenge, and it also frustrates her stated wish to conceive. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.rationale: Androgen excess evaluation belongs to women with hirsutism, acne or a raised luteinising hormone to follicle stimulating hormone ratio, and it would not explain a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge whatever the result. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

explanation.summary: Velamentous cord insertion describes the cord inserting into the membranes rather than the placental disc, so the vessels run unprotected by Wharton jelly for some distance before reaching the placenta. Its clinical significance splits into two quite separate problems that are frequently conflated. If those unprotected vessels happen to run across the internal cervical os the condition is vasa praevia, which is catastrophic if membranes rupture unrecognised and therefore demands planned preterm caesarean birth. If they do not cross the os, as here, the relevant association is with impaired placental transfer and fetal growth restriction, and the appropriate response is growth surveillance. Velamentous insertion is considerably more common in twin pregnancies and after assisted reproduction, and deliberately examining the os with colour Doppler whenever it is reported is what separates the two pathways.
key_points: Velamentous insertion means the cord inserts into membranes, leaving vessels without Wharton jelly
Colour Doppler over the internal os distinguishes vasa praevia from an isolated abnormal insertion
Isolated velamentous insertion is associated with fetal growth restriction and warrants serial growth scans
Vasa praevia requires antenatal corticosteroids and planned caesarean birth before labour
Incidence is higher in multiple pregnancy and after assisted reproductive technology
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is defined by fetal vessels running within 20 mm of the internal os, so ask explicitly for that measurement whenever a velamentous or marginal cord insertion is reported rather than accepting the insertion description alone.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum
RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

options.rationale: Early planned birth with admission is the pathway for confirmed vasa praevia, where unprotected vessels cross the internal os and can rupture at membrane rupture. It would be correct if colour Doppler had shown vessels over the os, which it specifically did not. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

Repeat localisation is the follow-up for a low-lying placenta, and this placenta sits 55 mm from the internal os, which is already well clear. Repeat localisation would be indicated if the lower edge were within 20 mm of the os. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.rationale: An abnormal cord insertion in isolation with normal anatomy and normal growth is not an indication for invasive testing. Amniocentesis would be considered if structural anomalies or soft markers were also present on the morphology scan. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

options.rationale: Velamentous cord insertion without vessels over the internal os is associated with fetal growth restriction rather than with vasa praevia, so serial growth surveillance is the intervention that changes management. Routine care otherwise continues because the mode and timing of birth are not altered by the insertion site alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

Aspirin is given for pre-eclampsia risk reduction and must be started before 16 weeks to be effective, so commencing at 20 weeks offers little benefit. It would be correct if started at the first visit in a woman with recognised pre-eclampsia risk factors, which are absent here. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist affects a substantial minority of pregnancies and is driven by the same fluid retention that produces peripheral oedema, with the carpal tunnel being a rigid compartment that tolerates little extra volume. The symptoms are worst at night because sleep tends to be spent with the wrist flexed, which further narrows the tunnel, and the classic history is waking to shake the hand out. The important clinical distinction is between sensory symptoms alone, which are self-limiting and managed conservatively, and motor involvement with thenar wasting, which risks permanent deficit and warrants escalation. Most cases resolve within weeks to a few months of birth as the fluid shift reverses, so the counselling message is as important as the splint. Symptoms persisting past 6 months postpartum should prompt reassessment, since the pregnancy explanation no longer holds.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history
Fluid retention narrows a rigid compartment, so the condition parallels peripheral oedema
Preserved thenar bulk and thumb abduction power indicate sensory-only involvement suitable for conservative care
Neutral position night splints are first-line; corticosteroid injection is second-line
Diuretics are not used, and nerve conduction studies are reserved for atypical or motor presentations
explanation.pearls: Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction converts this from a self-limiting nuisance into an indication for surgical referral during pregnancy, because axonal loss recovers poorly even after the oedema resolves.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms with motor involvement or failure of conservative measures after birth, and thenar bulk and power are preserved here. Decompression would be indicated for thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction or symptoms persisting well beyond the postpartum period. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.rationale: Injection is a reasonable second-line option but is not the initial step when a simple non-invasive measure has not been tried in a self-limiting condition. It would be appropriate if splinting failed and symptoms remained disabling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Diuretics do not relieve this compression and reduce plasma volume in a pregnancy that depends on expansion for placental perfusion, so they are avoided for physiological oedema. Furosemide has a place in pulmonary oedema complicating severe pre-eclampsia, not in dependent swelling. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Electrophysiology is unnecessary when the distribution and provoking features are typical and management would be conservative regardless of the result. It would be worthwhile if the distribution were atypical, symptoms were unilateral with wasting, or surgery were being planned. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.rationale: Pregnancy-related median nerve compression without motor loss is managed conservatively because fluid shifts reverse after birth and most women resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. Neutral wrist splinting worn overnight addresses the nocturnal flexion posture that provokes symptoms and is the first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Australian practice tests for hyperglycaemia in pregnancy with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks for everyone, and adds an early test for women whose risk profile makes previously unrecognised diabetes or very early gestational diabetes likely. Risk factors that trigger early testing include a body mass index above 30, previous gestational diabetes, previous macrosomia, a first-degree relative with diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds with high population prevalence. The most commonly misunderstood point is that a normal early test does not end the matter, because placental lactogen, progesterone and cortisol drive insulin resistance upward as pregnancy advances, and a woman who passes at 12 weeks may fail at 26. Glycated haemoglobin is unreliable in pregnancy because accelerated erythrocyte turnover lowers it independently of glycaemia. Detecting and treating hyperglycaemia reduces macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and pre-eclampsia, which is why the testing schedule is worth getting right.
key_points: Everyone is offered a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Early testing is added for body mass index above 30, previous macrosomia, previous gestational diabetes or a first-degree relative with diabetes
A normal early test must still be followed by the routine 24 to 28 week test
Glycated haemoglobin is lowered by accelerated red cell turnover and is not diagnostic in pregnancy
Capillary home monitoring manages established disease and does not diagnose it
explanation.pearls: Australian diagnostic thresholds on the 75 g test in pregnancy are fasting 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above, and a single value reaching any one of them makes the diagnosis.

sources.label: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
RANZCOG: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus

options.rationale: A body mass index above 35 with a previous macrosomic infant places her in the group for whom early testing is recommended so that unrecognised pre-existing hyperglycaemia is not missed through the first trimester. A normal early result does not exclude gestational diabetes developing with rising insulin resistance, so the routine test at 24 to 28 weeks is still required. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.rationale: Testing only in the routine window is appropriate for women without risk factors, but it delays detection of hyperglycaemia already present in the first trimester in a high risk woman. It would be correct for a woman with a normal body mass index and no previous macrosomia or family history. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.rationale: Glycated haemoglobin falls in pregnancy because red cell turnover accelerates, so it lacks sensitivity for gestational diabetes and is not a diagnostic test in this setting. It is useful for detecting overt pre-existing diabetes at booking when clearly elevated, not for excluding milder hyperglycaemia. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.rationale: Home monitoring is a tool for managing diagnosed gestational diabetes rather than for making the diagnosis, and capillary meters lack the accuracy required for diagnostic thresholds. It becomes appropriate once a diagnosis has been established on a laboratory test. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

options.rationale: Insulin resistance rises substantially through the second trimester under the influence of placental hormones, so a normal early result cannot substitute for the routine test. Omitting the later test would be reasonable only if the early test had already established the diagnosis. (Source: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy)
source_refs: ADIPS: Consensus guidelines for the testing and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Primary amenorrhoea is approached by asking first whether secondary sexual characteristics are present, because their presence establishes that oestrogen production and therefore the hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis are intact. When puberty has proceeded normally but menses have never appeared, the problem lies in the uterus or the outflow tract, and cyclical pain is the clue that a functioning endometrium is shedding into an obstructed space. Accumulating blood distends the vagina and then the uterus, producing a palpable mass and often urinary frequency or retention from bladder compression, which is a commonly missed presenting complaint. The differential includes an imperforate hymen, a transverse vaginal septum and cervical agenesis, and they differ substantially in surgical complexity, which is why the examination finding of a bulging membrane at the introitus matters. Prompt relief prevents further retrograde menstruation, which is associated with later endometriosis.
key_points: Normal secondary sexual characteristics with primary amenorrhoea point to a uterine or outflow tract cause
Cyclical pain indicates functioning endometrium shedding into an obstructed space
Urinary frequency or retention arises from bladder compression by the distended vagina
Normal gonadotrophins exclude hypogonadism and confirm the problem is mechanical
Relieving obstruction limits retrograde menstruation and the associated endometriosis risk
explanation.pearls: A bluish bulging membrane that protrudes on Valsalva localises the obstruction to the hymen, which is a straightforward repair, whereas a normal introitus with the same cyclical picture suggests a transverse septum or cervical agenesis needing preoperative magnetic resonance imaging.

options.rationale: Karyotype and androgen measurement investigate a disorder of sex development, which typically presents with absent or discordant pubic hair and no cyclical pain from retained menstrual blood. They would be appropriate for absent uterus on imaging with a raised testosterone and absent pubic hair. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Normal secondary sexual characteristics with cyclical pain, a palpable pelvic mass and a bulging bluish membrane indicate an obstructed but otherwise normal genital tract, and the treatment is surgical relief of the obstruction. Normal gonadotrophins confirm an intact hypothalamic pituitary ovarian axis, so the problem is mechanical rather than endocrine. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Hormonal suppression relieves the pain by stopping endometrial shedding but leaves an obstructed tract with accumulated blood and risks ongoing retrograde flow and endometriosis. It would be reasonable for primary dysmenorrhoea with an unobstructed tract and normal menses. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Waiting is reasonable for absent menses with no other findings, but cyclical pain with a palpable mass indicates accumulating blood that will continue to distend the tract and compress the bladder. Observation would be correct for primary amenorrhoea at 14 with normal examination and no cyclical symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable for complex or higher obstructions and duplicated systems, but the level of obstruction is already visible at the introitus here and imaging would delay treatment. It would be indicated if the introitus appeared normal and a higher transverse septum or duplication were suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

explanation.summary: Episiotomy has moved from routine to restricted use, and the remaining clear indication is to reduce severe perineal trauma at operative vaginal birth, particularly a first instrumental birth with a short perineum. The geometry of the incision matters more than whether one is performed at all. The perineum at crowning is stretched taut, so an incision that looks adequately angled at that moment straightens toward the midline once the tissue retracts after birth, and studies measuring post-delivery angles show that a cut made at 60 degrees ends up near the 45 degree mark associated with the lowest sphincter injury rates. Every incision should be followed by systematic examination including a digital rectal examination, because a proportion of sphincter injuries are recognised only when specifically sought. Repair technique, antibiotic cover and structured follow-up all influence long-term continence outcomes.
key_points: Mediolateral technique protects the anal sphincter complex; midline incision increases severe tears
Cut at crowning when the perineum is stretched, not before traction is applied
Incise at about 60 degrees from the midline so the healed angle sits near 45 degrees
Begin at the posterior fourchette rather than lateral to it
Perform a digital rectal examination after every operative vaginal birth to detect occult sphincter injury
explanation.pearls: A mediolateral episiotomy measured at 45 degrees or more from the midline after birth is associated with the lowest rate of obstetric anal sphincter injury, which is why the incision is made at around 60 degrees while the perineum is distended.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: The midline incision heals well and is less painful but extends directly into the anal sphincter and rectum with substantially higher rates of third and fourth degree injury. It is used in some overseas settings for spontaneous birth but is not recommended in Australia, particularly at instrumental birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: An angle this shallow at crowning finishes close to the midline once the perineum retracts after birth and carries a sphincter injury risk approaching that of a midline cut. Twenty five degrees would be the measured angle of a correctly placed incision assessed after delivery, not the angle to cut at. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Mediolateral incision directs the cut away from the anal sphincter complex and is the technique that reduces obstetric anal sphincter injury at operative vaginal birth. An angle near 60 degrees from the midline at the moment of crowning is required because the distended perineum straightens the incision, so a cut made at a shallower angle ends up close to the midline. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Cutting before the perineum is distended produces more bleeding over a longer interval and misjudges the final angle because the tissue has not yet stretched into its delivery position. The correct timing is at crowning when the perineum is thinned and stretched over the presenting part. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Starting lateral to the fourchette divides the vestibular tissue and Bartholin duct region rather than the perineal body, causing bleeding and poor healing without protecting the sphincter. The incision must originate at the posterior fourchette itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are roughly 10 to 20 times more susceptible to invasive listeriosis than the general adult population, because cell-mediated immunity is modulated to tolerate the fetus and Listeria monocytogenes is an intracellular organism controlled by that arm of immunity. The maternal illness is often unimpressive, amounting to fever, myalgia and gastrointestinal upset that looks like a viral syndrome, while the fetal consequences include miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. The key pharmacological fact is that cephalosporins, which dominate empirical sepsis regimens, have no activity against Listeria, so a standard ceftriaxone-based approach fails precisely when the diagnosis is missed. Blood cultures are the principal diagnostic test since stool culture is insensitive and not routinely performed. High risk foods in Australia include soft and semi-soft cheeses, pre-prepared salads and cut melon, cold cooked chicken, pate and smoked seafood, and dietary counselling is a standard part of antenatal care.
key_points: Pregnancy substantially increases susceptibility to invasive Listeria monocytogenes infection
Maternal illness is mild and non-specific while fetal loss and neonatal sepsis are the major risks
Cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria, so standard sepsis regimens can miss it
Benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is first-line, with gentamicin added for synergy in invasive disease
Blood cultures are the main diagnostic test; stool culture is insensitive
explanation.pearls: Any febrile pregnant woman treated empirically with ceftriaxone alone has no listerial cover, so add benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin whenever the history includes soft cheese, pre-prepared salad, cut melon, pate or cold cooked chicken.

sources.label: Food Standards Australia New Zealand: Listeria and food

options.rationale: All cephalosporins lack intrinsic activity against Listeria monocytogenes, so this regimen would leave the organism untreated despite being a reasonable broad spectrum choice for other causes of sepsis. Ceftriaxone would be appropriate for pyelonephritis, where the urinalysis would typically show nitrites or leucocytes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Nitrofurantoin only achieves therapeutic concentrations in urine and cannot treat a bacteraemic illness, and the urinalysis gives no evidence of urinary infection. It would be correct for asymptomatic bacteriuria or uncomplicated cystitis in the second trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Tetracyclines are avoided after the first trimester because they bind to developing bone and teeth, and doxycycline lacks reliable listerial activity in any case. Doxycycline would be considered for suspected rickettsial illness in a non-pregnant patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A febrile pregnant woman with a systemic illness after eating soft cheese and prepared melon must be treated empirically for Listeria monocytogenes, and benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin is the agent with reliable activity against it. Gentamicin is added synergistically once infection is confirmed, particularly for invasive disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antiviral therapy treats disseminated herpes simplex or varicella, which present with vesicular lesions or hepatitis rather than a febrile diarrhoeal illness after a food exposure. Aciclovir would be indicated for a pregnant woman with varicella pneumonitis or disseminated herpes infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitor cells, and in a fetus with a short red cell lifespan and rapidly expanding blood volume this can produce profound aplastic anaemia, high output cardiac failure and hydrops. Risk is greatest with infection before 20 weeks and falls substantially thereafter, which places this pregnancy in the higher risk window. Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity is the elegant non-invasive tool here: anaemic blood has lower viscosity and flows faster, so the velocity rises well before hydrops is visible, allowing intrauterine transfusion to be offered at a stage where survival is good. Maternal infection is frequently asymptomatic or presents only with arthralgia, and the classic slapped cheek rash is a childhood feature rather than an adult one, so exposure history and serology carry the diagnosis. Spontaneous resolution of fetal anaemia occurs in a meaningful proportion of cases, which is why surveillance rather than immediate intervention is the correct posture while velocities are normal.
key_points: Risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops is highest with maternal infection before 20 weeks
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises with anaemia before hydrops becomes visible
Serial weekly Doppler surveillance continues for 8 to 12 weeks after seroconversion
Intrauterine transfusion is indicated once velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops appears
Maternal infection is often asymptomatic or limited to arthralgia, with no rash in most adults
explanation.pearls: A middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median is the transfusion threshold for fetal anaemia from any cause, parvovirus and red cell alloimmunisation alike.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy
BMJ Best Practice: Parvovirus B19 infection

options.rationale: A single normal scan performed days after seroconversion cannot exclude anaemia that typically develops over the following 2 to 8 weeks, so discharging surveillance now risks missing hydrops at its treatable stage. Routine care would be appropriate if booking serology had shown pre-existing immunoglobulin G immunity. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.rationale: Invasive testing carries procedure-related loss risk and confirming viral genome in amniotic fluid does not change management, which is driven by the Doppler findings. Amniocentesis has a role where maternal serology is equivocal and fetal infection must be established to guide counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.rationale: Maternal immunoglobulin has no established role in preventing fetal parvovirus infection or anaemia and would delay the surveillance that actually detects deterioration. Immunoglobulin is used for chronic parvovirus infection in immunocompromised adults, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.rationale: Transfusion is the treatment for demonstrated severe fetal anaemia and carries significant procedural risk, so it is not undertaken while Doppler velocities remain normal. It becomes indicated when middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops develops. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

options.rationale: Confirmed maternal seroconversion requires serial Doppler surveillance because fetal anaemia develops silently and the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity rises before hydrops becomes visible. Surveillance is maintained for 8 to 12 weeks after infection, which is the interval within which almost all fetal complications appear. (Source: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, so serology results generate considerable anxiety and are frequently misinterpreted. The central problem is that immunoglobulin M is neither sensitive nor specific for recent infection: it can persist for six to nine months after primary infection, can reappear during reactivation, and can be falsely positive through cross-reactivity with other herpesviruses. Avidity testing solves this by measuring how tightly immunoglobulin G binds antigen, which increases as the antibody response matures, so high avidity in early pregnancy places the infection before conception. Vertical transmission risk after primary infection is roughly 30 to 40 per cent and is highest with first trimester infection, whereas non-primary infection carries a risk closer to 1 to 2 per cent. Australia does not screen routinely, so hygiene counselling for women in contact with young children remains the main preventive strategy.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M persists for months and cross-reacts, so it cannot date an infection alone
High immunoglobulin G avidity indicates infection more than about 3 months earlier
