Primary infection carries roughly 30 to 40 per cent vertical transmission; non-primary infection is far lower
Amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction is deferred until after 21 weeks and at least 6 weeks from infection
Routine antenatal screening is not performed in Australia; hygiene advice is the preventive measure
explanation.pearls: Amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction is falsely negative if taken before 21 weeks, because fetal diuresis must be established for virus to appear in the amniotic fluid at detectable levels.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection

options.rationale: High immunoglobulin G avidity in the first trimester indicates that infection occurred more than about 3 months earlier, which places it before conception and means the fetus is not at risk from that episode. Persistent immunoglobulin M is common for months after infection and is the reason avidity testing exists, so the discordance resolves in favour of past infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

Amniocentesis is the correct investigation for confirmed primary infection during pregnancy, but the high avidity result here excludes recent infection. It would be indicated if avidity were low or if seroconversion from a negative immunoglobulin G had been documented. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

High dose valaciclovir is an emerging option to reduce vertical transmission after confirmed periconceptional or first trimester primary infection, which has not occurred here. Treatment would be considered only once recent primary infection were established by low avidity or documented seroconversion. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

Paired testing is valuable when avidity is intermediate or unavailable, but a clearly high avidity result in the first trimester is already conclusive and repeating it delays reassurance. Repeat testing would be appropriate for an intermediate avidity index or an equivocal immunoglobulin G. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

Non-primary infection carries a much lower transmission risk than primary infection and does not warrant monthly growth surveillance in a structurally normal fetus. The described serology fits resolved past primary infection rather than active reactivation, which would not typically produce a symptomatic illness. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Mullerian agenesis is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhoea after gonadal dysgenesis, and it is diagnosed by the combination of normal secondary sexual characteristics, an absent uterus and female range androgens. The ovaries are derived from a different embryological origin and function normally, which means the girl ovulates, experiences no hormonal deficiency and needs no hormone replacement, points that are genuinely reassuring and often not explained clearly at diagnosis. Because the Mullerian ducts develop adjacent to the mesonephric system, renal anomalies such as a solitary or pelvic kidney occur in around a third of cases and skeletal anomalies in a smaller proportion, so imaging of the renal tract is part of the assessment. Management centres on creating vaginal length, usually with graduated dilator therapy as first-line and surgery reserved for failure, alongside psychological support. Fertility is possible through retrieval of the woman's own oocytes with gestational surrogacy, which is legally permitted on an altruistic basis in Australia.
key_points: Normal breast and sexual hair development with an absent uterus and female androgens defines Mullerian agenesis
Female range testosterone and normal sexual hair distinguish it from complete androgen insensitivity
Ovaries are of separate embryological origin, so ovulation and hormone production are normal
Renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases, warranting renal tract imaging
Graduated vaginal dilators are first-line management, with surgery reserved for dilator failure
explanation.pearls: Pubic and axillary hair is the bedside discriminator: it is fully developed in Mullerian agenesis and sparse or absent in complete androgen insensitivity, because sexual hair growth requires functioning androgen receptors.

options.rationale: Androgen insensitivity produces testosterone in the male range and absent or very sparse pubic and axillary hair because hair growth depends on androgen receptor function, whereas this girl has full Tanner stage 5 sexual hair and female range testosterone. Both conditions give an absent uterus and a blind vagina, but only androgen insensitivity gives male range androgens. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Female range testosterone with normal ovaries containing antral follicles and normal gonadotrophins establishes a 46,XX individual whose ovaries are working, so the absent uterus reflects failure of Mullerian duct development rather than androgen effect. The associated solitary kidney supports this, because the Mullerian and mesonephric systems develop in close association and renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Hypothalamic suppression gives low or low-normal gonadotrophins with low oestradiol and, critically, leaves the uterus present on imaging. It would explain secondary amenorrhoea in an athlete with a normal pelvic ultrasound and relative energy deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

Streak gonads produce little oestradiol, so gonadotrophins rise markedly and spontaneous breast development does not occur without replacement. Here the ovaries contain antral follicles and gonadotrophins are normal, which excludes primary gonadal failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

An obstructing septum leaves the uterus present and causes cyclical pain with accumulating blood, neither of which is present here. It would be the diagnosis in a girl with cyclical pain, a pelvic mass and a uterus visible on imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

explanation.summary: Type 3 cutting, in which the introitus is narrowed by an occlusive seal, creates specific obstetric problems: vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp electrode placement may be impossible, and labouring against a rigid scar risks anterior tears involving the urethra and severe perineal trauma. Deinfibulation divides the scar tissue anteriorly to expose the urethral meatus and restore access, and it is best done electively in the second trimester when it can be planned with the woman rather than improvised. Doing it antenatally also allows the conversation to happen properly, with a professional interpreter rather than a family member, since women frequently do not know what was done to them and have never been offered an explanation. Chronic sequelae including obstructed urinary flow, dysmenorrhoea, recurrent infection and dyspareunia are common and often never raised, so the antenatal visit is a genuine opportunity. Reinfibulation is a criminal offence throughout Australia, and declining it requires a clear and non-judgemental explanation.
key_points: Type 3 cutting obstructs examination, catheterisation and fetal monitoring during labour
Elective second trimester deinfibulation is preferred to intrapartum division
Previous genital cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean birth
Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions
Use a professional interpreter rather than a family member for these discussions
explanation.pearls: Mandatory reporting in this context is triggered by risk to a girl in the family, not by an adult woman's own history, so ask specifically about daughters and planned overseas travel rather than notifying on the basis of the woman's examination.

sources.label: Department of Health: Female genital mutilation in Australia

options.rationale: Deinfibulation in the second stage is an acceptable fallback when a woman presents late or declines earlier intervention, but it is performed under time pressure with less opportunity for genuine consent. It would be the plan for a woman first seen in advanced labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

Previous genital cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean birth, and recommending one avoids rather than addresses the obstruction while committing her to abdominal surgery in every future pregnancy. Caesarean birth would be indicated for a standard obstetric reason arising independently. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

Elective deinfibulation before labour allows the procedure to be done with adequate analgesia, informed discussion and an interpreter, and it permits vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp access during labour. The second trimester is the preferred window because the pregnancy is established and there is time to heal well before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions and must not be performed or promised regardless of a woman's request, though the request itself deserves a respectful explanation. Repair after birth restores the anatomy to its deinfibulated state only. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

Mandatory reporting obligations concern girls at risk of cutting rather than adult women who were cut as children overseas, so notification here is not triggered by her own history. A report would be required if there were concern that a child in the family was at risk of undergoing the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is substantially underdiagnosed, and the single biggest determinant of whether it is found is whether a systematic rectal examination and pill-rolling of the sphincter are performed after every vaginal birth, not only when a tear looks deep. The classification is not academic: it drives where the repair happens, who performs it, what antibiotics and laxatives are prescribed, and what the woman is told about future births. Grades 3a and 3b differ only in the proportion of external sphincter thickness torn, while 3c adds internal sphincter disruption, which carries the worst prognosis for continence because the internal sphincter maintains resting tone. Repair in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia allows adequate relaxation and exposure, and either end-to-end or overlap technique is acceptable for the external sphincter, while the internal sphincter is repaired end-to-end separately. Postoperative care includes a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy, and structured follow-up with symptom review before a subsequent pregnancy.
key_points: Any external anal sphincter disruption makes the tear third degree, regardless of perineal appearance
3a is less than half the external sphincter thickness, 3b more than half, 3c adds internal sphincter involvement
Fourth degree requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa
Repair belongs in theatre with anaesthesia, lighting, assistance and appropriate instruments
Digital rectal examination and pill-rolling after every vaginal birth is what makes the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Internal anal sphincter disruption, the 3c grade, is the finding that most strongly predicts long-term faecal urgency and incontinence, so identify it as a separate pale layer and repair it end-to-end rather than incorporating it into the external sphincter repair.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: A second degree tear by definition spares the anal sphincter complex entirely, and here external sphincter fibres are divided. This classification would apply if pill-rolling had confirmed an intact external sphincter beneath a torn perineal body. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: The subclassification 3b denotes external sphincter disruption of more than half its thickness, whereas less than half is torn here. The distinction between 3a and 3b turns purely on the proportion of external sphincter thickness involved. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: The subclassification 3c requires the internal anal sphincter to be torn as well, and it is described here as an intact pale layer. Recognising internal sphincter involvement matters because it predicts worse continence outcomes than external disruption alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: Any disruption of the external anal sphincter makes this a third degree tear, and involvement of less than half its thickness defines the 3a subclassification. Sphincter repair requires theatre conditions with adequate lighting, assistance, anaesthesia and instruments, because repair quality in the birth suite is consistently poorer and long-term continence depends on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: A fourth degree tear requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa, both of which are explicitly intact on rectal examination. That classification would apply if the examining finger were visible through the wound or mucosa were divided. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Managing Graves disease in pregnancy means trading two drug toxicities against each other across gestation. Carbimazole and its active metabolite methimazole are associated with an embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia and abdominal wall defects, concentrated in the 6 to 10 week organogenesis window, which is why propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester. Propylthiouracil, however, carries a small but genuine risk of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that can progress to fulminant failure, and this risk does not diminish with time on the drug. The resulting strategy is to use propylthiouracil through the first trimester and then switch back, which many clinicians forget to do. Treatment aims to keep free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy reference range on the lowest possible dose, deliberately accepting mild maternal hyperthyroidism, because both drugs cross the placenta and over-treatment causes fetal goitre and hypothyroidism.
key_points: Propylthiouracil in the first trimester avoids carbimazole embryopathy during organogenesis
Switch back to carbimazole after the first trimester because of propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity
Target free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy range on the lowest effective dose
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and ablates the fetal thyroid
A receptor antibody titre more than three times the upper limit predicts fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody at 18 to 22 weeks even in a woman rendered euthyroid or previously treated by surgery or ablation, because the antibody crosses the placenta and causes neonatal thyrotoxicosis independently of maternal thyroid status.

options.rationale: Propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity is idiosyncratic and can progress rapidly to hepatic failure requiring transplantation, so persisting with rising transaminases is not safe monitoring. Continuing would be defensible only in the first trimester if no alternative existed and liver enzymes were normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy causes miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction and thyroid storm, and her antibody titre is high, so stopping treatment exchanges one risk for a larger one. Withdrawal would be reasonable in late pregnancy for a woman whose disease has remitted with a low antibody titre on a minimal dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and ablates the fetal thyroid from about 10 to 12 weeks when it begins concentrating iodine. It is an option for definitive treatment once pregnancy and breastfeeding are complete, with conception deferred for 6 months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Corticosteroid does not treat idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury and adding it leaves the offending agent in place while introducing glycaemic and infective risks. Prednisolone has a place in thyroid storm and in Graves orbitopathy, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester to avoid carbimazole embryopathy, but that window has passed at 13 weeks and the guidance is to switch back to carbimazole for the remainder of pregnancy. Rising transaminases with other causes excluded make continuing propylthiouracil unsafe, since its hepatotoxicity can progress to fulminant failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is one of the preferred antiseizure medicines in pregnancy on teratogenicity grounds, but it has the most dramatic pregnancy-related pharmacokinetic change of the commonly used agents. Rising oestrogen induces uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase, so clearance can more than double and concentrations commonly fall by half or more by the third trimester even with perfect adherence. This is why pre-pregnancy baseline concentrations are worth obtaining: the target in pregnancy is the woman's own pre-pregnancy concentration at which she was seizure free, not a population reference range. Generalised tonic-clonic seizures carry real risk to both mother and fetus, including trauma, hypoxia and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, so breakthrough seizures are not something to observe. The postpartum reduction is the step most often missed: clearance falls rapidly after birth and women maintained on their escalated pregnancy dose develop toxicity with ataxia, diplopia and sedation within a fortnight, usually while caring for a newborn.
key_points: Oestrogen induces glucuronidation, roughly doubling lamotrigine clearance during pregnancy
Target the woman's own pre-pregnancy concentration rather than a population reference range
Obtain a baseline concentration before conception in any woman planning pregnancy on lamotrigine
Breakthrough generalised seizures warrant dose escalation, not observation or a change of agent
Plan the postpartum taper in advance, since clearance normalises within 2 to 3 weeks of birth
explanation.pearls: Write the postpartum lamotrigine taper into the birth plan at the time the pregnancy dose is increased, stepping back toward the pre-pregnancy dose over about 2 to 3 weeks after delivery, because toxicity typically appears around day 10 to 14.

options.rationale: Oestrogen-driven induction of glucuronidation increases lamotrigine clearance substantially through pregnancy, and the fall from 28 to 11 micromol/L with breakthrough seizures despite confirmed adherence is a pharmacokinetic problem requiring dose escalation to restore the pre-pregnancy concentration. Planning the postpartum reduction at the same time is essential because clearance returns toward baseline within 2 to 3 weeks of birth and toxicity otherwise follows. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Clearance continues to rise through the second and third trimesters, so maintaining the dose means concentrations will fall further and seizures will continue. Holding the dose would be reasonable only if she remained seizure free with a stable concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of any antiseizure medicine and is avoided in pregnancy whenever alternatives exist. Valproate also inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, which would raise lamotrigine concentrations unpredictably and increase rash risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Changing agent during pregnancy exposes her to breakthrough seizures during cross-titration when her current drug was fully effective before conception at an adequate concentration. Switching would be considered before conception, not as a response to a clearance problem that dose adjustment solves. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Adding a benzodiazepine treats the seizures without correcting the subtherapeutic concentration causing them, and it brings sedation plus neonatal withdrawal and floppy infant risk. Clobazam has a role as short-term seizure cluster cover, not as a substitute for optimising the primary agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lactogenesis proceeds after any birth beyond about 16 weeks gestation, so women who experience stillbirth, late miscarriage or neonatal death face the physical reminder of milk production during acute grief. Suppression is offered rather than assumed, because some women choose to express and donate milk as part of their grieving and that choice should be supported. When suppression is chosen, cabergoline given as a single 1 mg oral dose is the Australian first-line agent, most effective within the first few days postpartum. Blood pressure should be checked first, as dopamine agonists are avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and there is a recognised though uncommon association with psychotic symptoms. Supportive measures continue alongside the drug: a firm supportive bra, cold packs, simple analgesia and minimal expression for comfort only.
key_points: Cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose is the Australian first-line suppressant
It works best in the first days postpartum before lactation is fully established
Check blood pressure first; avoid dopamine agonists in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Bromocriptine and oestrogen have both been abandoned on safety grounds
Offer suppression rather than assume it, as some women choose to express and donate
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline has a terminal half-life of around 60 hours, which is why one 1 mg dose suppresses prolactin for two to three weeks while bromocriptine needed twice daily dosing for a fortnight.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Lactation suppression

options.rationale: Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin effectively but has been associated with hypertension, seizures, stroke and myocardial infarction in postpartum women, and it requires two weeks of twice daily dosing. Cabergoline has replaced it because a single dose achieves the same effect with a better safety profile. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A single 1 mg oral dose of cabergoline is the Australian standard for lactation suppression after stillbirth or neonatal death, and it works best when given in the first days postpartum before full lactogenesis is established. Normal blood pressure throughout the pregnancy matters because hypertensive disorders and a psychotic illness history are the two main cautions against a dopamine agonist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

High dose oestrogen was used historically to suppress lactation but was abandoned because it substantially raises the risk of venous thromboembolism in an already prothrombotic postpartum period. This woman has an additional thrombotic risk from recent birth and reduced mobility. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

Non-pharmacological measures are always offered and are the right answer for a woman who declines medication, but engorgement managed this way takes one to two weeks to settle. Withholding an effective and safe option from a bereaved woman who has explicitly asked for it is not neutral. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

Regular expression stimulates prolactin release and maintains supply, which is the opposite of the goal here, and it is advised only for women who choose to express and donate. Minimal expression for comfort only is the correct non-pharmacological approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

explanation.summary: Antenatal magnesium sulfate given shortly before very preterm birth reduces the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving children, an effect established by the Australasian ACTOMgSO4 trial and confirmed by later meta-analysis. Australian guidance recommends it for women at risk of imminent birth before 30 weeks gestation, whether the birth is spontaneous or planned, with imminent meaning expected within 24 hours. The regimen is a 4 g intravenous loading dose over 20 to 30 minutes followed by 1 g per hour, discontinued at birth or at 24 hours, and it is not repeated or continued postpartum. Monitoring is clinical, watching respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output for early magnesium toxicity, with serum magnesium levels reserved for renal impairment or suspected toxicity. Magnesium for neuroprotection is a separate indication from magnesium for eclampsia prophylaxis, and confusing the two regimens is a common source of error.
key_points: Give for imminent birth before 30 weeks, whether spontaneous or planned
Loading dose 4 g intravenously over 20 to 30 minutes, then 1 g per hour maintenance
Stop at birth or at 24 hours, whichever comes first, and do not continue postpartum
Monitor respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes and urine output rather than routine levels
Tocolysis has no role once the cervix is 4 cm with ruptured membranes and strong contractions
explanation.pearls: The first sign of magnesium toxicity is loss of the patellar reflex, which occurs at around 4 to 5 mmol/L, well before the respiratory depression that appears above roughly 5 mmol/L; calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously is the antidote.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: Continuing the infusion after birth is the pattern used for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia, where the maternal risk persists into the postpartum period. The neuroprotective effect operates on the fetal brain before and during birth, so there is no rationale for continuing once the baby is born. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of imminent birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in survivors, with a number needed to treat of about 63. The Australian regimen is a 4 g loading dose over 20 to 30 minutes followed by 1 g per hour, stopped at birth or after 24 hours, whichever comes first. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: A loading dose alone does not maintain the fetal serum concentration through the period of birth, which is when the neuroprotective effect is exerted. The trials that demonstrated benefit all used a loading dose followed by a maintenance infusion. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection Guideline)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate for Neuroprotection Guideline

options.rationale: Tocolysis is used to buy time for corticosteroids to act or for transfer to a tertiary centre, and it is not effective once the cervix is 4 cm dilated with ruptured membranes and strong regular contractions. Suppressing labour in the presence of ruptured membranes also raises the risk of chorioamnionitis. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

The second dose of the current course is due at 24 hours, not a whole repeat course, and birth is expected long before that. Repeat courses are considered only when a woman remains undelivered and at risk more than 7 days after the first course. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy presents with pruritus, classically of the palms and soles and worse at night, without a primary rash, and is confirmed by raised total serum bile acids with or without raised transaminases. The clinically important consequence is stillbirth, and the large 2019 individual patient data meta-analysis established that risk is concentrated almost entirely in women whose peak bile acids reach 100 micromol/L or more. That finding reshaped practice into a three-band approach: below 40 micromol/L birth at around 40 weeks, 40 to 99 micromol/L birth at 38 to 39 weeks, and 100 micromol/L or above birth at 35 to 36 weeks. Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and liver biochemistry modestly but the PITCHES trial showed it does not reduce perinatal death, so it is offered for symptoms rather than relied on for safety. Antenatal surveillance does not predict the event, and the condition resolves rapidly after birth with liver function checked at least 6 weeks postpartum to confirm normalisation.
key_points: Diagnosis rests on pruritus without a primary rash plus raised total bile acids
Peak bile acids of 100 micromol/L or more define the severe group with steeply raised stillbirth risk
Timing of birth follows the peak value: 40 weeks, 38 to 39 weeks, or 35 to 36 weeks by band
Ursodeoxycholic acid improves itch and biochemistry but does not reduce stillbirth
Cardiotocography and ultrasound do not predict the stillbirth of cholestasis
explanation.pearls: Recheck liver function and bile acids at least 6 weeks postpartum: persistent abnormality points to an underlying chronic liver disease such as hepatitis C or primary biliary cholangitis, which is found in a small but real minority of women labelled with cholestasis of pregnancy.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Obstetric cholestasis
BMJ Best Practice: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

options.rationale: Birth at 39 weeks is the plan for the mildest disease, where bile acids stay below 40 micromol/L and the stillbirth risk is close to background. Applying it to a peak above 100 micromol/L accepts a stillbirth risk several times the background rate across an extra month of pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

Birth between 38 and 39 weeks is appropriate for moderate disease with bile acids in the 40 to 99 micromol/L range, which is where this woman sat two weeks ago. Management follows the peak concentration reached, not the earlier value. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

Cardiotocography and ultrasound do not predict the stillbirth of cholestasis, which is a sudden arrhythmic event caused by bile acid toxicity to the fetal myocardium rather than a gradual hypoxic decline. Surveillance offers false reassurance and cannot substitute for timing the birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

A peak total bile acid concentration of 100 micromol/L or more marks the severe group, in which stillbirth risk rises steeply after 35 weeks, so birth is recommended at 35 to 36 weeks. Ursodeoxycholic acid is offered for maternal itch and biochemistry although it does not reduce the stillbirth risk, which is why the timing of birth carries the management. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

Serial monitoring is appropriate while bile acids remain below 40 micromol/L, and the result that would trigger action has already arrived. Awaiting spontaneous labour at term in severe disease exposes the pregnancy to the highest risk window. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its effect on the woman rather than by a measured volume, and the assessment separates structural causes, identified on examination and ultrasound, from non-structural ones including coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial disorders and iatrogenic causes. A coagulation screen with von Willebrand studies is warranted when heavy bleeding has been present since menarche or there is a personal or family bleeding history, as von Willebrand disease is found in a significant minority of these women. Treatment selection turns on whether contraception is wanted, because the most effective options are also contraceptive: the levonorgestrel intrauterine system first, then the combined pill or long cycle progestogen. For a woman trying to conceive, the non-hormonal options are tranexamic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, both taken only during menstruation, with tranexamic acid the more effective of the two. Iron deficiency is treated in every case, since it is the consequence that most often drives the symptoms of fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.
key_points: Whether contraception is wanted determines which treatments are available
Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by 40 to 50 per cent and does not affect fertility
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the other non-hormonal option and also help dysmenorrhoea
Endometrial ablation is only for women who have completed their family
Investigate for von Willebrand disease when bleeding has been heavy since menarche
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid is taken only on the days of heaviest bleeding, typically 1 g three times daily for up to 4 days, and it does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism in women without a thrombophilia, which is the commonest reason it is wrongly withheld.

options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding and would be first line for a woman who did not want to conceive. It is contraceptive, which makes it unacceptable to a woman actively trying for a pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

The combined pill reduces menstrual blood loss by around a third and is a reasonable second-line option, but it suppresses ovulation and is therefore incompatible with her stated goal. It would be the right choice if she also wanted contraception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Long cycle oral progestogen does reduce blood loss but it suppresses ovulation across most of the cycle and so acts as contraception at this dose and duration. Short luteal phase progestogen courses, by contrast, are ineffective for heavy bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Ablation destroys the endometrium and is offered only to women who have completed their family, with reliable contraception afterwards because a pregnancy in an ablated uterus carries a high risk of abnormal placentation. It is definitively contraindicated in a woman seeking pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

Tranexamic acid taken only on the days of bleeding reduces menstrual blood loss by around 40 to 50 per cent, has no effect on ovulation or on conception, and can be continued while she is trying for a pregnancy. Iron replacement is given alongside because a ferritin of 7 microgram/L means her stores are exhausted and repletion before conception matters for both her and the pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea for at least 4 months before the age of 40 with two follicle stimulating hormone measurements above 40 IU/L taken at least 4 weeks apart. About 90 per cent of cases have no identified cause, but the workup looks for Turner syndrome and other karyotypic abnormalities, the fragile X premutation, adrenal and thyroid autoimmunity, and iatrogenic causes including chemotherapy, radiotherapy and bilateral oophorectomy. Hormone therapy in this group is replacement rather than supplementation, and the risk-benefit balance is entirely different from that of women taking hormone therapy after a normal age at menopause, with benefits for bone, cardiovascular health, urogenital symptoms and quality of life. Treatment continues until at least the average age of menopause, around 51 years, at which point the decision is reconsidered on the usual grounds. Spontaneous ovarian activity returns intermittently in 5 to 10 per cent, so pregnancy remains possible and standard hormone therapy is not contraceptive.
key_points: Diagnosis needs amenorrhoea plus two follicle stimulating hormone levels above 40 IU/L a month apart
Replace with oestrogen plus a progestogen if the uterus is intact, continuing until about age 51
The risk-benefit balance differs entirely from hormone therapy started after a normal menopause
Investigate for karyotype abnormality, fragile X premutation and autoimmune disease
Standard hormone therapy is not contraceptive and spontaneous conception still occurs
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and carries no measurable excess venous thromboembolism risk, which makes it the preferred route in women who are obese, are migraineurs with aura, or have a thrombotic history.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Premature ovarian insufficiency

options.rationale: Two follicle stimulating hormone measurements above 40 IU/L a month apart with low oestradiol under the age of 40 confirms premature ovarian insufficiency, and systemic oestrogen replaces what the ovary would otherwise have produced until the average age of menopause. A progestogen is added because the uterus is intact, and physiological replacement at this age protects bone density and cardiovascular and cognitive outcomes rather than carrying the risk profile of postmenopausal therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

The combined pill is an acceptable alternative for a woman who also wants contraception, but its ethinylestradiol dose exceeds physiological replacement and the 7 day hormone free interval leaves a gap in bone protection. Standard hormone therapy is preferred when contraception is not the priority. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

Bisphosphonates target bone alone and leave the vasomotor, urogenital, cardiovascular and cognitive consequences of oestrogen deficiency untreated. They are reserved for women who cannot take oestrogen, and their long half-life raises concerns in women who may later conceive. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

Non-hormonal agents have a place when oestrogen is contraindicated, such as after hormone receptor positive breast cancer, and they do nothing for bone or cardiovascular risk. Withholding oestrogen from a 34-year-old with no contraindication accepts decades of avoidable deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

Baseline densitometry is worth arranging, but the decision to replace oestrogen rests on the diagnosis rather than on the density result, and a normal scan would not change it. Deferring treatment allows further bone loss during the interval. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Endometrial hyperplasia is classified by the presence or absence of cytological atypia, and that single distinction drives management. Without atypia the risk of progression to carcinoma over 20 years is under 5 per cent, so medical treatment with surveillance is appropriate; with atypia the risk is an order of magnitude higher and a substantial proportion already harbour occult carcinoma, so hysterectomy is recommended. The underlying driver is unopposed oestrogen, whether from obesity, anovulation, polycystic ovary syndrome, tamoxifen or an oestrogen secreting tumour, and identifying and addressing that source is part of treatment. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system outperforms oral progestogens for regression and is first line, with endometrial sampling at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative biopsies are obtained. The device is then retained for at least 5 years in women whose risk factors persist, with annual surveillance considered for those who remain obese or anovulatory.
key_points: Atypia versus no atypia is the distinction that determines medical versus surgical management
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line and outperforms oral progestogens
Resample at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative biopsies
Endometrial ablation is contraindicated when hyperplasia is present
Identify and treat the source of unopposed oestrogen, most commonly obesity or anovulation
explanation.pearls: Tamoxifen acts as an endometrial oestrogen agonist while antagonising the breast, so any abnormal bleeding in a woman taking it warrants sampling regardless of endometrial thickness, since the thickened heterogeneous appearance on ultrasound is unreliable in that setting.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is first line for hyperplasia with atypia, where up to 40 per cent harbour a concurrent carcinoma, and for hyperplasia without atypia only after medical treatment fails or the woman chooses surgery. Oophorectomy would also impose a surgical menopause on a premenopausal woman without indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Cyclical progestogen given for only part of the cycle produces lower regression rates than continuous progestogen exposure, because the endometrium is unopposed for the remainder of each month. Continuous oral progestogen is an acceptable second choice, but cyclical dosing is not. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

The levonorgestrel intrauterine system achieves regression of hyperplasia without atypia in over 90 per cent of women, exceeding oral progestogens, and simultaneously treats the heavy bleeding that brought her in. Surveillance biopsies are taken at 6 monthly intervals until two consecutive negative samples, with the device left in place for at least 5 years given her ongoing risk from obesity. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Ablation is contraindicated when hyperplasia is present because incomplete destruction can leave islands of endometrium behind adhesions, where disease progresses and subsequent sampling becomes unreliable. It is a treatment for heavy bleeding with benign histology only. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

Weight reduction addresses the peripheral aromatisation of androgens in adipose tissue that drives the unopposed oestrogen and is an important adjunct, but it is too slow and unreliable to be relied on as sole treatment. Observation alone is reserved for women in whom an identifiable reversible cause has been removed. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometrial hyperplasia)

explanation.summary: Cardiotocography is sensitive for fetal compromise but poorly specific, and fetal blood sampling exists to reduce the operative birth rate driven by that false positive burden. Australian units predominantly use scalp lactate rather than pH because it needs a much smaller sample volume and fails less often, with thresholds of less than 4.2 mmol/L normal, 4.2 to 4.8 mmol/L borderline and 4.8 mmol/L or above abnormal. Interpretation is always paired with an action interval: a normal result is repeated within an hour if the trace stays pathological, a borderline result within 30 minutes, and an abnormal result mandates birth. Conservative measures, meaning stopping oxytocin, repositioning, correcting hypotension and considering tocolysis for hyperstimulation, continue throughout because they may correct the underlying cause. Sampling is contraindicated in suspected fetal bleeding disorders, maternal blood-borne viral infection, prematurity below 34 weeks, and any acute event requiring immediate birth.
key_points: Australian scalp lactate thresholds: normal below 4.2, borderline 4.2 to 4.8, abnormal 4.8 or above
A borderline result is repeated within 30 minutes, a normal result within 60 minutes
The trend between two samples matters more than any single value
Conservative measures continue while sampling is being repeated
Sampling is contraindicated by acute events, maternal blood-borne virus or prematurity below 34 weeks
explanation.pearls: Fetal blood sampling is invalid during a prolonged bradycardia, because the lactate reflects the acid-base state up to the moment of sampling and will underestimate an injury that is happening right now; proceed straight to birth instead.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Fetal blood sampling
BMJ Best Practice: Fetal monitoring in labour

options.rationale: Immediate birth is indicated when the scalp lactate is 4.8 mmol/L or above, when sampling fails, or when there is an acute event such as prolonged bradycardia, abruption or cord prolapse. A borderline result in a stable woman with a working epidural does not justify a general anaesthetic. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Two hours is the interval used after a normal result when the trace remains pathological, not after a borderline one. Waiting that long allows a fetus already at the edge of compensation to decompensate unobserved. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

A scalp electrode improves the quality of the signal but adds no information about fetal acid-base status, which is the question the borderline lactate has raised. Continuing without resampling abandons the only test that can track the trend. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

A lactate between 4.2 and 4.8 mmol/L is borderline, meaning neither reassuring nor an indication for immediate birth, and the recommended action is to resample within 30 minutes while conservative measures continue. The trend between two samples is far more informative than either value alone, and a rising lactate then mandates birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Oxytocin increases contraction frequency and duration, which further reduces the placental perfusion window between contractions and worsens fetal acidosis. It was correctly stopped as part of the conservative measures and restarting it moves in the wrong direction. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

explanation.summary: Chronic hypertension complicates a growing proportion of Australian pregnancies and carries a threefold to fivefold increase in superimposed pre-eclampsia, fetal growth restriction and preterm birth. Pre-pregnancy or early pregnancy review has two tasks: switching to an agent with an acceptable safety profile, and starting the preventive measures that reduce the superimposed pre-eclampsia risk. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are stopped at the first knowledge of pregnancy, as is any direct renin inhibitor, while labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted alternatives with labetalol usually first. The CHIPS trial settled the target debate by showing that tight control reduces severe hypertension without harming fetal growth, so a diastolic target of 85 mmHg is now standard. Low dose aspirin from 12 weeks, calcium supplementation where dietary intake is low, serial growth scans and early morphology assessment complete the package.
key_points: Stop angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and receptor blockers at the first knowledge of pregnancy
Labetalol, methyldopa and nifedipine are the accepted alternatives; atenolol is avoided
Treat to below 140/90 mmHg; tight control does not increase small for gestational age babies
Start low dose aspirin from 12 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in chronic hypertension
Arrange serial growth scans because of the raised risk of fetal growth restriction
explanation.pearls: The renin-angiotensin fetopathy is a second and third trimester effect on fetal renal perfusion producing oligohydramnios and skull hypoplasia, so first trimester exposure alone, as here, warrants a detailed morphology scan rather than any discussion of termination.

options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are stopped as soon as pregnancy is recognised, not at an arbitrary later point, because exposure at any gestation carries risk and the second and third trimester fetopathy is the most severe. Continuing deliberately for another 6 weeks has no justification. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Blood pressure does fall physiologically in the first half of pregnancy, but a reading of 142/92 mmHg already meets the threshold for treatment and leaving it untreated risks progression to severe hypertension. Treatment of chronic hypertension continues throughout pregnancy with the agent changed, not paused. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are discontinued at the first knowledge of pregnancy because of oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, skull hypoplasia and limb contractures, and labetalol is the Australian first-line replacement with the largest safety dataset. Tight control to below 140/90 mmHg reduces progression to severe hypertension without increasing small for gestational age babies, as shown in the CHIPS trial. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Atenolol is the one beta blocker specifically avoided in pregnancy because first trimester exposure is associated with fetal growth restriction, an effect not seen with labetalol. Labetalol differs by virtue of its combined alpha and beta blockade and preserved uteroplacental flow. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

Aspirin is correctly indicated for her, since chronic hypertension is a high risk factor for pre-eclampsia, but it is started from 12 weeks and does not substitute for withdrawing a teratogenic agent. Dose reduction rather than cessation leaves the fetus exposed to the same mechanism at lower intensity. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates roughly 0.5 per cent of labours after a single lower segment caesarean section and is the complication that dominates counselling about vaginal birth after caesarean. The textbook description of sudden tearing pain with cessation of contractions is uncommon in practice, because most women labouring after caesarean have regional analgesia that blunts the pain and because oxytocin maintains the contraction pattern. The most reliable early sign is an abnormal cardiotocograph, present in the large majority of cases, and it is usually the first abnormality; loss of station of the presenting part, new constant pain breaking through a working block, maternal tachycardia, haematuria and vaginal bleeding follow. Induction and augmentation both raise the risk, and prostaglandin induction raises it most, which is why mechanical methods are preferred in this group. Management is immediate laparotomy with delivery of the fetus and repair or, if the defect cannot be repaired, hysterectomy.
key_points: An abnormal cardiotocograph is the earliest and commonest sign of scar rupture
Loss of station of the presenting part is highly suggestive and easy to miss
Pain breaking through a previously effective epidural is a warning sign, not a block failure
Oxytocin and prostaglandin both increase the risk of rupture in a scarred uterus
Treatment is immediate laparotomy; nothing medical relieves a defect in the uterine wall
explanation.pearls: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended for the whole of labour after a previous caesarean precisely because the cardiotocograph abnormality typically precedes the maternal signs by 10 to 30 minutes, which is the interval in which intact fetal survival is won or lost.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is a holding measure for a prolonged deceleration caused by uterine hyperstimulation, where the uterus is contracting excessively but intact. It does nothing for a defect in the uterine wall and delays the only definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Loss of station with an abnormal fetal heart rate, new constant abdominal pain breaking through a working epidural, maternal tachycardia with hypotension and fresh bleeding is uterine rupture until proven otherwise, and fetal and maternal outcomes depend directly on the interval to laparotomy. The oxytocin is stopped, blood is cross-matched and the massive transfusion protocol is put on standby while she is moved. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Sampling is contraindicated during a prolonged bradycardia because the result reflects the state before the acute event and will falsely reassure. It also consumes minutes that determine whether this baby survives intact. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum fetal surveillance)

Pain that breaks through a previously adequate epidural is one of the most specific warning signs of scar dehiscence, and deepening the block removes the signal rather than the cause. This is the classic mechanism by which rupture is recognised late in women labouring with regional analgesia. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.rationale: Oxytocin is already running and must be stopped, since augmentation raises intrauterine pressure across a scar that has failed. Planning an assisted vaginal birth also presumes descent, whereas the presenting part has risen. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Instrumental birth is classified by station and rotation into outlet, low, mid-cavity and the now abandoned high category, and any mid-cavity or rotational procedure should be conducted as a trial in theatre so that caesarean section can follow without delay. The decision to abandon rests on explicit stopping rules rather than on operator persistence: no descent with the first pull, three pulls without delivery, two cup detachments, or a total procedure time beyond about 20 minutes. Caput and moulding are the findings that unmask false reassurance from station, since a large caput can make a head that is genuinely at the level of the spines feel as though it has descended further. Sequential instrumentation carries the highest neonatal morbidity of any option at this point, and is only contemplated when the head is on the perineum and the failure was clearly from cup placement rather than disproportion. Whichever route is taken, the baby is examined for subgaleal haemorrhage and the woman assessed for third and fourth degree tears and postpartum haemorrhage.
key_points: Mid-cavity and rotational instrumental births are conducted as a trial in theatre
Abandon after two cup detachments, three pulls without descent, or about 20 minutes
Caput and irreducible moulding make the assessed station falsely reassuring
Sequential instrument use roughly doubles serious neonatal morbidity
Examine every vacuum-assisted baby for subgaleal haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: Subgaleal haemorrhage can hold most of a newborn's circulating volume because the subaponeurotic space is unbounded, so a vacuum-assisted baby with a boggy scalp that crosses suture lines needs hourly head circumference measurement and observation for at least 8 hours.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Assisted birth
BMJ Best Practice: Operative vaginal delivery

options.rationale: Sequential use of a second instrument after a failed vacuum roughly doubles the rate of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage and significant birth trauma compared with either instrument alone or caesarean section. Rotational forceps are an option for an occiput transverse position when there is no prior failed attempt and the operator is trained in their use. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

A vacuum procedure is abandoned after two detachments or after three pulls without progressive descent, and raising the pressure does not overcome a mechanical mismatch. Repeated cup application increases scalp trauma, cephalohaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Manual rotation followed by direct traction is a reasonable technique for a malpositioned head before any instrument has been tried, and it depends on there being room for the head to rotate and descend. Here the caput and irreducible moulding indicate cephalopelvic disproportion, and reapplication would still be a third vacuum attempt. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

A further hour of pushing is appropriate when the trace is reassuring and descent is occurring, neither of which applies with absent variability and a head that has not moved. The trial was undertaken precisely because expectant management had already been exhausted. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

Caput of 2 cm with irreducible overriding parietal bones at station plus 1 indicates that the station is falsely reassuring and reflects scalp swelling rather than true descent, and two cup detachments without descent meet the stopping rule. Proceeding directly to caesarean in a theatre already prepared avoids the sequential instrument morbidity, and the trial was deliberately conducted in theatre so this transition can be immediate. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is approached by asking at which level the axis has failed: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary or hypothalamus. Normal gonadotrophins with a normal oestradiol point away from the ovary and away from the pituitary, and a progestogen challenge that produces no bleeding in a woman with adequate oestrogen localises the problem to the uterus. Intrauterine adhesions, also called Asherman syndrome, follow instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus, with the risk highest when curettage is performed on an infected or puerperal uterus rather than on an empty non-pregnant one. Presentations range from hypomenorrhoea through amenorrhoea with cyclical pain to recurrent miscarriage and infertility, and the cyclical pain reflects functioning endometrium trapped behind an obstructed cavity. Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis is both diagnostic and therapeutic, usually followed by measures to prevent re-adhesion such as an intrauterine balloon or device and a course of oestrogen to promote re-epithelialisation.
key_points: Normal follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol with no progestogen withdrawal bleed localises to the outflow tract
Curettage of an infected or puerperal uterus is the classic precipitant of intrauterine adhesions
Cyclical pain without bleeding indicates functioning endometrium behind an obstruction
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic test and the treatment
Re-adhesion prevention with a barrier and oestrogen follows adhesiolysis
explanation.pearls: The risk of intrauterine adhesions after curettage is highest between 2 and 4 weeks postpartum, which is why medical management of retained products or hysteroscopic resection is preferred over sharp curettage in the puerperium wherever the clinical situation allows.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Intrauterine adhesions

options.rationale: Normal gonadotrophins with an oestradiol in the follicular range mean the axis and the ovary are working, so a failed progestogen challenge localises the problem to the outflow tract, and cyclical pain indicates the endometrium is still responding behind an obstruction. Curettage on an infected puerperal uterus is the classic cause of intrauterine adhesions, and hysteroscopy both confirms the diagnosis and treats it under direct vision. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

These tests belong to the workup of premature ovarian insufficiency, which would show a follicle stimulating hormone above 40 IU/L with a low oestradiol. Her gonadotrophins and oestradiol are unambiguously normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

Exogenous hormones cannot produce a bleed through an obliterated cavity, so a withdrawal bleed will not occur and six months of treatment will delay diagnosis while adhesions mature. Hormonal treatment has a place only after the cavity has been restored. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

Pituitary imaging is indicated for hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia or visual field loss, and would be the right test if she had a low follicle stimulating hormone with a low oestradiol. Her normal prolactin and normal gonadotrophins exclude that pathway. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

Treating with a dopamine agonist presupposes hyperprolactinaemia, which has already been excluded on a normal prolactin. Prolactin would be the target if she had galactorrhoea with a raised level, neither of which is present. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are graded as 3a when less than half the external sphincter thickness is torn, 3b when more than half is torn, 3c when the internal sphincter is also involved, and fourth degree when the anorectal mucosa is breached. The grading matters because it dictates the repair technique and predicts continence outcome, and it can only be determined by a per rectum examination, which is why that examination is recommended after every vaginal birth regardless of how the perineum looks. Risk factors include first vaginal birth, birth weight above 4 kg, occipito-posterior position, prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia and instrumental birth, with forceps carrying a higher risk than vacuum. Repair is performed in theatre with a broad spectrum antibiotic, using either end-to-end or overlap technique for the external sphincter and end-to-end for the internal, with long-acting absorbable suture. Postnatal care includes laxatives for 10 to 14 days, physiotherapy, and a follow-up review at which the woman is counselled about mode of birth in a future pregnancy.
key_points: Grade 3a is under half the external sphincter, 3b over half, 3c includes the internal sphincter
Perform a per rectum examination after every vaginal birth to avoid missing an occult injury
Repair all sphincter injuries in theatre with adequate anaesthesia and a trained operator
Give a broad spectrum antibiotic and prescribe laxatives for 10 to 14 days afterwards
Forceps carries a higher sphincter injury risk than vacuum extraction
explanation.pearls: Avoid constipating agents and rectal examinations in the first days after repair, and prescribe lactulose rather than a bulking agent alone; a hard first stool passed against a fresh repair is a recognised cause of breakdown.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Perineal repair
BMJ Best Practice: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.rationale: A defect involving more than 50 per cent of the external anal sphincter with an intact internal sphincter is a 3b tear, and every obstetric anal sphincter injury is repaired in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, good lighting, appropriate instruments and an operator trained in the technique. Repair in these conditions materially reduces the rate of persisting faecal incontinence compared with repair attempted in the birth room. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Birth room repair under local infiltration suits a genuine second degree tear, which by definition spares the anal sphincter complex. Repairing the muscle layer over an unrecognised sphincter defect is the commonest route to a persisting occult injury and later faecal urgency. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Healing by secondary intention is an accepted option for superficial first degree tears and labial grazes that are haemostatic and well apposed. A divided sphincter will not reappose spontaneously and delayed secondary repair has substantially worse continence outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Deferring sphincter repair for six weeks allows retraction and fibrosis of the divided muscle ends, which makes secondary repair technically harder and functionally inferior. Primary repair at the time of birth is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Faecal diversion is reserved for extensive cloacal-type injuries, gross faecal contamination or breakdown of a previous repair, and it is not required for a routine sphincter injury. Primary repair without diversion heals well in the great majority of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: High and total neuraxial block follows unintentionally extensive spread of local anaesthetic, most often when an epidural catheter has migrated intrathecally or subdurally and is then topped up with a surgical dose. The presentation is a recognisable sequence rather than a single sign: paraesthesia and weakness in the hands as the C6 to T1 roots are blocked, a weak whispery voice and difficulty breathing as intercostal and then phrenic function is lost, bradycardia from blockade of the cardioaccelerator fibres at T1 to T4, and profound hypotension from sympathectomy. It is distinguished from local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, which is a central nervous system excitation syndrome with no motor block, and from anaphylaxis, which produces tachycardia with cutaneous or airway signs. Management is airway first with intubation and ventilation, then circulation with vasopressors, atropine and fluids, maintaining left uterine displacement and proceeding to birth. The block wears off over one to three hours, so the woman needs continued sedation and ventilation until motor function returns.
key_points: Hand paraesthesia and loss of grip mark ascent of the block to the lower cervical roots
A weak voice with shallow breathing signals impending respiratory failure, so secure the airway early
Bradycardia with hypotension reflects blockade of the T1 to T4 cardioaccelerator fibres
Distinguish from local anaesthetic toxicity, which causes seizures without a motor block
Keep left uterine displacement throughout and continue ventilation until the block recedes
explanation.pearls: An epidural catheter that has previously worked normally can still migrate intrathecally, so a test dose is repeated before every top-up intended to produce a surgical block rather than only at insertion.

sources.label: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block
RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium
BMJ Best Practice: Complications of neuraxial anaesthesia

options.rationale: Anaphylaxis is the other cause of sudden profound hypotension in this setting, but it produces tachycardia with warm vasodilated shock accompanied by rash, wheeze or angio-oedema, and it does not produce a symmetrical ascending motor block. Bradycardia with a demonstrable C6 sensory level points to sympathetic blockade of the cardioaccelerator fibres instead. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.rationale: Intravascular injection of local anaesthetic announces itself with perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, agitation and then seizures or ventricular arrhythmia, none of which has occurred here. Lipid emulsion treats that syndrome and does nothing for drug that has tracked into the wrong compartment intact. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.rationale: Sitting a woman upright once the sympathetic block is established removes venous return from an already vasodilated circulation and can precipitate cardiac arrest. Head-up positioning is used in the first minute or two of a hyperbaric spinal to limit spread, not as rescue for an established high block with hypotension. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.rationale: Magnesium is given for eclamptic seizure prophylaxis, and she is normotensive by history with no proteinuria and no seizure. Magnesium would additionally worsen the hypotension and potentiate the neuromuscular weakness she already has. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

options.rationale: A block ascending to C6 with hand paraesthesia, loss of grip, a weak voice and shallow breathing is a high neuraxial block that has reached the phrenic and intercostal supply, so the airway is secured and ventilation taken over before respiratory arrest occurs. Bradycardia with hypotension reflects blockade of the T1 to T4 cardioaccelerator fibres and is treated with a vasopressor plus atropine, keeping left uterine displacement and preparing for immediate birth once she is stable. (Source: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block)
source_refs: ANZCA: Management of high neuraxial block

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage, and it occurs because the gland roughly doubles in size during pregnancy while remaining supplied by a low pressure portal system that is vulnerable to hypotension. Failure of lactation is usually the earliest clue because prolactin secreting cells are among the first lost, followed by amenorrhoea from gonadotrophin deficiency, then the insidious fatigue of secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency. The biochemical signature is a low target hormone with an inappropriately normal or low trophic hormone, so a free thyroxine of 6.1 pmol/L with a thyroid stimulating hormone of 1.2 mIU/L is diagnostic of central rather than primary hypothyroidism. Hyponatraemia in this setting comes from glucocorticoid deficiency releasing antidiuretic hormone from its normal cortisol mediated restraint, which is why it corrects with hydrocortisone rather than with saline. Presentation is often delayed by months or years, so the postpartum haemorrhage history must be actively sought in any woman of childbearing age with unexplained hypopituitarism.
key_points: Failure to lactate after a major postpartum haemorrhage is the earliest and most specific clue
Low free thyroxine with a normal thyroid stimulating hormone indicates central hypothyroidism
Hyponatraemia in cortisol deficiency corrects with glucocorticoid, not with saline or fluid restriction
Always give glucocorticoid before thyroxine, as thyroxine can precipitate an adrenal crisis
Posterior pituitary function is usually spared, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon
explanation.pearls: Take the cortisol and thyroid samples before the first hydrocortisone dose if it can be done within minutes, but never delay treatment for them: a random cortisol below 100 nmol/L in a shocked patient is diagnostic enough to act on.

options.rationale: Thyroid hormone increases the metabolic clearance of cortisol, so replacing thyroxine in an unrecognised or untreated cortisol deficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis. The sequence is fixed: glucocorticoid first, thyroid hormone second. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A low cortisol with hypoglycaemia, hypotension and hyponatraemia is secondary adrenal insufficiency, and glucocorticoid replacement corrects the blood pressure, the glucose and the sodium because cortisol deficiency is what is driving the inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Thyroxine is added once glucocorticoid replacement is established, since giving it first can precipitate an adrenal crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for hyponatraemia with seizures or deep coma, and correcting the sodium without correcting the cortisol treats the consequence rather than the cause. Fluid restriction is actively harmful here because she is hypotensive and volume depleted from vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Desmopressin treats cranial diabetes insipidus, which produces hypernatraemia with large volumes of dilute urine, the opposite biochemical picture to this. Posterior pituitary function is usually preserved in postpartum pituitary necrosis because it has a separate blood supply. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Vasopressin receptor antagonists are used for euvolaemic hyponatraemia from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion after adrenal insufficiency has been excluded. Using one in undiagnosed cortisol deficiency risks rapid overcorrection without addressing the hypotension or the hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Genito-pelvic pain and penetration disorder, historically called vaginismus, is characterised by involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor and perineal muscles on attempted penetration, producing pain, fear and avoidance in a self-reinforcing cycle. The examination is the diagnostic tool: normal vulval architecture, a negative cotton swab test at the vestibule and a visible or palpable levator contraction distinguish it from provoked vestibulodynia, dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus, atrophy and infection. Treatment centres on pelvic floor physiotherapy with progressive dilator use, which retrains the muscular response while gradually reducing the anticipatory fear, and psychological therapy is added where avoidance, relationship distress or trauma is prominent. Attempting a forced examination is both unhelpful and harmful, since it confirms the patient's expectation that examination is unbearable. Outcomes are good with structured therapy, and most women achieve comfortable penetration within several months.
key_points: The cotton swab test separates pelvic floor overactivity from provoked vestibulodynia
Diagnosis rests on observing involuntary levator contraction, not on investigations
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded dilators is first line
Psychological therapy is added for prominent fear, avoidance or relationship distress
Stop the examination when the patient withdraws rather than persisting under duress
explanation.pearls: Offer the woman control of the dilator and of the pace of every examination, because patient-controlled insertion consistently outperforms clinician-led insertion in this condition and is the single most important element of the physiotherapy protocol.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.rationale: Structural anomalies such as a transverse septum usually present with primary amenorrhoea or cyclical obstructed menstruation, and she menstruates normally. Examination under anaesthetic also removes the conscious muscle response that is the diagnostic finding. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

A negative swab test with normal vulval skin and a visible involuntary levator contraction identifies the problem as pelvic floor overactivity rather than a vestibular or dermatological disorder, and graded dilator work with pelvic floor physiotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence. Psychological therapy is combined with it where distress or avoidance is prominent. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

Topical anaesthetic is used for provoked vestibulodynia, which is defined by localised tenderness on the cotton swab test, and her swab test is negative. Anaesthetising normal tissue does nothing about the muscle contraction that is actually obstructing penetration. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary atrophy, which produces pallor, loss of rugae and friability in a hypo-oestrogenic woman. This woman has regular cycles and a normally oestrogenised vulva, so there is no deficiency to replace. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis can cause introital pain, but it produces erythema, fissuring or discharge, none of which are present, and empirical antifungal therapy for normal appearing skin delays effective treatment. Swabs are worth taking only if the examination suggests infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea arises from endometrial prostaglandin release at menstruation causing myometrial contraction and ischaemic pain, and it characteristically begins within a year or two of menarche once cycles become ovulatory. The pain is central, starts within hours of the onset of bleeding, lasts one to three days and is absent at other times in the cycle. Features that should raise the possibility of endometriosis or another secondary cause include onset well after menarche, pain outside menstruation, progressive severity, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, and failure to respond to adequate medical therapy. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs work best when started before or at the very onset of symptoms and taken regularly rather than as required, and this timing point is frequently the reason an apparently failed trial was not a real one. Combined hormonal contraception used continuously is the usual next step, and persistent pain despite both warrants specialist referral rather than escalating analgesia.
key_points: Prostaglandin mediated pain responds best to anti-inflammatory therapy started before onset
Regular dosing for the painful days outperforms as-required dosing
Non-menstrual pelvic pain, dyschezia or progressive severity suggest a secondary cause
Transvaginal imaging is inappropriate when the adolescent is not sexually active
Failure of adequate medical therapy, not first presentation, is the trigger for referral
explanation.pearls: Advise starting naproxen 250 to 500 mg roughly twenty four hours before the expected bleed in a woman with predictable cycles, since prostaglandin synthesis begins before flow and pre-emptive dosing converts many apparent treatment failures into responders.

options.rationale: Laparoscopy is considered when pain persists despite adequate medical therapy or when there are features suggesting endometriosis such as non-menstrual pelvic pain, dyschezia, deep dyspareunia or progressive severity. None of those apply and she has had no adequate medical trial. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

Imaging is indicated when the history suggests a structural cause, and a transvaginal approach is inappropriate in a girl who is not sexually active and has declined pelvic examination. A textbook primary dysmenorrhoea pattern does not require imaging before treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

Paracetamol does not inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissue to a clinically meaningful degree, so increasing its frequency addresses neither the mechanism nor the timing problem. Heat has modest benefit but is an adjunct rather than a treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
